2026-10-29.title: Departure: Orlando — Lisbon
text: Friends, let me start with the main thing: we have taken off. In the evening, from Orlando, without any incidents. For the start of a journey, that is already quite something.

We left home around six in the evening; the plane was at 22:40. We are flying via Lisbon, with a connection there, and then on to Rome, where we are scheduled to land tomorrow at 18:45. The whole trip is a little over two weeks; we return home on November 14, also via Lisbon.

There are three of us: me, Yana and Masha. Masha, though, is on her own flight. We bought the tickets at different times, so in Lisbon our paths will briefly part. Masha is twenty-one, a grown-up, she'll manage. Why am I stressing this, you ask? You'll find out tomorrow.

The luggage was a little lesson too. At first we were sure we were each checking a 23-kilogram suitcase. On the day of departure we reread the conditions once more: checked baggage is included only on my ticket, Yana has none. So between the two of us one suitcase goes in the hold, and the rest is on our shoulders. The moral is simple: read your ticket conditions before you start packing your suitcases, not after.

We rented a car in advance; we'll pick it up right at Fiumicino airport. We took out separate insurance, just in case. We also looked into whether an international driving permit is needed in Italy. It is. We're not planning to drive around Rome, though: the car will stay by the hotel. You can't take it into the center — there are ZTL zones there, which only locals with a permit may enter. Drive in out of ignorance, and half a year later a letter arrives at your home with a fine and a pretty Italian stamp.

We thought about accommodation for a long time. We even wrote to a pilgrim house at a monastery right in the center, near Navona. In the end, for the first nights we'll be staying near the Vatican, about twenty minutes' walk from St Peter's Square.

We had a plan for the trip. Several plans, in fact. Yana and I have a shared list of places — what each of us wants to see. Separately there are ideas for day trips from Rome without a car, thirteen screenshots. Everything sorted, everything thought through. As will turn out later, life will rework almost all of it. And that is probably the most honest thing you can say about any plan. Man proposes, God disposes — tested more than once.

October 29 in the church calendar is the feast of the martyr Longinus the Centurion. That very Roman soldier who stood at the Cross and said: “Truly this was the Son of God.” A Roman who became a Christian at Golgotha. To my mind, a good heavenly fellow traveler for those flying to Rome.
Tomorrow evening we'll be in Rome.

2026-10-30.title: Rome as a Quest
text: A night on the plane, a connection in Lisbon — and in the evening we're in Rome. Fiumicino airport is full of people, as if the whole world had decided to fly into Rome on the same evening.

First of all we rushed to find where to pick up the rental car. That turned out not to be simple. It's somewhere in some Terminal 3 where nothing is signposted. In the end we figured it out: you have to go out of the first exit, cross the road, stand and wait — they'll come for you. We stand, we wait. They came. The first small victory: we have the car. Now we have wheels in a country where, as will turn out later, wheels are not always an advantage.

And at that very moment Masha calls from Lisbon. She went to the wrong terminal, and there are about ten minutes until departure. Remember I said yesterday that she's a grown-up and will manage? Well, here she is, managing. We tell her: skip the line, go up to people, ask, they'll let you through. Ten minutes, a different terminal, a foreign country — anyone would get flustered. And on top of that she's embarrassed. How can you — skip the line, past everyone? We barely talked her into it. And she made it. Afterwards you think: shame is a good feeling, but sometimes it misses the plane along with you.

Next, the hotel. Which nowhere says it's a hotel. No sign, no plaque. No parking, of course. I drove into some courtyard, and it was impossible to drive out of it forwards. I reverse out, by some miracle not touching the tiny Italian cars, which are parked as if someone had placed them by hand. It worked out, not a single scratch. My guardian angel, I think, worked overtime that evening.

Then the real game begins. On the door — someone else's login and password; you enter them and hope. The keys are in the mailbox. Then the stairs and the third floor, which in Italian is not the third at all. Their ground floor is called piano terra, the “earth floor,” and doesn't count. So their third is our fourth, and you climb one more flight with a suitcase than you'd counted on.

Our room is number twelve. We walk down the corridor, and the numbers on the doors start at thirteen. There is no twelve. We found one door with no number at all. That was twelve. Why it's like that — don't ask. Probably so that life wouldn't seem too sweet from the very first evening.

In short, friends, if you've never played quest games, you've got no business in Italy. Although, to be honest, it all ended well: we have the car, we have the keys, the room was found. What more does a person need after a night on a plane?

In these days I started keeping travel notes. I called them “Roman Holiday,” like the old film with Audrey Hepburn. Though for now it's not a holiday for us, more of a survival course for beginners. But everything is still ahead.

We're not taking the car into the center of Rome — yesterday I explained about the ZTL zones. Let it stand by the hotel, and we'll walk. Although tomorrow morning parking at the hotel will have its own story too.
And now we're driving back to the airport to meet Masha. At night. So far we've seen Rome only from the car window, and mostly in reverse at that.
Tomorrow — the Vatican.

2026-10-31.title: The Vatican
text: The morning began with parking the car, but I've already written about that. Then breakfast from the hotel, which in fact turned out to be a croissant with coffee at the nearest café around the corner. The croissant, by the way, was tasty, and so was the coffee. So no complaints.

Then on foot, about twenty minutes, to St Peter's Square. You can't put into words how monumental those colonnades are. You really feel like a little speck of fluff. In everything you sense the greatness of the Church that built this, and the smallness of a cog in this huge mechanism. We had no guide. Yana and Masha took pictures of themselves against everything, and I looked and tried to fit at least something into my head. You can't see it all or take it all in. You touch not even the summit, but just the edge of a great culture.

We went into the shops. Almost everywhere they have the Kazan icon of the Mother of God. And October 31, by the way, is the feast of the Apostle Luke, who, according to tradition, painted the first icons of the Mother of God. A nice echo.

The line at the basilica is enormous; you could spend a whole day there. We hesitated for a long time whether to stand in it or not. But we went in. The basilica astonishes both with its size and its beauty. The main dome is about forty meters in diameter. And the small dome at the very top, above it, is almost the same as the dome of the church in Tishki. Only in Tishki it seems big, and here, up top, it's tiny.

In the bookshop there was a separate shelf in Slavonic and Russian, and editions from '62 at that, just from the time of the Second Vatican Council. I bought “Guidance for the Celebration of Orthodox Divine Services.” Interesting, isn't it? They've kept it to this day and sell it in the Vatican shop.

Below, under the basilica, are the tombs of the popes. Including those we talk about at our Friday talks. On one grave it is written that the most important thing in this man's life was that he “promoted reconciliation with the Eastern Church.” And the tomb of Alexander VII, the one who built the colonnade — Death under a red stone shroud, and Truth covered by a bronze veil the color of white marble. You can't look at it enough.

A sea of tourists, from every country. The staff strictly make sure nobody sits down anywhere even for a minute. I asked one of them why they chase people away. He, irritated: they block the whole staircase. Also true.

However much you'd like to think you imagined it — no. The cult of the Pope really does exist. In the bookshop almost everything is about him; the letters two meters high at the base of the dome are about him. A little unusual. On the other hand, throughout the basilica there are statues of the founders of orders. A good idea — to single out those who started each direction of ministry. In this, it seems to me, lies part of the secret of the Western Church's success in mission and social work.
We had lunch at a small restaurant we would never have found on our own. We chose the local Roman pasta. To me, macaroni is macaroni, like in Orlando, no better.

In the evening, Castel Sant'Angelo — built as the mausoleum of Emperor Hadrian, it later became a papal residence and fortress. Right by the entrance is the Pope's hall (the Pope again); on the walls little figures are doing all sorts of things. Probably a medieval Instagram feed. I can just picture it: a rocking chair, a dog, a fireplace, and over a year the Pope goes through all the walls, then starts again. And at the end of the day — a sunset with the basilica in the background.
Only half of today's plan happened, and that's fine.
Tomorrow — ancient Rome.

2026-11-01.title: Ancient Rome
text: Sunday. For Catholics it's the feast of All Saints, and also the first Sunday of the month, when museums let you in for free. We didn't go to the Liturgy this time — we hadn't prepared and hadn't brought anything for the service with us. The priest is on vacation; that happens too. We gave the whole day to ancient Rome.

We approached the Colosseum and immediately understood: free admission is wonderful, but not for us. The line was such that we looked at it from outside. Never mind, it has been standing there for almost two thousand years, it can wait.

We walked along the Sacred Way, the Via Sacra, past the columns of the Temple of Venus and Roma. A design by Emperor Hadrian himself. According to tradition, the architect Apollodorus, who laughed at this design, was later executed. Criticism was a risky business in ancient Rome.

On the ruins of this temple stands the church of Santa Francesca Romana. There is the tomb of St Frances of Rome — a wife, a mother, she served the poor, and beside her is her guardian angel. An icon of the Mother of God from the twelfth century, of the “Sweet Kissing” type, and under it they found an even more ancient one, an encaustic one, from the fifth or sixth century. And a stone on which, according to tradition, the Apostle Peter knelt when the demons lifted Simon Magus into the air. That's what it says, in Italian. There is also a medieval tombstone of a prelate, on which you can see the whole “pattern” of the vestments: a bell-shaped chasuble, an amice, pontifical gloves. For me, as a priest, this is especially interesting to look at. We stood for a little while at the feast-day Mass — there was almost nobody there.

Nearby are the excavations of Vespasian's Temple of Peace, where the menorah and the table of the shewbread from the Temple in Jerusalem were once kept. And behind them is Santi Cosma e Damiano, the first church on the Forum, the year 527. A sixth-century mosaic: Christ descends on fiery clouds, Peter and Paul lead the holy physicians to Him, below are twelve lambs. And it is precisely today, the first of November, that is the feast of the Unmercenaries Cosmas and Damian. You can't arrange a coincidence like that. On the mosaic there is an inscription with the word salus — in Latin it means both health and salvation. For unmercenary physicians you couldn't put it more precisely.

There is also a tombstone: an eighty-six-year-old father buried his son of forty-four. And the inscription — “so overturned is the order of nature.” The Latin is short, and there's nothing more to say.

Then the Imperial Forums: of Augustus, of Nerva, of Trajan. On the Forum of Nerva there's a frieze with weavers and Minerva — remember the myth of Arachne? And on top of Trajan's Column now stands the Apostle Peter. The emperor would probably have been surprised.

At Trajan's Markets we walked along a real Roman street, the Via Biberatica, past shops with travertine frames. There are stamps on the bricks; on one roof tile, the stamp of King Theodoric and a chi-rho, the monogram of Christ. There's also a colossal head, said to be of Trajan's mother. From the terrace you can see all the forums at once.

We had lunch at a café by the forums. Then the bronze Aeneas carrying his father Anchises on his shoulders at Palazzo Valentini, and at the end we went up the Vittoriano, to the Altar of the Fatherland and the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier. There, up top, we decided: next we head south — Naples, Pompeii, Amalfi, Matera, Bari to the relics of St Nicholas. Getting ahead of myself, I'll say: life will rework this plan too.
Tomorrow we leave Rome.

2026-11-02.title: The Appian Way and Montecassino
text: In the morning we packed our things, loaded everything into the car and left the hotel before eleven. We left the city by the Appian Way — that very one, the ancient one, along which legions once marched, and later the apostles too.

The first stop was the little church of Domine Quo Vadis. It stands where, according to tradition, the Apostle Peter, leaving Rome to escape persecution, met Christ and asked: “Lord, whither goest thou?” And heard that the Lord was going to Rome to be crucified again. Peter returned and accepted martyrdom. Hence the title of Sienkiewicz's famous novel “Quo Vadis.” Inside is a stone with the imprints of feet. It's a copy; the original is kept in the Basilica of San Sebastiano. But the place is no less for that. We didn't go to the Catacombs of St Callixtus this time — we had been there before.

And here's what's interesting, friends. The Gospel read that day was precisely about Peter: “But whom say ye that I am?” — “The Christ of God.” You stand at the stone where Peter asked “whither goest thou,” and you remember how he once answered the main question. A coincidence, you'll say. Maybe.
We had lunch right there, at a trattoria on the Appian Way. Scialatielli with porcini mushrooms, tagliolini with guanciale and spinach risotto.

Then we got onto the A1 motorway. At the entrance the barrier was open, and I didn't take a ticket. And in Italy, exiting without a ticket means a conversation with an operator. We prepared a phrase for this case in advance: “Sono entrato senza biglietto, la barriera era aperta” — “I entered without a ticket, the barrier was open.” Sounds like the beginning of a detective story.

Then Montecassino, the abbey of St Benedict. Here in the sixth century Benedict founded a monastery and wrote his Rule, by which most of Western monasticism later lived. In the crypt are the relics of Benedict and his sister Scholastica. The monastery was destroyed four times: by the Lombards in 577, by the Saracens in 883, by an earthquake in 1349 and by the bombing of 1944. And each time it was rebuilt anew. Their motto is “Succisa virescit,” “cut down, it grows green again.” To my mind, this is not only about the monastery, it's about the Church in general. Nearby is the Polish cemetery: in May of '44 it was the Poles who took this mountain, and many of them stayed there.

And in the evening, Naples. Friends! If the thought ever occurs to you to drive into Naples by car, think again. And then again. The driving there is a nightmare, the parking is a separate nightmare. To everyone who will be planning Naples: stay somewhere in Ercolano or Torre del Greco, where you can park the car, and come into the city as guests.
This time our apartment is big, three bedrooms, each of us has our own. After the Roman room without a number — sheer luxury.

We went to dinner at the trattoria “Da Nennella.” There's a huge line there, and the waiters dance on the tables. I'm serious — right on the tables. The line, by the way, didn't stop us. After the Colosseum we take lines philosophically, but here we decided to wait it out.
Tomorrow we just walk around the city.

2026-11-03.title: Naples on Foot
text: Why Naples, you ask? Yesterday evening, behind the wheel, we asked ourselves the same question. Whoever has driven around Naples will understand me. Whoever hasn't — better not to. There's no parking, the streets are narrow, and every driver is sure the rules were invented for somebody else. We got to our place, and thanks for that.
But today we left the car alone and went on foot. And the question went away by itself.

Naples in general is a city not for the steering wheel but for the feet. From the car window it seems noisy, peeling and senseless. But when you walk slowly, it turns out that behind every shabby facade stands a church some seven hundred years old. There are hundreds of churches here, they say, and almost every one is worth looking into.

We started with San Domenico Maggiore. It and Santa Chiara stand almost next to each other, on an old straight street called Spaccanapoli — “the one that splits Naples.” It runs exactly along the line of the ancient city: Naples was founded by the Greeks, after all, and the name itself means “New City.” The New City, by the way, is about two and a half thousand years old.

So, San Domenico Maggiore. It's a large Dominican church, built back under the Angevin kings. In the monastery attached to it Thomas Aquinas lived and taught. According to tradition, it was here that the crucifix spoke to him: “Thou hast written well of me, Thomas.” One can have different views of Latin theology, but when you stand where a man prayed for years and thought about God, the place is special all the same, for an Orthodox priest too.

Then Santa Chiara. It was built in the fourteenth century by King Robert of Anjou and Queen Sancha. In 1943, after a bombing, the church burned out, and it was restored almost from scratch, this time without the Baroque decorations. Austere Gothic — after the motley Neapolitan streets it's even a rest for the eyes.

Then we went down to the sea. Piazza del Plebiscito is huge, as if it had been built for some other, more solemn city. On one side is the Royal Palace, on the other the church of San Francesco di Paola with its semicircular colonnade. Anyone who has been to Rome will immediately recognize the Pantheon in it. We've just come from Rome, so we recognized it.

From the square it's a stone's throw to the waterfront and to Castel dell'Ovo — a castle that stands right on a small islet off the shore. It's the oldest castle in Naples. The name translates as “Egg Castle”: according to legend, the poet Virgil hid an egg in its foundations, and as long as it is intact, the city stands. Judging by the fact that Naples is still in place, the egg is fine.

That, really, was the whole day. No feats, no lines or tickets. San Domenico, Santa Chiara, the square, the castle by the water. We just walked and looked. And you know, sometimes on a journey it's exactly days like this that are needed — when you're not late for anything and aren't “ticking off” anything on a list. Rome is usually taken by storm. Naples can't be taken by storm, and it doesn't surrender. With it you can only stroll.

Friends, if you're going to Naples, my advice is simple, learned the hard way: leave the car somewhere outside the city and go on foot yourselves. The city will show you everything itself. Your nerves will be in better shape, and you'll see more.
Tomorrow, one more day in Naples.

2026-11-04.title: One More Day in Naples
text: We decided to stay in Naples one more night, and the whole plan shifted by a day. Never mind, a plan is written precisely in order to be changed. Yesterday we walked around the city and realized that one day isn't enough for it.

In the morning we went to the Gesù Nuovo. From the outside this church looks more like a fortress: the whole facade is in faceted stones, as if it had been laid with huge diamonds. Once it was the palace of the noble Sanseverino family; then it was given to the Jesuits and rebuilt as a church. They kept the facade, and rightly so. Inside, on the contrary, it's all Baroque: marble, gilding, frescoes. The contrast is such that for a second it seems you've walked in through the wrong door.

Then the street of San Gregorio Armeno. This is that very street where nativity scenes and figurines for them are sold all year round. Christmas never ends here. The street is named after the old monastery of St Gregory the Armenian — that same Gregory the Illuminator who baptized Armenia. So even here it's not without saints. Besides shepherds, magi and little sheep, the craftsmen model bakers, fishermen, merchants, and, they say, footballers and politicians while they're at it. A Neapolitan nativity scene is not only Bethlehem, it's the whole city around the manger. And there's something very true in that: Christ is born not in a museum but in the middle of ordinary life, with its bazaar and noise.

Next — the Pio Monte della Misericordia. It's an old Neapolitan confraternity of mercy, and in its church hangs Caravaggio's “Seven Works of Mercy.” The painting was made in 1607 for this very altar and since then, as far as I know, has never left. The works of mercy are from the Gospel of Matthew, from the Lord's words about the Last Judgment: to feed the hungry, give drink to the thirsty, take in the stranger, clothe the naked, visit the sick and the prisoner. The seventh, burying the dead, the Church added later. In Caravaggio all seven happen at once, on one dark Neapolitan street, and from above the Mother of God with the Child looks on. No solemnity — people helping people, each as best they can. A ready-made sermon, only without words.

Then the cathedral. Here the blood of St Januarius, the patron saint of Naples, is kept. And inside the cathedral there is another church — Santa Restituta, an ancient fourth-century basilica. The cathedral later grew up around it, and it ended up inside, like a matryoshka doll. Such places are especially dear to me: here Christians of the still-undivided Church prayed, when there were neither “Orthodox” nor “Catholics,” but simply the Church.

In the evening we wanted to go up to the Vomero, the hill from which all of Naples can be seen from above. We confidently arrived at the Montesanto funicular. The funicular is closed for repairs until May. We did manage to buy tickets, though — six of them at 1.90 euros each. The lesson cost us little, only eleven euros forty cents, and it goes like this: before going somewhere, check whether it's working at all. There are four funiculars in Naples, by the way, and the Centrale and Chiaia funiculars, and the metro, also go up to the Vomero. We'll remember for next time.
Tomorrow we move on, to the sea.

2026-11-05.title: Pompeii and the Road Up
text: Pompeii. It seems everyone knows about it: Vesuvius, the year 79, a city under ash. We covered that at school. But here's what is usually forgotten: the city we walked through today is much older than Rome as we know it. It was founded by the Oscans, some six hundred years before the Nativity of Christ. Then the Greeks lived nearby, then the Samnites came, and only for the last century and a half of its life did Pompeii live as an ordinary Roman town.

Ordinary — that, perhaps, is the whole point. Pompeii is not a capital and not a holy place. It's a provincial town with streets, shops, baths and taverns, which one day simply stopped. In Rome you look at the great ruins of a great empire. Here you look at someone's house, someone's bakery, someone's street with cart ruts and stepping stones across the roadway so you don't get your feet wet in the rain. Two thousand years have passed, and everything is arranged very understandably.

The eruption was described in detail by Pliny the Younger; he saw it from the other side of the bay. His uncle, Pliny the Elder, commanded the fleet, sailed off to rescue people and died. Excavation of the city began only in the eighteenth century, and it's still being excavated. In the nineteenth century archaeologists thought of filling with plaster the hollows left in the ash by people — that's how the famous casts came about, which still make you uneasy today. And above all this, as if nothing had happened, stands Vesuvius. It, by the way, hasn't gone anywhere and hasn't gone to sleep: it last erupted in 1944, within our grandfathers' memory.

And one more thought, this time from a priest. Less than twenty years before the eruption, very close by, in Puteoli — that's today's Pozzuoli, on the other side of Naples — the Apostle Paul came ashore when he was being taken to Rome. In Acts it says just that: “Where we found brethren.” That is, there were already Christians on this bay. Who knows, maybe some of them walked these very streets too. It can't be proved, but it's hard not to think about it.

Friends, the advice is simple: come to Pompeii with time to spare and in comfortable shoes. The city is large, the pavements are made of real Roman stone, and you could never call them even. And it's good that we're here in November and not in August: Pompeii is one of the most visited places in Italy, and under the summer sun on these stones it's probably not pleasant at all.

And towards evening we went up to Agerola, high above Amalfi. The road up is a serpentine, bend after bend. Agerola is a few villages on a mountain plateau, about six hundred meters above the sea. From here, by the way, begins the famous Path of the Gods, which runs above the coast. We decided to stay here, up top, for two nights. Why not down below, by the sea, where everyone is? Because here there's somewhere to park the car. And I don't drive into town centers any more. The lesson of Naples has been learned.

Originally, to be honest, Pompeii and Agerola were supposed to happen a day earlier. But we stayed longer in Naples, and the plan simply shifted. Nothing terrible: Pompeii has waited almost two thousand years, it waited one more day.
Tomorrow we'll go down to the sea.

2026-11-06.title: By Old Paths to Amalfi
text: In the morning, dawn over the Gulf of Salerno. You don't see that every day, so we decided to take a fifteen-minute walk. The fifteen-minute walk turned into a descent along old paths all the way to Amalfi. Friends, if on the Amalfi Coast someone suggests you “walk for fifteen minutes,” clarify right away: down or up, and how far.

We set out from San Lazzaro — that's one of the villages of Agerola, high above the sea. Then Tovere, the fork where paths 361 and 317 meet (the paths here have numbers, like in real mountains), then Vettica. These paths are old, truly old. The road along the coast was built only in the nineteenth century, and before that people walked for centuries between the mountain villages and the sea just like this, on foot, over stones and steps. We went the same way, only without a mule and without a load.
By noon we were standing at the cathedral in Amalfi. Masha, a wise girl, stayed home. The girl is twenty-one, but for her dad, as is well known, that changes nothing.

Amalfi today is a small resort town squeezed between cliffs. But once it was a maritime republic, one of the first in Italy, and its merchants traded a great deal with Byzantium. So the ties with Constantinople here are old ones, and that will come in handy in our story.

The Cathedral of Amalfi is several churches at once. The Cloister of Paradise with its arches — it was built in the thirteenth century as a cemetery for the noble families of Amalfi, hence the name. The Basilica of the Crucifix — the old cathedral, which is now a museum. Kept there is an Angevin miter, all embroidered with pearls. And below is the crypt, where the relics of the Apostle Andrew the First-Called lie.
My heavenly patron.

The relics were brought here from Constantinople in 1208, after the crusaders sacked the city. A story, I'll say honestly, that isn't easy for an Orthodox heart. But the apostle doesn't stop being an apostle because of that. Andrew is the first whom Christ called. And the first thing he did was find his brother Simon and say to him: “We have found the Messias.” And he brought him to Christ. That's how Simon became Peter. It seems to me this is all of Andrew: to find Christ and at once bring another to Him. According to tradition, he preached in our lands too and blessed the hills on which Kyiv later rose. He suffered a martyr's death in Greek Patras, on a diagonal cross. And here in Amalfi, according to tradition, an oily moisture called manna seeps from his tomb.
You stand at the relics of a saint you've been reading about in the Gospel all your life, whose name you bear — and you think: when will you ever be this close again.
We have a separate story about the apostle; you can listen to it below.
We went back up by SITA bus. From November 2 they're on the winter timetable, so if you go in the off-season, check in advance when the last bus is. Our legs said thank you.
So that's how a fifteen-minute walk led me to my saint. The most important thing, as often happens, happened not according to plan.
Tomorrow Herculaneum, and then north.

2026-11-07.title: Herculaneum and the Road to Orvieto
text: Our plan changed again. In the morning, still in the south, we sat down and honestly counted: Bari, Apulia, the Liturgy in Naples, and then Venice or Pisa as well. How many hours behind the wheel is that? It came out that we would be seeing Italy mostly through the windshield. So we put Bari off, set the bustle aside and decided differently: one base, drives of no more than an hour. There were many options on the table, and we chose the simplest. I think rightly.

On this trip I realized a simple thing about myself. I don't like driving a lot. And I especially don't like driving in city centers. After Naples, where the driving and parking are, to put it mildly, a nightmare, to any “come on, let's pop into the center” I respond with a counter-question: and where do we park the car?

Behind us are Naples, Montecassino, the paths above Amalfi and the crypt with the relics of the Apostle Andrew the First-Called. The week turned out packed, and we've had more than enough serpentines.

But on our last day in the south there was also Herculaneum. It's Pompeii's neighbor, and Vesuvius covered it on the same day in the year seventy-nine. Only Pompeii was buried in ash, while Herculaneum was flooded by hot flows, in a layer some twenty meters deep. The town is smaller than Pompeii, but it preserves what has hardly survived in Pompeii: charred wood, beams, here and there second floors. On top lives ordinary modern Ercolano, and the ancient town lies beneath it, in a huge pit. Two thousand years of difference — vertically, about twenty meters.

Then the long road north. About three hundred kilometers, almost the whole day in the car. Yes, I remember that I just wrote about “no more than an hour.” But this was the last big drive, I promise. Well, almost promise.

At that point we were driving with a plan for the Val d'Orcia: Pienza, the field from “Gladiator,” Montepulciano, Montalcino, hot springs. Spoiler: this plan too will live less than a day. But more on that tomorrow.

We were to spend the night at an agriturismo outside the town. The hostess wrote in advance: navigate by Google Maps or Waze, just not by Apple Maps. Apparently someone had already tried. And also check-out is before eleven — also important information when you're used to a family pace of getting ready.

You first see Orvieto from below. In the middle of the plain stands a huge rock, and on it, as if on a tray, the whole town with its cathedral. The rock is tuff, that is, compressed volcanic ash. The Etruscans lived here before the Romans, and in the Middle Ages the popes more than once left Rome to come here and hide — you can't climb a rock like that uninvited. So we didn't climb it by car either. We left it below, at the foot of the rock, and went up to the old town on foot.

We had dinner in old Orvieto. After a whole day on the road, dinner in a town on a rock is a reward in itself. Vesuvius in the morning, an Etruscan rock in the evening — that's the kind of day we had, and the south suddenly stayed somewhere very far away.
The tenth day of the trip, Saturday. Tomorrow is Sunday, and we need to find somewhere to pray.

2026-11-08.title: Porano, Civita and Bolsena
text: Sunday, the eleventh day of the trip. The morning began not with the road but with a decision. We didn't go to the Val d'Orcia. We're so happy near Orvieto that we're staying two more nights — we arranged it directly with the hostess, without any websites. And then three nights in Etruscan land, near Tarquinia and Viterbo: tombs, thermal baths, and about an hour from there to the airport. That's what our “one base” looks like. There are already two bases, true, but we don't have to drive far — and that's the main thing.

Then — to church. We were at Mass in Porano, a small town near Orvieto. The service isn't ours, the language isn't ours, but Sunday is Sunday. In the church there's a fourteenth-century fresco. That is, people have been praying beneath it for over six hundred years. Generations come and go, and it hangs there.

Next, Civita di Bagnoregio, “the dying town.” It stands on a lonely tuff rock, and only a long footbridge leads to it. There is no other road. Year after year the rains wash away the clay under the rock, the edges crumble, and the town gradually goes away with it. It was founded by the Etruscans, and St Bonaventure came from Bagnoregio. Only a handful of permanent residents remain there now, but there are tourists aplenty. We, as you can see, also made our contribution.

We had lunch right there, and the lunch was local: stracotto d'asino. Put simply, stewed donkey. The donkeys in Civita, by the way, once turned the millstones of the olive press. They worked for people all their lives. Such is the gratitude.

After lunch — Bolsena, a little town on the shore of a large lake. The lake, by the way, isn't an ordinary one: it's the largest volcanic lake in Europe, an almost round bowl in place of collapsed volcanoes. And in the town is the Basilica of St Christina. We venerate her too, the Great Martyr Christina. According to tradition, she was from here, from Bolsena: a very young girl, the daughter of a pagan ruler, she suffered for Christ back in the third century. To meet your own saint in a foreign country is like meeting an old acquaintance.

And in 1263, here, in this church, something happened that later changed the calendar of the whole Western Church. A priest who was traveling from Prague to Rome and doubted the Sacrament — whether Christ Himself is truly present in the bread and wine — was celebrating Mass and saw blood on the Holy Gifts. The blood seeped onto the linen cloth, the corporal. The cloth was taken to Orvieto, to the pope, and a year later Pope Urban IV established the feast of Corpus Christi. The texts for it, according to tradition, were written by Thomas Aquinas, who was also living in Orvieto at the time. And it was for the sake of this cloth that the cathedral in Orvieto was later built. But that's a story for the coming days.

Here's how I think about it. Everyone has doubts, including the one who stands at the altar. And the Lord answered this doubt not with an argument and not with a book, but in such a way that the answer is still kept in a silver reliquary. The doubting priest, strangely enough, turned out to be a very necessary person in this story.
You can listen to the stories about Orvieto and about Civita and Bolsena below. We're staying near Orvieto for two more nights.
Tomorrow morning, horses.

2026-11-09.title: Horses, Hot Springs and a Pigeon
text: Monday began with horses. At half past nine we were at an equestrian club near Orvieto, in a place called La Cacciata, and for two hours we rode around the surrounding countryside. The guide spoke Italian, the horses, it seems, did too, but everyone came to an understanding. We rode and liked it very much. There's nothing more to add — if it's good, it's good.

By noon our next question had ripened: where are the warm pools? We want to swim. The answer was found in San Casciano dei Bagni. This is real Tuscany now, not that far from Orvieto, a little hilltop town that lives on hot water. There are dozens of springs there; the Etruscans and Romans bathed in them. And a few years ago archaeologists pulled a whole collection of bronze statues out of an ancient sacred pool — they had lain in the hot mud for more than two thousand years.

Around half past one we had lunch at the restaurant Daniela on the square. A Tuscan menu, no compromises: pecorino with truffle, pici — a thick hand-rolled pasta, pappardelle with wild boar. All of this is what we were advised to order. Tuscany knows how to feed you so that after lunch you don't much feel like swimming any more, but you very much feel like lying down.

But we came to swim, after all. We went to look for the famous free bathing pool. I find a stone basin under a canopy, there's water, the stone is old, everything is genuine. I take a photo and send it: “Is this it?” Turns out — it isn't. It's an old washhouse, a lavatoio, where the local women washed laundry for centuries. Good thing I asked before I climbed in. Picture it: an American priest in swimming trunks sitting in a medieval washhouse, waiting for it to get warm.
In the end we swam at Fonteverde, a paid thermal pool. The water is about thirty-eight degrees. In November, getting into water like that is the right decision; there's nothing even to argue about.

In the evening we returned to Orvieto and, you won't believe it, couldn't find the cathedral. In a town where the cathedral can be seen from the plain several kilometers away, we walked the little streets and couldn't understand where it had gone. We found it. And around half past seven we stood in front of the facade under its night lighting.

This is, without exaggeration, one of the most beautiful facades in Italy. The cathedral was built over almost three hundred years, and the first stone was laid on November 13, 1290 — which makes it almost exactly seven hundred thirty-six years ago, this week. The chief master of the facade was the Sienese Lorenzo Maitani. Below are four marble pillars, and they are the Bible in stone: on the left the creation of the world, on the right the Last Judgment. Above is the rose window by the Florentine Orcagna and gold mosaics that blaze under the lights. And the central bronze doors are quite new, from the sixties, the work of Emilio Greco; on them are the works of mercy. The town argued about them for some ten years, and now the cathedral is unimaginable without them.

And this whole cathedral was built for the sake of one linen cloth from Bolsena, where we were yesterday. For the sake of one doubt that the Lord did not leave unanswered. We stood, listened to the story about the cathedral and looked up.

We had dinner at the trattoria del Moro Aronne. I had pigeon alla ghiotta — it's an Umbrian dish, and I kept checking: is it really pigeon, not partridge? Pigeon. Well, after yesterday's donkey, nothing surprises me any more.
Tomorrow, the cathedral from the inside and the move to Etruscan land.

2026-11-10.title: Montefiascone, Capodimonte, Tuscania
text: In the morning we went to Orvieto Cathedral again, inside this time. It was raining. Inside, the walls are striped — black basalt and light travertine, as if the church had been drawn in pencil. In the Chapel of the Corporal is kept that very cloth from Bolsena. Two days ago we stood where the blood fell on it, and now we stood before it itself. The circle closed. Opposite is the Chapel of San Brizio, where Luca Signorelli painted the Last Judgment. They say Michelangelo came here to learn before painting his own in the Sistine Chapel. Then we walked around the town following a list drawn up in advance.
We booked the accommodation for the last three nights only this morning. We live without a margin, but with parking by the house, and for me that's the main thing.

Around two we left Orvieto and all the way listened to a story about these places. Lake Bolsena is a collapsed volcano. On the small island of Martana in 535 the Gothic queen Amalasuntha was strangled, and that started a twenty-year war. And in Montefiascone there's a wine called “Est! Est!! Est!!!” A bishop's servant, who marked the taverns with good wine, wrote “it is” on the door here three times, and the bishop never went on to Rome.

We did stop in Montefiascone. The first thing I did was proudly park the car right under a sign “eccetto titolari permesso NRP,” that is, for locals only. We moved it. We went up to the Rocca dei Papi, the summer papal fortress. The view of the lake from there, they say, is the best. They say — because there was fog and rain. I asked about local news: during the day near Acquapendente, very close by, there had been a small earthquake, a 2.6.

From four to five we sat on the waterfront in Capodimonte and watched the sunset over the lake. Opposite is the island of Bisentina, nearby the castle of the Farnese — the very family that produced Pope Paul III.

In the evening we checked in in Tuscania. I asked: was D'Artagnan a Tuscan? No, a Gascon. And we, for the record, aren't in Tuscany at all. Tuscania is Lazio, the region of Tuscia, the old land of the Etruscans. We had dinner at the restaurant “Beer and Meat”: Morellino and Grechetto, Neapolitan starters — arancini, frittatina, cuoppo, then steaks and the “Rasna” board. Rasna is what the Etruscans called themselves. On a Tuesday evening Tuscania is empty. Nowhere to go, nobody around.

But Stefano turned up, the husband of our apartment's hostess. For fifty euros he drove us to the free hot springs of the Piscine Carletti near Viterbo and waited while we bathed. I translated through my phone, by voice, and we talked about everything. About how our months come from the Romans. I told him: when my ancestors lived in dugouts, yours were building temples, forums, Pompeii; a great country and a great history; it's a great honor to be here. Then about small Italian cars and American trucks. Gasoline in Italy is now two twenty to two fifty a liter, and it used to be a euro twenty. Stefano's car runs on gas. I told him that in Ukraine I also drove on gas, and in America gasoline was a dollar seventy-five a gallon, now four. And about the police: in America they chase you with flashing lights; in Ukraine they would stop you and offer a fine or a bribe. Stefano also learned how in San Casciano we nearly bathed in a washhouse.

In the evening there were only men at the springs. We asked why. Stefano: I don't know, generally both men and women come. He also recommended a restaurant for tomorrow, I Tulipani: they feed you well there, and fish too, tell them you're from Stefano, she knows me well.
Tomorrow, the Etruscans and the necropolis of Tarquinia. And for lunch, it seems, we'll go “from Stefano.”

2026-11-11.title: Tarquinia: Necropolis, Museum and the Sea
text: Today was the day of the Etruscans. From Tuscania to Tarquinia is twenty-five minutes, and all the way we listened to a story about the city of the dead, which for two and a half thousand years has looked across the valley at the city of the living. Right by the necropolis, in a yard under an olive tree, we saw a block of stone: a bearded man reclining as if at a feast, around him owls, horses, animal faces. At first we thought it was ancient. It turned out to be modern work by a local craftsman; nearby stand a van and plastic chairs. But it's done with real knowledge.

From the outside, the Monterozzi necropolis doesn't look at all like a city of the dead: a green meadow, cypresses, and in the grass little houses, like sheds. You open the door, and there's a steep staircase down into the tuff. Below there's glass, you press a button, the light comes on, and out of the darkness step people who were painted five hundred years before the Nativity of Christ. They feast, dance, play double flutes.

I came up with my own tour. I photographed the sign at the entrance, and a minute later in my earphones there was already an account of what to look for on the left, on the right, above the door. So we went from tomb to tomb: the Leopards, the Lionesses, the Bacchantes, the Hunter, where the whole room is painted like a hunting tent, and through the painted fabric a roe deer grazes. In the Tomb of Hunting and Fishing there are two rooms and one door, and that very youth who dives from a cliff into the sea can't be seen from the first room. We had to look at him in a photo on the phone. You stand a meter away from him and look at your phone.

And you can see very clearly how the Etruscans changed. In the early tombs there's only feasting, dolphins, birds and joy. But two hundred years later, when Rome was taking their cities from them one after another, demons with hammers already stand at the painted door to the afterlife, and the dead are led by the arms. In the Tomb of the Two Roofs the deceased is seen off by a she-demon with a torch, and at the gates of Hades he is met by his own, who died earlier. To my mind, this is the hope most understandable to us of all that we saw.

Then there was a separate story with lunch. The navigator led us straight through a ZTL, and we didn't want to risk a fine, so we parked the car by the Barriera San Giusto gate and went on foot. The restaurant I had picked turned out to be locked up. The second one too. November, Wednesday, Italy. The third one was found, with the local acquacotta soup on the menu and with a note under the carbonara saying that the one who loves you is not the one who talks about love, but the one who silently cooks you carbonara.

After lunch we went to the museum, in Palazzo Vitelleschi. It was built in the fifteenth century by a cardinal who led the papal armies and ended his life in Castel Sant'Angelo. Inside is everything that was taken out of the ground. An urn in the shape of a hut; through its little window the ashes of a warrior can still be seen. A bronze helmet with a crest like a flame. The tomb of the Versna family with a chariot, spears and dishes for an eternal feast. And, of course, the Winged Horses. They were found in '38 as a heap of fragments and put together like a jigsaw puzzle. After a whole day underground it was like a breath of air: light, wings and movement upwards.
And upstairs, in the medieval halls, there was a fresco of the Mother of God. Beneath it in Latin: “When you come to the image of the Most Pure Virgin, as you pass by, do not forget to say: Hail.”

Towards evening we drove to the sea, to the old salt pans and to Lido di Tarquinia. We just wanted to sit with a hot tea and look at the cold sea. Somewhere beyond the salt ponds, they say, flamingos spend the winter.

2026-11-12.title: Viterbo: The Papal Hill in the Rain
text: It was raining in Viterbo. Not a downpour, but that Italian November drizzle that makes the cobblestones shine as if varnished and the yellow leaves stick to the stones. We climbed up to the Colle del Duomo, the cathedral hill. This is the oldest place in the city: according to tradition, first there was an Etruscan sanctuary here, then a fortress, and in the thirteenth century the popes came.

Why would the popes want Viterbo, you may ask? Rome was dangerous at the time. Noble families fought right in the streets, and a mob could drive out even the pope himself. Viterbo, on the other hand, was loyal, rich and well fortified. For almost a quarter of a century the popes lived here, and from those years the loggia remains, from which they blessed the people: seven pointed arches on slender paired columns, stone lace, with the sky showing through it.

This is also where the word “conclave” was born. In twelve sixty-eight Pope Clement the Fourth died, and the cardinals sat down to elect a new one. They sat for a year. Then a second. The townspeople got fed up and locked the cardinals in a hall with a key, cum clave. It didn't help. Then they were put on bread and water. It didn't help. Then the roof was taken off the hall. In the thirty-third month a pope was finally elected, and what's more, a man who was not a cardinal and was in fact in the Holy Land at the time. And the new pope later wrote down a rule: from now on, lock them in straight away.

I went around with my own home-made tour: I photographed the map and the signs, and the story played in my earphones. In the museum I asked for the rest to be sent as text. Reading is faster than listening, and in a museum there is never enough time.

The cathedral museum is small, but it has everything at once. A golden Gothic folding altarpiece: the Mother of God enthroned, with Peter, the Forerunner, John the Theologian and Paul on either side. Essentially our Deesis, only gathered into a single frame. A small Madonna on a gold ground; the Child has coral beads around His neck and a goldfinch in His hand. Relics of St Lawrence, the archdeacon to whom the cathedral here is dedicated: a bone in a wooden casket with glass and a handwritten label. And a Roman Artemis of Ephesus, the very one about whom, in Acts, they shouted for two hours: “Great is Diana of the Ephesians!” Now she stands by the wall of the papal palace, hung all over with her strange clusters, and nobody shouts in front of her.

Two things I examined longer than the rest, for professional reasons. The first: a red chasuble, embroidered all over with gold and silver, with a coat of arms at the bottom. I stood in front of the case counting stitches the way someone else might count money. The second: “The Dead Christ”, a painting from eighteen seventy-six. The body on a slab, a white shroud, the removed crown of thorns on the floor. This is our epitaphios, only painted in oil. We stitch it and carry it out on Great Friday, and here it hangs in a museum gallery, and next to it you want to fall silent just the same.

In the evening we returned to Tuscania and went to dinner at the same place as on the first evening. We ordered Chianti. On the label was a beast very much like the Etruscan Chimera of Arezzo. We are, of course, still not in Tuscany, but the Etruscans caught up with us even here.
Tomorrow is our last day with the car. We want to make it to Cerveteri, to the Etruscan burial mounds, and we need to be at Fiumicino by one in the afternoon.

photos/2026-10-31/1.alt: Bernini's tomb of Pope Alexander VII in St Peter's Basilica
photos/2026-10-31/1.description:
At first the eye catches on the red “carpet,” and only then do you realize it is stone. A huge mottled drape of jasper flows down from the pedestal, and from under it a gilded skeleton climbs out and raises an hourglass above its head. At the top Pope Alexander VII kneels, hands folded in prayer; he doesn't even look at death. On the left is a female figure with an infant at her breast, this is Charity, on the right another, who has set her foot on the globe. And under this whole mass is a perfectly ordinary wooden door, which is still in use today. Bernini essentially turned a service passage into an image: death comes out of the door through which everyone will one day enter.

I stood behind the red rope and for a long time couldn't step away. In the morning we had entered the square through the colonnade that this same pope commissioned from the same Bernini, so all day we were, as it were, walking around inside his design, and in the basilica we ended up at his grave as well. The tomb was finished in the late 1670s, when the master was already nearly eighty, and it is one of his last great works. The old man knew what he was sculpting about.

What moved me most was that the pope is shown not in glory but in prayer. Facing the hourglass held by a bony hand, you couldn't think of anything wiser. On the right a random tourist in a light T-shirt got into the frame, and it looked like he, too, had something to think about.

photos/2026-10-31/2.alt: A Roman fountain with a lion's head
photos/2026-10-31/2.description:
Morning, we are still only walking to St Peter's Square, and on the way we come across this fountain built right into the wall. Old yellow stone, a lion's face with a mane of stone curls, and from a pipe a stream runs into a long marble basin. The water in the basin is dark, the bottom green, and the sides are overgrown with moss of every shade, from emerald to rusty red. You can tell at once that it hasn't been flowing here for just a year or two. On the right a woman has bent down and is holding a bottle under the next stream.

In Rome this is an ordinary thing. Everyone drinks water from the city fountains, locals and visitors alike, and an empty bottle is carried around here as routinely as sunglasses. The famous cast-iron hydrants are affectionately called “big noses” by the Romans, nasoni, and they say there are more than two thousand of them around the city. And stone fountains with lions like this one are their older and more elegant relatives. Lions are everywhere in Rome anyway: on fountains, by doors, on coats of arms, and after so many centuries nobody, it seems, has grown tired of them.

All this water came into the city by aqueducts. The ancient Romans brought them from dozens of kilometers away, later many of them fell into ruin, and it was the popes who restored them one after another, placing ornate fountains with their own coats of arms at the end. So taking a drink in Rome is, in essence, partaking of other people's centuries-old labor, and all of it free.

I looked at this little stream and remembered the Samaritan woman at the well and Christ's words: “Whosoever drinketh of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst.” In front of a huge basilica, something as simple as water by a wall turned out to be very welcome. Plus twenty had been forecast, a long day lay ahead, so the bottle was definitely not superfluous.

photos/2026-10-31/3.alt: On the steps at the entrance to a shop
photos/2026-10-31/3.description:
My two fellow travelers sat down on the marble steps at the entrance to a shop and made it look as if this was exactly how it had all been planned. One, in black, with a striped bag at her feet, has propped her head on her hand and is looking thoughtfully to the side. The other, fiery red-haired, in a beige trench coat and light blue jeans, holds her phone on her knees and gazes into the lens as if it were her own shop. Behind them, through the wide-open glass doors, are shelves of framed icons, souvenirs, a string of lights under the vault, a salesman and customers. On either side, shop windows in brass frames.

This was in the morning, on the way to St Peter's Square. The shops around the Vatican are a genre of their own: rosaries, medallions, candles, postcards with the pope. And almost everywhere, which surprised and pleased me, the Kazan Icon of the Mother of God is on sale. Probably not by chance. An old copy of the Kazan Icon was kept for many years by Pope John Paul II, and in 2004 the Vatican handed it over to the Russian Church, and now it is in Kazan. So for the sellers here this image has long been their own.

And the thirty-first of October in our church calendar is the feast of the Apostle Luke. According to tradition, he was the first to paint an image of the Mother of God. The Kazan Icon is of the Hodegetria type, “She Who Shows the Way,” and tradition also attributes the first Hodegetria to Luke. So here is a kind of echo: an Orthodox feast, a Catholic shop, and in the window an image that links the one with the other.

I also like this shot because there are no columns or domes in it. Just steps, morning, our own people. It is from minutes like these that a journey is later made up, and the basilicas, as everyone knows, will stand and wait.

photos/2026-10-31/4.alt: The sculpture “Angels Unawares” in St Peter's Square
photos/2026-10-31/4.description:
From a distance it looks as if a boat packed with people has moored in St Peter's Square. You come closer and begin to make out faces. An old man with a staff, a boy in a cap, a woman in a headscarf, many holding suitcases and bundles, someone pressing a child to themselves. Clothes from different centuries and different countries, some barefoot, others in sandals. And in the middle of the crowd two large wings rise up. The angel himself is not visible, only the wings above the heads, and you can't tell at once which of these people they belong to.

This is a sculpture by the Canadian Timothy Schmalz; it was placed here in 2019, on the World Day of Migrants and Refugees. The title is taken from the Epistle to the Hebrews: “Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares.” In English that is exactly how it sounds, angels unawares.

You want to walk all the way around it and peer into every face. I liked that the angel doesn't stand apart on a pedestal but is hidden among the refugees. It's a good thought for a traveler to keep in mind. After all, we are strangers here too, with backpacks and tickets on our phones, and in a foreign country you depend entirely on the kindness of strangers. And at home, in Orlando, it is often others who turn out to be the strangers, and then it depends on us whether we make out the wings.

Next to the bronze crowd stood a living one, from all over the world, also taking pictures. Two crowds side by side, and it's an open question which of them looks more like the one in the boat.

photos/2026-10-31/5.alt: Bernini's colonnade in St Peter's Square
photos/2026-10-31/5.description:
Here it is, the colonnade I later wrote can't be put into words. The columns stand four rows deep, and when you walk between them they merge into a forest of stone, while above, along the whole roof, statues of saints are lined up. The sky that morning was bright blue, the travertine almost white in the sun, and under the vaults a cool shade. People sit on the steps between the columns, some with phones, some just resting. Here, outside, nobody forbids sitting yet. Inside the basilica, as we found out later, the attendants make everyone get up who sits down even for a minute.

Bernini built the colonnade under Pope Alexander VII, in the 1650s–1660s. Two hundred and eighty-four columns, and above them one hundred and forty statues of saints. Bernini himself explained his idea simply: the two semicircles are the motherly arms of the Church, embracing all who come, believers to strengthen them, and the lost to bring them back. It seems this is that rare case when architecture really does what is said about it. You enter the square and feel that you have been taken into an embrace, only a very large and very stony one.

They say that if you stand on a special round stone in the pavement between the obelisk and the fountain, the four rows of columns line up into one and the colonnade becomes transparent. Next time I'll be sure to look for it. But this time it was enough for us that we walked for about twenty minutes, came around a corner and suddenly found ourselves inside this gesture.

photos/2026-10-31/6.alt: A Swiss Guard at the Arch of the Bells
photos/2026-10-31/6.description:
The sun is still low, the light slanting and warm, long shadows stretching across the cobblestones. To the left of the basilica's façade, at the service entrance, by all appearances at the Arch of the Bells, a Swiss Guard stands on duty. A uniform in broad stripes, blue, red and yellow, a black beret, in his hand a halberd taller than he is. On either side two gray sentry boxes, behind him wrought-iron gates and a passage under an arch with a balustrade. Beyond that begins the state of Vatican City itself, where a tourist can't go without business. The arch's name is simple: above it, in the left part of the façade, hang the basilica's bells.

The shot was taken from far away, and I like that the guard in it is very small and the stones around him are enormous. That's probably how it really is.

The Guard was founded by Pope Julius II in 1506, and the first Swiss came to Rome on foot. Ever since, it has remained Swiss. It is made up of young men, necessarily Swiss and Catholic, who have done military service back home. There are only a little over a hundred of them in all; it is said to be the smallest army in the world. People often say the uniform was designed by Michelangelo. A beautiful legend, but the uniform got its present look at the beginning of the twentieth century from a commander of the Guard, inspired by old Renaissance frescoes. It came out so convincingly that everyone still believes in Michelangelo.

Today the halberd is, of course, more of a symbol. But there is something touching in the fact that for five hundred years in a row people from one small mountain country have come here to stand at the gates. Service is rarely glamorous anyway. More often it is just this: to stand while everyone walks past, and not to leave.

photos/2026-10-31/7.alt: A shelf of liturgical books in the Vatican bookshop
photos/2026-10-31/7.description:
For an Orthodox priest this is perhaps the most unexpected shelf in the whole Vatican. A sign at the top in Italian, LITURGIA, and under it stacks of books in paper covers the color of baked milk. I read the spines: “Trebnik” (the Book of Needs), volume three, volume four, volume five, “Sluzhebnik” (the Service Book). Next to them the Greek “Agiasmatarion,” the book of the rites of the blessing of water and various blessings, and above it the “Anthologion.” On many covers it says in Latin “Recensione volgata,” that is, the familiar, commonly used recension of the text. The covers are plain, the typeface old, the paper already yellowed; you can see they haven't been lying here for just a year. And below, for contrast, bright flip calendars for 2027.

Rome printed these books in its time for the Eastern Catholics, whose services are the same as ours, in Slavonic or in Greek. That's why their Trebnik is ours and their Sluzhebnik is ours, except perhaps with Roman publication details. You look at them with the same feeling you have when you meet someone from your hometown in a strange city. In this same shop I bought “Guidance for Celebrating Orthodox Services,” the 1962 edition, from the time of the Second Vatican Council.

It's amazing that all this wasn't written off and sent for pulping, but is kept on a shelf and sold. Someone in the Vatican evidently decided that a book like this doesn't need to be fashionable; it's enough for it to be right. And here I quite agree with him.

photos/2026-10-31/8.alt: Crowds in St Peter's Square, the obelisk in the center
photos/2026-10-31/8.description:
This is what St Peter's Square looks like on an ordinary October Saturday if you look at it from inside the line. Wooden barriers, endless heads, dark glasses, backpacks, someone has opened an umbrella against the sun. Beyond the people a fountain, further on the curve of the colonnade with white statues on the roof, and in the center of it all stands the obelisk with a cross on its top. The sky looks as if it had just been washed.

We spent a long time deciding whether to join this line or give up and go on walking. It's there, I think, for the whole day. In the end we joined it and didn't regret it, though by evening our feet remembered it.

The obelisk is a story in itself. It was brought from Egypt back under the Emperor Caligula and set up in the circus that Nero later finished building. According to tradition, it was somewhere near this circus that the Apostle Peter was crucified, upside down. For fifteen hundred years the stone stood in its old place, and in 1586 Pope Sixtus V ordered it moved here, to the center of the square. The architect Domenico Fontana moved it for several months, with winches, horses and hundreds of workers, and raised it under the strictest order to keep silence. A cross was set on top.

I like this thought. A stone that saw Peter's execution now stands before his tomb and bears a cross. The pagan monument lost nothing; it just changed its owner. The obelisk, by the way, is the only one of Rome's that has never once fallen in all that time. Standing in line next to such a neighbor is easier, after all.

photos/2026-10-31/9.alt: The sarcophagus of Pope Marcellus in the grottoes beneath the basilica
photos/2026-10-31/9.description:
Down below, under the basilica, in the grottoes where the popes rest, it was noticeably quieter than above. This sarcophagus stands behind a red rope by a light-colored wall. A simple stone chest, with wavy grooves on the sides like frozen ripples on water, in the center a relief with three figures, and one more at each corner. On the lid, in large Latin letters: MARCELLVS PAPA II. The chest itself is noticeably older than the inscription; such chests were carved back in the first Christian centuries, and it seems it was simply taken and reused. In Rome nothing goes to waste.

Marcellus II was pope for a very short time, in the spring of 1555, and reigned only about three weeks. He was a strict and honest man and only managed to show what he would have liked the papacy to be. In those days he ordered the pomp at court cut back and more modest conduct. Then he died, and the promise remained a promise.

He did, however, leave music behind. Palestrina named his Mass in his honor, the Missa Papae Marcelli, and there is a beautiful tradition that it was this Mass that persuaded the fathers of the Council of Trent not to ban polyphony in church, because every word can be clearly heard in it. Historians doubt the story, but the music is still sung.

At our Friday talks we happen to be discussing the popes, and standing at their tombs turned out to be not at all the same as reading about them. Twenty-two days on the throne, and then five hundred years of silence underground. Here you understand very clearly how short any power is.

photos/2026-10-31/10.alt: The dome of St Peter's Basilica from inside
photos/2026-10-31/10.description:
You stand under the dome, tilt your head back, and your neck soon starts to complain. But it's hard to tear yourself away. The dome is divided by ribs into sections, and along them in tiers run mosaic figures in medallions and at full height: saints, angels, apostles. At the top a ring of golden stars on blue, and above it the bright lantern with an inscription running around it. Through the windows in the drum falls a ray of sunlight, slanting and almost tangible, as if someone had stretched a ribbon of light across the whole basilica. Below you can see the top of Bernini's bronze baldachin with its angels, and in a round medallion on the pendentive sits one of the Evangelists.

Around the base of the dome runs an inscription in enormous letters. The end of it got into the frame: TIBI DABO CLAVES REGNI CAELORUM, “and I will give unto thee the keys of the kingdom of heaven.” These are Christ's words to the Apostle Peter from the sixteenth chapter of the Gospel of Matthew. The letters there, they say, are about two meters high, but from below they look like a neat line of text. We Orthodox read these words a little differently than they do here, but under this dome I somehow didn't feel like arguing.

The dome was conceived by Michelangelo, and it was completed after his death by Giacomo della Porta and Domenico Fontana, in 1590. It is about forty meters in diameter. And here is what struck me more than all the figures. The small dome at the very top, that same lantern, is almost the same size as the dome of the church in Tishki. Only in Tishki it seems big, and here, at such a height, it is quite tiny.

Everything depends on what you have been set over. A good thought, I think, for a priest looking upward in someone else's cathedral.

photos/2026-10-31/11.alt: St Bruno, founder of the Carthusians, refusing the miter — a statue in St Peter's Basilica
photos/2026-10-31/11.description:
In a niche of a huge marble pier stands a monk. Pale marble, the hood thrown back onto his shoulders, his tonsured head bowed. With his left hand he holds a skull, and he has raised his right hand palm outward, as if saying: “No, don't.” And at his feet a little angel holds out to him a bishop's miter and crozier. Below are rows of transparent plastic chairs set out for some service, and a barrier rope.

If I understood correctly from the pose and the inscription, this is St Bruno, the founder of the Carthusians. The statue was made by the French sculptor René-Michel Slodtz in the middle of the eighteenth century. Bruno lived in the eleventh century and was a well-known teacher of theology, and then he left everything and with a few companions went into the mountains near Grenoble, to a hermitage that was called the Chartreuse. Later his former pupil became Pope Urban II and summoned his teacher to Rome. Bruno was offered the post of archbishop; he refused and ended his life as a hermit in Calabria. It is this refusal that the sculptor carved in marble: an angel with a miter, and the saint pushing it away with his hand.

The Carthusians still live in almost complete silence, each in his own cell. Their motto: “The Cross stands while the world turns.”

I've already written that the statues of the founders of orders throughout the basilica are a good idea. To single out those who began each direction of service. And here it's especially amusing: in the most famous and noisy church in the world stands a man who all his life sought silence, and under him rows of chairs for the crowd. I think he would have smiled. Or kept silent, which for a Carthusian is the same thing.

photos/2026-10-31/12.alt: A papal tomb in a niche of St Peter's Basilica
photos/2026-10-31/12.description:
Above a door in a side part of the basilica stands a whole marble scene. In the center Christ sits enthroned and blesses with both hands, on either side two apostles, Peter and Paul, as I understand it. Below, at their feet, a pope in a mantle kneels, hands folded, his face intent. On the cornice beneath him is the inscription: PIO VIII PONTIFICI MAXIMO, and next to it the name of Cardinal Giuseppe Albani, who erected this monument. On either side of the door are two more figures in niches, virtues, as is customary here.

Pius VIII was pope for a very short time, not quite two years, in 1829–1830, and textbooks usually give him a line or two. But he got a very fine monument. I liked that the pope here does not sit enthroned or command but kneels before Christ, and the apostles above him are something like witnesses. That's how it should be.

The door below is open, and through it you can see a lit passage, leading, it seems, to the sacristy and the inner rooms of the basilica. Attendants in dark suits walk there, tourists scurry back and forth. Above, eternity; below, a working day. Everything in this basilica is like that: amid endless marble someone carries a folder of papers, someone looks at a phone, someone checks whether you've sat down somewhere on a step.

There are so many papal tombs in the basilica that after an hour they begin to merge into one. But this one sticks in the memory, probably because the scene is clear without any guidebook. A man before God, and nothing more.

photos/2026-10-31/13.alt: A mosaic with acanthus, roses and a wind face in St Peter's Basilica
photos/2026-10-31/13.description:
Yana took this shot, and it's good that she did: in a basilica where your gaze is pulled upward all the time, toward the dome, things like this right by the floor are easy to miss. In front of us is a corner of a mosaic in a gilded frame with beading. An ivory background made up of thousands of tiny stones. Across it wind green and brown acanthus leaves, and in the very center of a scroll a large red flower, like a peony, has bloomed. Above are sprays of roses tied with a golden bow, and three little golden stars. And in a separate field on the left a chubby face with puffed-out cheeks blows on ears of grain and flowers. That is how the wind was depicted in the old days. At the side you can see the edge of a white cloth, so I think this is the facing of some altar, but I can't say for sure.

Step back a pace, and it looks like embroidery or painting. Come right up close, and you see that every petal is made of stones the size of a grain of rice, each with its own shade. The basilica has had its own mosaic workshop for almost three hundred years, and they say several tens of thousands of shades of smalto are kept there. Mosaic fears neither candle soot nor damp, which is why it is so loved here.

What I liked most was this little face of the wind. The ears of grain bend, the flowers bow, but the wind itself can't be seen; you only see what it does. Christ spoke to Nicodemus about exactly this: “The wind bloweth where it listeth, and thou hearest the sound thereof, but canst not tell whence it cometh, and whither it goeth.” The craftsman may not have been thinking of the Gospel and was simply decorating a corner. But it came out very much in the spirit of the Gospel.

photos/2026-10-31/14.alt: A coffered arch from the nave into a side aisle of St Peter's Basilica
photos/2026-10-31/14.description:
If you stop in the middle of the nave and look up into one of the arches leading into a side aisle, this is what you see. The vault of the arch recedes into the depth like a telescope, and it is coffered all over: octagonal recesses with gilded rosettes, row after row. At the very end, in the opening, a small dome of the side aisle glows with its windows. Above the arch two white female figures recline, allegories of virtues, and higher still runs a frieze with huge letters; in the frame you can read PETRE and IESVS, apparently words from the Gospel conversation of Christ with Peter. Above all this is the golden coffered ceiling of the nave. On the sides fluted pilasters, statues in niches, medallions on colored marble. And through all of it a ray of sunlight falls on a slant.

Coffers were invented by the ancient Romans. In the Pantheon they were needed not only for beauty but to lighten the vault: the less stone at the top, the less it presses on the walls. Here, in the basilica, they are more for beauty and rhythm; the eye runs along them into the depth and of its own accord is drawn toward the light.

It's interesting that this long nave didn't appear right away. Michelangelo planned the basilica in the form of a Greek cross, with equal arms, and at the beginning of the seventeenth century Carlo Maderno lengthened it, and the basilica became a Latin cross. That's why, if you stand at the entrance, Michelangelo's dome is almost invisible; the façade hides it.

To be honest, views like this make your head spin, and not only from the height. You can't take it all in. You touch not even the summit but the edge of an enormous culture, and that is probably as it should be: we wouldn't have had enough in us for everything at once.

photos/2026-10-31/15.alt: An altarpiece in St Peter's Basilica
photos/2026-10-31/15.description:
One of the altars in a side aisle of the basilica. Above the altar table, a large image in a gold frame: in the center elders in blue and gold robes, one of them has raised his hand high, the others are looking in one direction. Below, at their feet, lies a fallen man, head down, as if he had just crashed down from a height. And above, on a cloud, a reclining figure and around it some flying creatures. In front of the image, six tall candles in candlesticks with a crucifix in the middle, and below that a marble balustrade with twisted balusters.

I'll be honest, I never did make out the subject for certain. It looks like one of the miracles of the Apostle Peter, but I won't venture a guess from memory in a basilica where there are dozens of such altars. Especially since many of the “paintings” here are actually mosaics, put together from tiny pieces of smalto, and from a distance you can't tell them from painting. Over the centuries candle soot and damp ruin canvases, but mosaic endures.

The most interesting thing in the frame is perhaps the man in the foreground. A random visitor sits beneath the image with his hand over his mouth, looking off to the side. It seems he, too, was trying to understand what was depicted, or was simply tired, as all of us were by that time. The basilica is so huge that after a couple of hours you stop being amazed and just start sitting. If, of course, the attendants allowed sitting.

Shots like this are dearer to me than postcard ones. Great art, and before it an ordinary tired man. It is for such people, properly speaking, that all this was built.

photos/2026-10-31/16.alt: The three of us on the steps by St Peter's Basilica
photos/2026-10-31/16.description:
A rare shot with all three of us together. A selfie on stone steps, right in the thick of the crowd. The blue backpack I carried around the whole Vatican that day, my girls beside me, and all around constant movement: someone going down, someone going up, behind us a girl in a pink T-shirt and glasses with a lollipop in her mouth, and above the heads an ocher Roman house glows. The sun was already sinking; you can tell from our faces that it had been a long day.

Exactly which steps these were you can't tell from the picture; in Rome there are so many of them that you can't remember them all. The main thing is something else: our feet were aching, and we finally sat down. After the basilica, where the attendants made sure nobody sat down anywhere even for a minute, this was almost a celebration. I asked one of them then why they were so strict. He answered with annoyance that otherwise the tourists would block the whole staircase. And looking at this picture, I understand him: that's exactly what we're doing.

Yana and Masha spent the whole day taking pictures of themselves against everything in sight, while I mostly looked and tried to fit at least something into my head. So this shot turned out to be a bit of chance justice: in at least one picture I'm not behind the camera but next to them.

When you travel as a family, the most important photos later turn out to be not the ones with colonnades but ones like this, where everyone is a little tired and tousled, sitting on steps and squinting into a phone. The colonnade will stand another three hundred years, but this day we have only once.

photos/2026-10-31/17.alt: A mosaic icon of the Nativity in a gold frame
photos/2026-10-31/17.description:
A small icon of the Nativity behind glass, in a heavy gilded frame that looks like a twisted rope. The picture itself is perhaps the size of a palm, and it is made of hundreds of tiny pieces of smalto. The Mother of God in a blue maphorion has bent toward the Child; she has a golden halo, and so does He. The Child is swaddled and lies in a red manger that looks like a stone box. From above, an ox and an ass lean over Him, and from the sky a bluish ray descends. Behind, a little house with a triangular pediment, and mountains. Around the edge a red border with little blue and green squares, like precious stones on an icon cover.
