The icon stands on a stand behind glass, and you can study it for a long time: how the craftsman laid out the folds of the clothing and the shadows on the face with stones smaller than a grain of rice. Roman micromosaic is an old local craft, it is valued here, and the Vatican still has its own mosaic workshop.

To me, as an Orthodox, this iconography is very dear and familiar. The manger in the shape of a little coffin, swaddling clothes like grave clothes, the dark cave, the ox and the ass, of whom Isaiah says: “The ox knoweth his owner, and the ass his master's crib.” All of this is in our icon of the Nativity too, though we more often paint it differently, with the cave and the shepherds.

It was strange and good to see the Nativity on the last day of October, when the feast is still two months away. But in an icon time doesn't matter. In it Christ is being born now, in Rome, and in Orlando, and anywhere where people look at Him.

photos/2026-10-31/18.alt: The street leading to St Peter's Basilica
photos/2026-10-31/18.description:
A straight, wide street, and at its very end, as if in a theater's proscenium, stands St Peter's Basilica. The dome slightly hazy, the façade in shadow, and on either side two symmetrical buildings, like stage wings. Above it all a high, bright sky with clouds, and along the cobblestones a solid stream of people walks toward the basilica. In the foreground a young guy in dark glasses accidentally got into the frame, but the basilica is no less majestic for it.

This street is called Via della Conciliazione, the Street of Reconciliation. It was laid out in the twentieth century, after the Holy See and the Kingdom of Italy signed the Lateran Treaty in 1929 and ended a long-running feud. For the sake of a straight avenue a whole old quarter was demolished that used to stand between the Tiber and the square. In the past people approached the basilica through narrow lanes and the square opened up suddenly, and now you can see it from far away. Romans still argue about which was better. I would probably have chosen the lanes, but nobody asked me.

I liked the name. That same day, already in the basilica, I saw the tomb of a pope of whom it was said that the main thing in his life was that he furthered reconciliation with the Eastern Church. A street of reconciliation leads to the tomb of the apostle, and that is a good image. Only reconciliation, unlike an avenue, isn't laid out in a couple of years by knocking down everything that's in the way.

Along this street, from the square toward the Tiber, you can walk to Castel Sant'Angelo, where we ended our day.

photos/2026-10-31/19.description:
A wall completely hung with notes. Thousands of slips of paper and handkerchiefs, rolled up and tied in knots on cords, hang so densely that the wall itself can hardly be seen. Among the white, here and there, you can glimpse rosaries, little icons, photographs, a child's drawing, a red felt heart, a wooden heart with an inscription. On the right the gold of the church furnishings flashes, lamps are burning, and at the very edge of the frame an electronic terminal glows, apparently for donations. The twenty-first century doesn't doze in this place either. A hand in a black sleeve reaches toward the notes.

I looked at this wall for a long time. In every knot is someone's trouble: an illness, a child who still hasn't come, a job that hasn't been found, someone who has gone away. In all sorts of languages, including ones I don't know. And to be honest, this moves me more than any marble. The great basilicas were built by popes and kings, but walls like this are built by ordinary people, one slip of paper at a time.

In our Orthodox churches notes are handed in differently, at the candle desk, and then the names are read at the Liturgy and at a moleben. But the essence is the same: a person can't keep their trouble inside and gives it to God, sometimes literally, on paper. And the terminal next to it, I think, doesn't trouble the Lord. What matters more to Him is what is written on the slip of paper, not how the candle was paid for.

If I were asked what was the most alive thing in Rome that day, I would probably name not the marble but this wall.

photos/2026-10-31/20.alt: Sunset over the Tiber and Rome from Castel Sant'Angelo
photos/2026-10-31/20.description:
Evening, the upper terrace of Castel Sant'Angelo. The sun is setting right behind the hills, the sky shifting from yellow to peach, the clouds lit with pink. Below is the Tiber, with the bridge and the sky reflected in it, and along the embankment a continuous ribbon of people, all walking to the castle or away from it. On the right, above the rooftops, the dark silhouette of the dome of St Peter's. And in the foreground a construction site, barriers, machinery; around the castle they are digging something and landscaping. Rome is never quite finished, and that even suits it.

All day we were in a hurry, and only half the plan got done. And then you stand on this terrace, watch the sun set behind the basilica, and think: well, never mind, it's fine, for a sunset like this it was worth missing something.

The castle began as the mausoleum of the Emperor Hadrian, in the second century. Then it was turned into a fortress, then a prison, then a refuge and residence of the popes. And it got its name from a tradition of the late sixth century. Plague was raging in Rome, and Pope Gregory the Great was leading a procession through the city. Above the mausoleum the Archangel Michael appeared to him and sheathed his sword, and the plague stopped. Ever since, an angel with a sword has stood on the summit, and the castle is called the Castle of the Holy Angel.

I like that the main name of this building was given not by an emperor or a pope, but by a procession. People prayed, and this was remembered for a long time, longer than Hadrian himself.

photos/2026-10-31/21.alt: The dome of St Peter's in a loophole window of the castle, pigeons on the sill
photos/2026-10-31/21.description:
The thick wall of the castle, a narrow loophole window in it, and in the opening, like a painting in a frame, the dome of St Peter's against a yellow sunset sky. In front of it a modern building with rows of windows, lawns, cars, all ordinary, but through this ancient hole in the wall all the ordinariness falls into a composition. And on the sill, two pigeons. One stands looking at the basilica, the other is pecking at something right at its feet. They, of course, don't care at all about the dome; they have their own concerns.

The castle's walls are so thick that the sill in the loophole is more like a small room. Once guards and gunners looked out at the city from windows like this, because for centuries the castle was the main fortress of Rome, and in hard times it was here that the popes took refuge. Now tourists with phones look out of the loophole, and the pigeons hold the defense.

If you think about it, the result is a photograph not of the Vatican with pigeons in the background, but of pigeons with the Vatican in the background. And that, I think, is more honest.

There is something of the Gospel in it. A great basilica, the heart of Western Christianity, and in the foreground the fowls of the air, which sow not, neither do they reap, and the heavenly Father feeds them. And we spent the whole day running about, hurrying, worrying that we weren't making it in time. While they simply sat in the loophole and watched the sunset.

photos/2026-10-31/22.alt: The dome of St Peter's at sunset from the castle terrace
photos/2026-10-31/22.description:
The same dome, but now from the terrace and a little later, when the sky had turned completely orange. Shot from under a dark stone arch, which became a frame all by itself. Michelangelo's dome stands over the city calmly and confidently, as a dome should; around it roofs, houses, and all of it gently dissolving into a golden haze. In the foreground, other people's heads from behind: someone in glasses, someone with a phone, arms raised, filming the same view. All of Rome stands in the evening photographing one and the same sunset.

On the right you can see a long brick wall on arches. This is apparently the Passetto, a covered passage along the top of the city wall that connects the Vatican with the castle. It was built back in the Middle Ages so that the pope could quickly escape to the fortress in case of danger. The best-known occasion was in 1527, during the sack of Rome by the emperor's troops. Pope Clement VII fled along this passage to the castle while below, by the basilica, the Swiss Guards who were covering his retreat were dying. Since then, they say, recruits of the Swiss Guard take their oath on 6 May, in memory of that day.

During the day we were inside the basilica looking up from below, and in the evening we look at it from the side, from afar, and it seems even bigger. In the morning I wrote that you feel like a speck of fluff. From the castle terrace the feeling is the same, only calmer. The speck of fluff has sat a while, rested, and is watching the sunset.

photos/2026-10-31/23.alt: Two girls resting by the wall of Castel Sant'Angelo
photos/2026-10-31/23.description:
My girls have settled right down on the stone slabs at the foot of the wall of Castel Sant'Angelo. One is hugging her knees, squinting into the sun and smiling; the other has her nose in her phone. Bags beside them, tired feet in sneakers, and above them a tall, sun-bleached wall with white stone bands, a row of semicircular arches at the bottom and round openings ringed with white stone. Whether they were vents or loopholes for shooting, I never figured out, and I no longer had the strength to look for a sign.

By evening the day was taking its toll. We had been on our feet since morning: the square, the line, the basilica, the grottoes, the bookshop, lunch, walking again. In the basilica they don't let you sit down; the attendants are strict about it. Here, by the wall, nobody chases you off, and the girls sat down right where they stood. I understand them perfectly.

I like this photo precisely for its simplicity. The castle is almost nineteen centuries old. It was begun as the tomb of Emperor Hadrian, then it was faced, built up, fortified; people sat in it under siege and in captivity, and today two travelers from Orlando are resting at its foot, and the stone puts up with it indulgently. To it we are all like that, just passing through. It saw Hadrian, it saw the popes and their enemies, and it will see the ones who come next.

Afterwards there was the sunset over the basilica from the upper terrace, and it was worth it. But this shot, where they are just sitting, I love perhaps more than the sunset ones.

photos/2026-10-31/24.alt: The three of us at dinner in a Roman restaurant
photos/2026-10-31/24.description:
The end of a long day. The three of us are in a little restaurant, and the setting feels as if we had walked into the living room of an old Italian auntie. The walls are painted a deep emerald, copper pans and molds hang on the wall, heavy golden curtains with fringe and tassels over the window, armchairs in worn leather. On the table, a red crocheted tablecloth, a bottle of wine, glasses of red and a little jug of flowers. Outside the glass it is already night, car lights and a scooter by the door.

You can see in the photo that everyone is nearly out of strength. Each of us is holding a phone, and I can guess what's on them: the day's photos that urgently need to be sent to someone. The girls had been taking pictures all day, so there was plenty to look through. I'm no better.

At lunch we had Roman pasta, and I confess I wasn't thrilled: pasta is pasta, no better than at home in Orlando. But in the evening everything tastes better, because it's no longer about the food. You sit there, your feet buzzing, a glass of wine, your own people beside you, and there is plenty to remember. The colonnade, the tombs of the popes, the books in Slavonic, the sunset over the basilica. We managed only half of the day's plan, and, honestly, that's fine. The other half can wait; Rome isn't going anywhere.

The Lord, I think, arranged it very well that the day ends with supper. Even in the Gospel the most important conversations often take place at table. Ours were not so important, but for us they were the most needed. Tomorrow, ancient Rome.

photos/2026-11-01/1.alt: Apse mosaic of Santi Cosma e Damiano: Christ on the clouds
photos/2026-11-01/1.description:
The church of Santi Cosma e Damiano, the first Christian church on the Forum, was consecrated in 527. If you raise your head, you see three eras at once in one picture. At the very top is a gilded coffered ceiling, much later, with a papal coat of arms under the tiara and keys. Below, on the arch, is a mosaic on a subject from the Apocalypse: on the throne the Lamb, before Him the book sealed with seven seals, on either side seven candlesticks, angels and the winged symbols of the evangelists. And under the arch, in the blue half-dome of the apse, is Christ Himself. He comes down to us on clouds, fiery red and pink, in golden robes, with His right hand raised. On either side are the apostles Peter and Paul, leading the holy physicians Cosmas and Damian to Him. The apse and the arch date from the sixth and seventh centuries, yet the colors look as if they were laid on yesterday.

For me, an Orthodox priest, this image is utterly familiar. The throne with the book and the Lamb on the arch is very close to what we call the Hetoimasia, the prepared throne, the image of the Judgment to come. And Christ on the clouds is the Second Coming, only painted not menacingly but brightly. He comes not to judge but to meet us.

And the main thing: we got here on the first of November, and today is precisely the feast of the unmercenaries Cosmas and Damian. We hadn't planned it. We walked into the church, raised our heads, and there were the saints of the day greeting us. You can't arrange a coincidence like that, and all that's left is to quietly congratulate them in your own way.

photos/2026-11-01/2.description:
The Colosseum. An overcast Sunday morning, heavy clouds, and against them the ancient travertine looks gray and warm at the same time. Three tiers of arches, at the top a fourth level with small windows, the sky showing through the openings; in the sun it probably glows all golden, but that morning we got no sun. My girls are hugging at the edge of the road, posing, and around them ordinary Roman life: tourists with backpacks, a cyclist at the crossing, a woman in black with a phone.

We walked up to the Colosseum and understood right away that we wouldn't get inside today. The first Sunday of the month, free admission, and a line so long you couldn't see the end of it. Free admission is wonderful, but not for us. We decided to look at it from outside. It has stood here almost two thousand years; it can wait for us too.

Emperor Vespasian began building it, and his son Titus opened it in 80 with great games that went on for a hundred days. Officially it was called the Flavian Amphitheater, and the name Colosseum came later, most likely from the huge statue of Nero, the Colossus, that stood nearby.

For Christians this place is special. Here, according to tradition, martyrs met their death, and in the eighteenth century a pope dedicated the amphitheater to their memory, and a cross was set up inside. To this day, on Good Friday, the pope leads the Way of the Cross here. The stones over which a crowd once roared now listen to prayer. That is perhaps the best thing that can be done with such a place.

photos/2026-11-01/3.alt: Icon of the Mother of God in Santa Francesca Romana
photos/2026-11-01/3.description:
Above the main altar of the church of Santa Francesca Romana, deep in the apse, stands an icon of the Mother of God with the Child. The doors of its shrine are thrown open like shutters, and in the half-light the gold background shines brightly. The Mother of God looks straight at us: large dark eyes, a crown on her head, a necklace. The Child in a red chiton nestles against His Mother. Before the icon is a gilded tabernacle that looks like a little church with a small dome, tall candles in golden candlesticks, and fresh flowers below.

The icon is from the twelfth century. Our iconographers would call its type “Sweet Kissing,” in Greek “Glykophilousa,” when the Child caresses His Mother. And the most amazing thing is that during restoration another one was found underneath it, much older, painted in wax colors in the fifth or sixth century. One icon beneath another, like layers of one and the same prayer that has been repeated for fifteen hundred years now.

As a priest I love things like this. We are used to saying that an icon is a window into eternity, and here it is literally a window with shutters. And when they are opened, you are looked at by eyes that have seen all the Romans from the Middle Ages to our Sunday.

The church is named after St Frances of Rome. She lived in the fifteenth century, was a wife and mother, served the poor all her life and, according to tradition, always saw her guardian angel beside her, who gave her light in the dark. For this, in the twentieth century, she was declared the patron saint of motorists. For us, with our car and Roman parking, such a patron certainly won't hurt.

photos/2026-11-01/4.alt: Golden apse mosaic with the Mother of God and saints
photos/2026-11-01/4.description:
The apse of Santa Francesca Romana as a whole. A golden twelfth-century mosaic: in the center, on a throne, the Mother of God as Queen with the Child on her knees; on either side, under little arches, stand apostles, two on the left and two on the right, each holding a book or a scroll. Above them is a blue dome scattered with small figures, and at the very top the Chi-Rho, the monogram of Christ. Below the mosaic you can see the altar area, and at the very bottom of the frame, in the open shrine, glows that same ancient icon of the Mother of God that I later photographed separately. At the sides of the apse are frescoes with little angels, marble columns and pilasters.

I liked the inscription above the arch. If you read it closely, it says in Latin that in 1953, under Pope Pius XII, this new ceiling was made at the expense of the Italian Republic. The Republic, long since secular, pays for a ceiling in an ancient church and honestly writes so on the wall. Perhaps in our parish, too, we should sign every repair like that, so that our descendants know whom to thank.

This church stands on the ruins of the Temple of Venus and Roma, which was designed by Emperor Hadrian himself. Above the ruins of a pagan sanctuary of the goddess of love and the goddess who protected the city, the Queen of Heaven now sits enthroned, and in my opinion Rome has only gained from the exchange. There was almost no one inside; Mass was being celebrated for the feast, and we stood at it for a little while. For me it was a quiet island in the middle of the noisy Forum. The mosaic is nearly nine centuries old, and it still looks calmly at those passing by.

photos/2026-11-01/5.alt: Mass on the feast of All Saints
photos/2026-11-01/5.description:
The Catholic feast of All Saints, the first of November, Mass at Santa Francesca Romana. Hardly anyone there, just us and a few other people. At the altar, covered in white lace, a priest in light vestments reads from a book lying on a red stand. On the right a second monk in white has stretched his hand over the altar. On the left, kneeling, is a young monk with a censer. All three are in white; the monks here, Olivetan Benedictines, wear white habits. Behind the altar is a marble angel, on the wall a large painting in a gold frame, candles are burning, and on the left stands a tall silver processional cross. On the floor is a red and gold carpet.

We didn't go to the Liturgy this time. We hadn't prepared, hadn't brought anything for a service with us, hadn't let anyone know in advance. The priest is on vacation; that happens too. So standing for a little while at someone else's service was a quiet comfort.

As an Orthodox, I found it interesting to watch the small things. The censer, the lace on the altar, the candles, the kneeling at an important moment of the service. Much is familiar, much is different. And a great deal of silence: a small church, a few people, no pomp, just people praying on a feast day.

We Orthodox celebrate All Saints in our own way, on the first Sunday after Pentecost. And here I found myself at the feast at the beginning of November, in a Roman church where everything speaks of the holiness of ordinary life: Frances of Rome was a wife, a mother, and served the poor. Perhaps that is the best sermon for All Saints' Day, when holiness is close by, in the house next door.

photos/2026-11-01/6.alt: Sixth-century mosaic: apostles and the holy physicians, lambs below
photos/2026-11-01/6.description:
A fragment of the apse of Santi Cosma e Damiano, close up. On the left stands a pope holding a model of the church, above him the inscription SANC FELIX PAPA: this is Pope Felix IV, who set up the church here in the sixth century. Next to him walks one of the holy physicians holding a martyr's crown, and behind him, in a white himation, the apostle who is leading him to Christ. The background is dark blue, and at the top hangs a palm branch with orange fruit. And at the bottom is a golden band, and along it walk lambs, one after another, white, curly, quite alive. In the center of this band, outside the frame, stands the Lamb, and the twelve sheep on either side are the apostles, coming out of Bethlehem and Jerusalem.

Under the lambs you can see part of a Latin inscription that runs around the whole apse. It begins with words saying that the house of God shines with the beautiful brilliance of metals, and the light of faith shines in it more precious still. The mosaicist, it seems, understood well that his gold was only the setting.

I was especially touched by Pope Felix. He holds the model of the church in his hands like a gift and carries it to Christ. That is how ktitors, the builders of churches, were depicted in ancient times, and in our frescoes it's the same: a prince holds a little church. You bring to God what you have built, although in fact it was He who gave you all of it.

The church, by the way, is set up right in a hall of the ancient Temple of Peace, on whose wall there once hung a huge marble plan of Rome. The Romans in general knew how to build so that their buildings could later become churches.

photos/2026-11-01/7.alt: Ruins of the Temple of Peace with fallen columns
photos/2026-11-01/7.description:
A hollow, fenced off with railings, and in it columns scattered over the grass. Not standing but lying in pieces, drum after drum, on concrete supports, as if someone had laid them out to dry. You can see the stone is pinkish, gray in places, chipped here and there. On the left, brickwork rises in steps, a concrete entrance to some service tunnel with a fire extinguisher inside, and along the railing above, people crowd. Behind them, ordinary Roman houses with tiled roofs, trees and an overcast sky.

These are the excavations of the Temple of Peace, which Emperor Vespasian built after the Jewish War. The columns were of pink granite brought from Egypt, from near Aswan. A few columns here have already been set back up, and the rest are lying for now. The temple itself was not so much a temple as a huge garden-museum: long porticoes, flower beds, pools of water, and famous works of art were kept in its halls.

And the main thing for us Christians. Here, according to Josephus, the treasures from the destroyed Temple in Jerusalem were brought: the golden seven-branched candlestick and the table of shewbread. They were carried through Rome in the triumph and depicted on the Arch of Titus. Where they went afterwards, no one knows for certain.

You stand at this railing and think. The emperor called his building the Temple of Peace and stored the trophies of war in it. Almost five hundred years later, in one of its halls, a church was set up for the holy unmercenaries, who healed for free. Peace did come to this place after all, only not at all the kind Vespasian had in mind.

photos/2026-11-01/8.alt: Artistic reconstruction of the Temple of Peace
photos/2026-11-01/8.description:
This is not a photograph but an artistic reconstruction of how Vespasian's Temple of Peace might have looked in its best days. The details are approximate; it was made from archaeologists' descriptions, and I added it so that the stones lying today in the grass behind the railing would have something to be compared with. Long porticoes of pink granite columns, a garden between them: channels of water, fountains, flower beds with roses and cypresses, bronze statues on pedestals. At the back, the main hall with a pediment, and behind it, above the roofs, you can see the Colosseum. Romans in togas stroll along the paths, talking and looking at the statues.

That, apparently, is how it was: not a temple in our sense, but a huge square-garden where you could hide from the heat, sit by the water, and look at the famous sculptures that Vespasian gathered from all over the empire. Pliny the Elder, a contemporary, considered this place one of the most beautiful in the world. There was also a library here, and later a huge marble plan of Rome, carved on slabs, was hung on one of the walls.

Compare this with the columns we saw in the grass, drum after drum. For me, pictures like this are needed so that my head can keep up with my feet. You walk around the Forum, and it's all made of ruins, and it's very hard to imagine that all this was once a living city with fountains and flowers.

Here I am reminded of the Apocalypse, where the Heavenly Jerusalem is described as a garden-city, with the river of life and a tree in the midst of it. The Romans, without knowing it, also dreamed of a garden.

photos/2026-11-01/9.alt: The Roman Forum from the terrace
photos/2026-11-01/9.description:
The Roman Forum from above. In the foreground, a chaos of stones: fragments of columns, pieces of marble floor, railings, walkways for archaeologists, grass in the cracks. Further on, a green open space with remains of pedestals and lone columns scattered across it. On the horizon, umbrella pines and cypresses, the Palatine Hill with brick ruins, bell towers and domes of later churches. On the left a single column sticks up on a white base. On the right is a tall brick building with plain walls and a window at the top. The sky is overcast, but the clouds are already starting to part.

This tall brick building is the Curia, where the Roman Senate met. It survived almost whole, though everything around it was destroyed, and it survived only because in the seventh century it was turned into a church. As long as the building was a church, it wasn't taken apart for stone. Later, in the twentieth century, the church was removed and the Curia was given back its ancient look.

I looked at this for a long time. It turns out that of everything that stood on the Forum, what has survived best is what once became a church. Pagan temples, basilicas, arches — all were taken apart, burned for lime, hauled off for new buildings. But what was consecrated still stands. The Pantheon, the Curia, the Temple of Peace, where Cosmas and Damian are now. So the Church, without planning it, turned out to be the chief keeper of ancient Rome.

From up high the Forum seems small. A few hundred paces long, and yet here the fate of the whole world of that time was once decided. Senators, consuls, emperors. Their voices fell silent long ago, and we, visitors from Orlando, walk among the stones and try to read what is written on them.

photos/2026-11-01/10.description:
Trajan's Markets in the midday sun. A huge semicircle of red brick rising in tiers up the slope of the hill. At the bottom a row of arches, each of which once held a shop, above that another floor with small windows, and above them medieval and later houses built right on top. Over all of this rises a tall brick tower, the Torre delle Milizie, built in the Middle Ages. In the foreground, the lumpy remains of the forum's walls, grass, a few columns. The sky is clear and bright blue; after the overcast morning it's as if someone had changed the scenery.

The complex was built at the beginning of the second century, under Emperor Trajan, and it is usually attributed to the same architect, Apollodorus of Damascus, who also built the Forum of Trajan itself. The very Apollodorus who, according to tradition, was later executed by Hadrian for mocking his design for the Temple of Venus and Roma. In the morning we had walked past the columns of that temple, and in the afternoon we came to the best work of its critic. That's history for you: first you laugh at an emperor, then you are executed, and nineteen centuries later your building is still standing, while no more is left of the emperor's temple.

This was something like a shopping center: more than a hundred rooms on several levels, shops, offices, storerooms. Inside you can still see the travertine door frames. You can walk along the corridors and imagine how oil, wine and cloth were traded here.

By this time the weather had cleared. The overcast morning at the Colosseum seemed to have made way on purpose for this shot.

photos/2026-11-01/11.alt: Colossal female head from the Forum of Trajan, thought to be Trajan's mother
photos/2026-11-01/11.description:
A huge marble head stands on a black cube by a brick wall. A woman's face, calm, turned slightly to one side; above the forehead, rows of tight ringlet curls that look like snails; behind the ears, long locks fall onto the neck. The eyes are smooth, without pupils: in those days they were most likely painted in. Behind it is a large window, and in it an old brick wall with a bricked-up little window. These are the halls of Trajan's Markets, where the Museum of the Imperial Forums is now.

I read the label on the pedestal carefully later, from the photo. The head was found on the Forum of Trajan and made around 112 from Carrara marble. The hairstyle is in the manner of Agrippina the Younger, Nero's mother, but for Trajan such a figure would have been odd. So it is thought that this is the mother of Trajan himself. Almost nothing is known about her, not even her name. Only because her daughter was called Marciana is it supposed that the mother was called Marcia. At the back of the neck there is a large hollow: a pin went into it, by which the colossal statue, almost five meters tall, was fixed to the wall.

That's fate for you. The son is one of the most famous emperors of Rome, his column still stands, and of the mother there remains a head in a museum and a guess at her name. Five meters of marble, and no name.

At that moment I remembered how we in the Church commemorate the departed. Not with statues, but by name, at every Liturgy, in the notes handed in at the candle desk. “Memory eternal” is not about marble, after all. Marble, as we see, did not keep the name. But prayer keeps the names even of those whom no one on earth remembers anymore.

photos/2026-11-01/12.alt: The Roman street Via Biberatica in Trajan's Markets
photos/2026-11-01/12.description:
A real Roman street. Not a reconstruction, not a museum path, but the very pavement people walked on almost nineteen centuries ago. Large dark slabs of volcanic stone, polished smooth by thousands of feet, uneven, slightly convex, with grass pushing through between them. The street climbs uphill and runs off into the distance. On the left and right are tall brick walls with doorways in white travertine frames. These were shops. Above are windows where the merchants probably lived or kept their goods. The sky above the street is bright blue, the sun strikes from the side, and every stone casts its own shadow.

The street is called the Via Biberatica. The name is late, medieval, and no one really knows where it comes from. Some say it's from the Latin for “to drink,” because there were taverns here selling wine; others say it's from “pepper,” which was also sold here. I prefer the version with the taverns. It's somehow human: a great emperor builds a forum with a column reaching to the sky, and next to it ordinary people drink wine and talk about prices.

We walked along it slowly. Your feet can tell this isn't asphalt: every stone has its own shape, you step carefully, especially in sneakers. I thought that perhaps some of the first Roman Christians walked on these stones. The apostle Paul wrote to the Romans when these markets didn't exist yet, but half a century later their grandchildren were coming here to shop. And among them, surely, there were those who secretly gathered for prayer in houses.

photos/2026-11-01/13.description:
A long vaulted corridor inside Trajan's Markets. On the left, arched windows with the sun streaming through; on the right, a brick wall with doorways in travertine frames, former shops or offices. The light falls on the walls in slanting golden stripes, and the floor, worn down, uneven, polished in places, looks sandy. The vault overhead is massive, concrete, like in a bunker. Deep in the corridor walk two of our companions, one with fiery red hair, the other fair-haired, in dark coats. Behind them a few more visitors, and at the edge of the frame, on the left, a bit of someone's dark sleeve.

I like this shot better than many postcard ones. It has scale: such high vaults, such long corridors, and such small people. And most of all, it has light. The morning was gloomy, but by midday the sun had broken through, and in this corridor it put on a real show.

The Romans knew how to build with concrete in a way we hardly know how to anymore. Their concrete with volcanic ash has stood for almost two millennia, while modern concrete often starts to crumble after a few decades. Scientists are still studying what the secret is. And this whole corridor is, in essence, an ordinary shopping arcade. Shoppers, clerks, porters with baskets walked here. Nothing heroic, just the everyday life of an empire.

In places like this I always think that the most durable things on earth are not palaces but what is needed for simple life: roads, markets, aqueducts. And of the grand designs, the ones that usually stand are those dedicated to God.

photos/2026-11-01/14.description:
The ruins of the Imperial Forums toward evening. In the foreground, a heap of marble fragments: cornices, pieces of friezes, slabs, stacked by archaeologists like firewood. On the right, a green open space with capitals and pedestals scattered across it, and next to it the remains of an ancient pavement. Further on rises Trajan's Column, with a small figure at its top. Behind the column is the dome of a church, on the left the white Vittoriano building with Italian flags, and a row of umbrella pines against the sky. On the right is a big orange house with green shutters, where people live right above the ruins. The clouds are white, cumulus, the sky is blue, the sun already low and warm.

Trajan's Column has stood since 113. A relief band winds around it in a spiral, telling in scenes of Trajan's war with the Dacians, in what is now Romania. Inside is a spiral staircase, and in the base, it is said, the urn with the ashes of the emperor himself was once kept. Originally Trajan stood at the top, and at the end of the sixteenth century Pope Sixtus V placed a statue of the apostle Peter there. The emperor would probably have been surprised.

I really like this change. The column is dedicated to victory, blood, conquest. And now at the top is a fisherman from Galilee, who denied thrice and was forgiven. Not a Roman soldier, but a simple man whom Christ made the rock of the Church.

At the end of the day we went up the Vittoriano, which you can see here on the left, and there, at the top, we decided where to go next. But more on that in the following chapters.

photos/2026-11-01/15.alt: Steps of a Roman church with a turquoise door
photos/2026-11-01/15.description:
The entrance to one of the churches by the Imperial Forums. Wide travertine steps, huge columns and a tall door painted a rich turquoise. On a step right by the door sits one of ours, fair-haired, in black. Other passers-by are resting on the steps nearby; on the right sits a man in a green cap. In front of the stairs stands a young olive tree in a terracotta pot. On the left, around the corner, you can see another church, with a dome and a lantern, against a cloudy sky.

Above the door is a carved Latin inscription, which I didn't read right away. It speaks of a plenary indulgence, daily and perpetual, for the living and the dead. For Catholics this is an important concept; for us Orthodox it is foreign. But here is what's interesting: “pro vivis et defunctis,” for the living and for the departed. And this on the first day of November, on the eve of the second, when Catholics remember all the faithful departed. In these days the whole city thinks a little about those who have gone.

We have the memorial Saturdays, they have All Souls' Day. Different calendars, different theological concepts, but the prayer is one: Lord, grant rest. In this sense we and the Catholics are much closer than it seems when you read the disputes of theologians.

But the photograph is really about something else. The day was long; we had walked half of Rome on foot. The door may be closed, but the step at the threshold of a church is always open. You can sit down and rest for a while, and, unlike at St Peter's Basilica, no one chases you off here. The olive in the pot is a good sign too: peace, and eternal rest, and simply a breather.

photos/2026-11-01/16.alt: Artistic reconstruction of the Forum of Trajan
photos/2026-11-01/16.description:
Another artistic reconstruction, one of those I added to this day so that my head could keep up with my feet. The details are approximate; it is a picture-guess based on archaeologists' descriptions, not an exact drawing. This is how the Forum of Trajan might have looked at the beginning of the second century. A huge square paved with white marble, with an equestrian statue of the emperor on a tall pedestal. Further on, the colonnade of a large building with gilded statues on the roof: this is the Basilica Ulpia. Behind it rises the column, the very one that still stands today, with a golden figure at its top. On the right, porticoes, a legionary with a spear, and in the distance on the hill the brick tiers of the markets. And everywhere people in white togas, some with a red stripe: that is how magistrates dressed.

In the afternoon we saw all this in real life, only without the marble and without the people. The column is still there, the markets are still there, and of the square there remain fragments of columns and slabs in the grass.

The forum was built with the spoils of the Dacian wars, and it was the last and largest of the Imperial Forums. Over two hundred years later, in 357, Emperor Constantius II came to Rome for the first time. The historian Ammianus Marcellinus writes that on the Forum of Trajan he was struck dumb with amazement and said that the only thing he could reproduce was Trajan's horse. And the Persian prince Hormisdas, standing nearby, replied: “First, sire, build a stable like this.” And, according to the same Ammianus, Hormisdas also said that the only thing he liked about Rome was that here, too, people die.

Bitter wisdom, but accurate. All that golden splendor has passed, and people have remained the same. The glory of the world passes. The column, it's true, still stands, only it is no longer the emperor at the top.

photos/2026-11-02/1.alt: Mosaic dome in the crypt of Montecassino
photos/2026-11-02/1.description: To take this shot I had to crane my neck until it cracked, but it was worth it. This is the ceiling of the crypt of Montecassino, right above the place where the relics of St Benedict and his sister Scholastica lie. All this turquoise, gold and checkered border around the edge is mosaic, as fine as beadwork. In the center is a blue cross in a red circle, on either side four angelic faces with wings, and a Latin inscription runs around the ring. You have to read it letter by letter, slowly turning around on the spot like a compass needle: “Fratres, si mortui sumus cum Christo, credimus quia simul etiam vivemus cum Christo.” This is the Epistle to the Romans, chapter six: “If we be dead with Christ, we believe that we shall also live with him.” Only the word “brethren” has been added at the beginning — and it comes out as if the abbot were addressing his monks. For a crypt where saints await the resurrection, you couldn't think of better words. I never fully deciphered the letters around the cross — the Benedictines have their own system of monograms, and you can't make it out here without a local monk. The crypt was painted at the beginning of the twentieth century by artists of the Beuron school. Beuron is a Benedictine abbey in Germany, and its masters have a very recognizable style: strict geometry, flat figures, an almost Egyptian solemnity. Upstairs, in the basilica, everything is Baroque, golden and noisy, but here, below, it is quiet and austere. The monastery has lain in ruins four times, and the inscription on the ceiling says exactly the same thing as its motto: what is cut down grows green again, what has died with Christ will come to life.

photos/2026-11-02/2.alt: Statue of St Cecilia in a niche of the crypt, Catacombs of Callixtus
photos/2026-11-02/2.description: In a dim niche of old Roman brick lies a marble girl. She lies on her side, knees slightly bent, arms stretched forward, her head wrapped in a veil, and her face turned toward the floor, so that it can't be seen at all. On either side two little lamps hang on chains, beneath her is a floor of multicolored marble fragments, and the light falls so that the statue is the only bright spot in the whole underground. This pose can't be mistaken for anything else: this is how, in 1600, the Roman sculptor Stefano Maderno carved St Cecilia. The story goes like this. In 1599 in Rome her tomb was opened in the church of Santa Cecilia in Trastevere and, according to tradition, her body was found incorrupt, lying exactly like this. Maderno, they say, saw it with his own eyes and carved her just as he saw her, even with the mark of the sword on her neck. According to her Life, the executioner struck three times and could not cut off her head, and she lived for three more days. The original is in Trastevere, and this copy is in the Catacombs of St Callixtus, in the very crypt where the martyr was once buried, until in the ninth century her relics were moved into the city. She is in our calendar too: the martyr Cecilia, commemorated on November 22. In the West she is considered the patron saint of church music, because her Life says that on her wedding day, while the instruments were playing, she sang to God in her heart. So, choir directors and singers, this is your saint. And here is what's remarkable: the sculptor never showed her face, and this silence makes it clearer what martyrdom is than many words do.

photos/2026-11-02/3.alt: Ancient fresco with the face of Christ
photos/2026-11-02/3.description: The plaster has fallen off in chunks, the paint has faded, the brick is showing through, but the gaze has remained. This is an ancient fresco from the same Roman underground as the marble Cecilia. Christ in a golden halo with a cross, His right hand blessing, in His left the Gospel in a jeweled cover. Next to Him, in a separate frame, another saint with a halo, his face almost worn away, and below, a very small figure that can't be made out at all. I couldn't read the inscriptions, so I won't guess at names. But to an Orthodox eye everything here is familiar. This is the Pantocrator, after all, the same image that we have in the dome of a church and on the iconostasis to the right of the Royal Doors. Large eyes, a straight, severe nose, a blessing hand, a book in a cover — that is how they painted both in the East and in the West, when the Church was still one. Paintings like this appeared in the Roman catacombs after the persecutions, when the underground cemeteries became places of pilgrimage to the tombs of the martyrs: the Roman bishops decorated the crypts, and pilgrims came here from all over the Christian world. I don't know the exact date of this fresco and won't make one up; let it simply be “very long ago.” The main thing is something else. For centuries people stood before this face who had come to venerate the martyrs, and they prayed with the same words as we do. This is not a museum exhibit; it is an icon, only without a shrine and a lamp. The face of Christ has outlived damp, and cave-ins, and crowds of tourists with phones — including me.

photos/2026-11-02/4.alt: The Basilica of San Sebastiano on the Appian Way
photos/2026-11-02/4.description: A white facade with no particular frills: three arches of a portico on paired columns, a triangular pediment with a coat of arms, and a cross at the very top. In front of the church is a cobbled square, old brick walls on the sides, a cypress, and over it all a gray November sky. If you squint, above the portico you can read a Latin inscription with the name of Cardinal Scipione Borghese and a date in Roman numerals — 1612. It was he, the nephew of Pope Paul V, who rebuilt the ancient basilica into the form we see today. But the Basilica of San Sebastiano itself is much older; it has stood on the Appian Way since the fourth century, right above the catacombs. At first it was called the Basilica of the Apostles: according to tradition, during the persecutions the relics of the apostles Peter and Paul were kept here for a time, and ancient inscriptions by pilgrims calling on them are still found in the underground. Later the church came to bear the name of the martyr Sebastian. He was a Roman soldier who openly confessed the faith under Diocletian; he was shot with arrows, survived, and then he was beaten to death. We commemorate him on December 18. And one more detail for which this church is worth remembering: it is here that the original of the stone with the footprints is kept, a copy of which we saw in the little church of Domine Quo Vadis. Both churches stand on the same ancient road, quite close to each other. San Sebastiano is one of the seven pilgrim churches of Rome, which pilgrims for centuries walked around on foot in a single day. We sinners made do with the car.

photos/2026-11-02/5.alt: A town on a mountainside on the way to Monte Cassino
photos/2026-11-02/5.description: This was taken on the move, from the car window, so everything in the foreground is blurred: bushes, wires, some reddish grass. But further off, on a green hill, sits a little town. Yellow and pink houses, tiled roofs, a bell tower, a couple of dark cypresses at the edge, and behind the town a bare grey mountain with clouds on its top. I never did find out its name, and I won't guess. There are dozens of towns like this on the road south from Rome, and each one seems to have climbed as high as it could on purpose. It isn't for the sake of beauty. For centuries armies, bandits and marsh fever passed through the valleys below, while up above it was both drier and safer, and the bell could be heard throughout the whole area. This is already southern Lazio, the land the Italians call Ciociaria. In '43 and '44 the front ran through here: the Germans held a defensive line across Italy, and its center was precisely the mountain of Monte Cassino, where we were heading. Many towns in these parts suffered badly then and took a long time to rebuild. At that moment, I confess, my head was occupied not with the scenery but with how I was going to explain to the attendant at the motorway exit why I had no ticket. I had prepared the Italian phrase for the occasion in advance, and I kept turning it over in my mind like a schoolboy going over a poem before class. And the town looked down on us calmly and, I think, a little condescendingly. It is nothing new for it to watch strangers drive past with their own worries.

photos/2026-11-02/6.alt: The high altar of the basilica of Monte Cassino
photos/2026-11-02/6.description: Marble of every color there is, gilding, angels beneath the vaults, a painted dome overhead, and in front a staircase to the high altar, closed off with a rope. This is the basilica of the abbey of Monte Cassino. Beneath the altar, below in the crypt, rest St Benedict and his sister Scholastica, so this whole shining church is, in essence, a huge reliquary over their tomb. Behind the altar you can see organ pipes, on the altar tall candles, and on either side columns faced with patterned marble inlays. You stand with your head tilted back, and it is hard to believe that all this is not the 17th or 18th century but postwar work. In February 1944 American bombers razed the monastery to the ground; only rubble remained. After the war it was rebuilt from old drawings and photographs, on the principle of “where it was and as it was.” Craftsmen reassembled the marble inlays and repainted the vaults, and in 1964 Pope Paul VI consecrated the new basilica and at the same time proclaimed St Benedict patron of Europe. As an Orthodox priest I usually feel a little cramped in this kind of Baroque — the eye has nowhere to rest. But here you think about something else. The monks could have left the ruins as a monument to the war, and that would have been understandable. Instead they built the church again, so that services would be held in it again. That is their motto “Succisa virescit” in action: what is cut down grows green again. And outside that day it rained without stopping.

photos/2026-11-02/7.alt: The head of a statue in the abbey museum
photos/2026-11-02/7.description: Under glass, on dark blue velvet, lies a face. White, of ivory, with huge eyes in which mother-of-pearl gleams, with finely drawn lashes and brows, in a silver veil that falls like a fan over the shoulders. Beside it, separately, hands folded in prayer. The label in the abbey museum explains: work of the Beuron school, 1900–1913, the face and hands of St Scholastica, the remains of a statue that stood in the crypt, bombed on 15 February 1944. Ivory, silver, mother-of-pearl and amber. That is all that is left of a whole statue. Looking at it is a little unsettling: as if the saint had been pulled out from under the rubble. The cracks on her cheek and fingers show what she has been through. Scholastica was Benedict's own sister, by tradition even his twin, and she herself headed a community of women nearby. St Gregory the Great tells a touching story about them. Brother and sister saw each other once a year, and at their last meeting Scholastica asked Benedict to stay and talk with her all night about the Kingdom of Heaven. He refused — the Rule does not allow spending the night outside the monastery. Then she bowed her head and prayed, and at once such a storm broke that it became impossible to leave. Three days later she died, and Benedict saw her soul rising to heaven as a dove. On the day of our visit, by the way, it was raining over Monte Cassino too. Not a storm, of course, but I thought that Scholastica, it seems, still knows how to get her way.

photos/2026-11-02/8.alt: The cloister of the abbey of Monte Cassino in the rain
photos/2026-11-02/8.description: Wet stone paving, arched galleries with balustrades, a well under a small arch in the middle of the courtyard, two statues on pedestals on either side, and beyond the far arches, instead of a wall, emptiness: the valley and the mountains in haze. The sky is grey and low, and two people are trudging across the courtyard under a yellow umbrella. That yellow umbrella, it seems, was the only bright spot on the whole mountain that day. Monte Cassino stands on a summit almost half a kilometer above the valley, and the monastery courtyard is laid out so that, as from a balcony, you can see the whole surrounding country. I didn't make out the statues at first: the one on the right holds a pastoral staff, so it is an abbot, and most likely Benedict himself — in his monastery it is hard to imagine any other master. Benedict came here around 529, when the remains of a pagan sanctuary still stood on the mountain, and founded the community that became the mother of Western monasticism. Here he wrote his Rule, whose essence later came to be expressed in two words: “pray and work.” Everything we see in this shot is new, built after 1944, but built so carefully that without being told you would never guess. If you go further on, from the monastery wall you can see the Polish cemetery on the neighboring hill: in May '44 it was the Poles who took this mountain, and many of them stayed there. It rained without stopping that day. To a monastery that has survived four destructions, rain is of course no obstacle. But we had to cross the courtyard in short dashes, from arch to arch.

photos/2026-11-02/9.alt: A cook preparing dough in a Neapolitan snack bar
photos/2026-11-02/9.description: Our first evening in Naples. Behind the window glass of a small snack bar, rows of golden pieces of dough lie on trays, and a young man in a black T-shirt is going over them with a sprayer that looks very much like a painter's spray gun. What exactly he had filled it with — oil, syrup or egg wash — I never figured out. But he did it with such pleasure, as if he were painting not buns but the Sistine Chapel. And he was grinning from ear to ear the whole time. Behind him is a wall of colorful tiles, cans of tomatoes on a shelf, a huge orange bottle next to them, and on the lower shelves of the counter, trays of something already cooked. This is how Naples wins you over. A moment ago you were cursing everything on earth behind the wheel in the narrow streets, looking for somewhere to squeeze the car in, and thinking you would never come back here. And then you go out on foot, see a fellow like this with his sprayer, and the irritation somehow goes away. Neapolitan street food is a culture of its own. Here they fry and bake right in front of passers-by, and eating something on the go, wrapped in paper, is a perfectly normal supper. It was the same a hundred and two hundred years ago, when poor families in the cramped quarters simply had no kitchen, and the city fed itself on the street. Pizza, incidentally, comes from here too, from this street poverty. I watched him and thought: here is a man in his right place, doing his work with joy. That, I think, is already a little sermon on labor, and without a single word.

photos/2026-11-02/10.alt: The window of a Neapolitan pastry shop in the evening
photos/2026-11-02/10.description: A pastry shop window in the evening, and here I realized that Neapolitans don't know how to do anything by halves. The walls are faced with maiolica in blue and yellow patterns, under the ceiling there is a crystal chandelier and a whole garden of flowers and leaves, and behind the counter, right up to the top, shelves of liqueur bottles. And in the glass display case, pastries are arranged in tiers: orange balls, flaky shells, little tartlets, some sort of cream domes. In the corner stand funny little gnome figures in blue and red caps, and next to them a blackboard with something written in chalk. Right beside all this splendor, literally half a meter away, an ordinary Neapolitan wall begins: peeling, grey, marked by time. All of Naples in one shot. The flaky shells, if I identified them correctly, are sfogliatella, the chief Neapolitan sweet. Its dough is folded in the thinnest layers, and after baking it crunches like autumn leaves, while inside there is a soft filling of ricotta with candied fruit. According to tradition, it was invented by nuns in a convent on the Amalfi Coast, and only later did the recipe reach the city. In general, a great many European sweets were born behind monastery walls: monks and nuns baked for feast days for centuries, and fast days forced them to be inventive. I'll honestly admit that you can easily stand at a window like this longer than at many a church. But after a day that began on the Appian Way and continued at Monte Cassino, that is forgivable, I think.

photos/2026-11-02/11.alt: Trattoria Da Nennella in the evening, a full room
photos/2026-11-02/11.description: This is the dining room of the trattoria “Da Nennella” at the height of the evening, and the noise, unfortunately, doesn't come across in the photo, which is a pity. The tables stand close together, all with red-and-white checked tablecloths, with bread, water bottles and paper menus on them. Waiters in red T-shirts rush between the tables, and from the ceiling hang huge copper discs with light bulbs that look like flying saucers. On the wall in the right corner there is some figure in a frame, and a painting next to it. At one table a customer is holding a small white dog in his arms, and nobody sees anything strange in that — this is Naples. I have already told about the queue outside and about the waiters dancing on the tables. Here I'll add something else. A trattoria is not a restaurant at all in our sense. It is a place where people eat simple home cooking, without pretensions, at long tables, and where you may be seated next to strangers. Neapolitan cuisine is at heart a poor one: pasta, beans, potatoes, tomatoes, cheese — what ordinary people had, but cooked so that people queue for it. Everything here is loud: orders are shouted across the whole room, everyone talks at once, and nobody tries to speak more quietly. At first it feels as if you have stumbled into a stranger's wedding. But half an hour later you already feel like an invited guest. In the Gospel the Lord often compares the Kingdom of Heaven to a feast to which everyone is called, from the streets and the crossroads. Looking at this room, I thought that the Neapolitans seem to have taken this parable literally, and there is something right in that.

photos/2026-11-03/1.alt: A maiolica bench in the cloister of Santa Chiara
photos/2026-11-03/1.description: Blue, yellow, orange and lots of sun. This is one of the maiolica benches in the cloister of the monastery of Santa Chiara. On its back, painted across the tiles, there is a whole little scene: country men in broad-brimmed hats, one sitting on the ground, another standing by a brick building, on the right a man aiming a gun, and in the middle, on a rock, a fortress tower with birds flying above it. The frame is Baroque scrolls and sea waves. In places the tiles are cracked, the paint has flaked off, and you can see where they were repaired. All the more touching. This cloister was rebuilt in the 1740s by the architect Domenico Antonio Vaccaro, and the tiles were painted by the Neapolitan maiolica masters Giuseppe and Donato Massa. Octagonal pillars, benches along the walks — everything is covered in maiolica: flowers, vines, scenes of country life, hunting, outings. And the most interesting thing: this was the courtyard of the Poor Clare nuns, a strict enclosed order. They did not go out into the world, so the world came to them by itself, painted on tiles. And the subjects on the benches are not biblical but everyday: peasants, hunters, travelers. I thought for a long time about why that is. Probably because the world you deny yourself for God's sake does not become bad because of it. You can leave it and still love it, and even keep it before your eyes as you sit on a bench with your prayer beads. Trees all around, people walking along the paths. It was warm and quiet, even though Spaccanapoli with its motor scooters is just a stone's throw away.

photos/2026-11-03/2.alt: A Neapolitan house with green shutters
photos/2026-11-03/2.description: A blue sky and a Neapolitan house at full height. Tall, four stories, pink walls, or rather once pink, and now streaked, stained and with peeling plaster. Dark green shutters, wrought-iron balconies on every window, with flowerpots and air conditioners on them. Below, an entrance arch, signs, an awning over a shop. I took it from up high, directly opposite, and the house came out as plain as day, as if it had posed on purpose. In Naples there are façades like this at every step, and at first they seem neglected. You want to take a bucket of paint and tidy things up. And then you realize that this is exactly the face of the city. Neapolitan palaces, palazzi, were built to last for centuries, with high ceilings and thick walls, and all sorts of people lived in them: shops and workshops below, wealthier families higher up on the “noble floor,” and under the roof whoever got what was left. The green shutters here are not for decoration. In summer the sun in Naples is such that without them you couldn't survive in the rooms, and yet air and light still come through the slats. That is why during the day the city often stands with its eyes closed and comes to life in the evening, when the windows and balconies open. I caught myself admiring a shabby house more than some palaces. Probably because people live in it, laundry dries on it, geraniums bloom, and someone comes out onto the balcony in the evening for a smoke. Beauty that is not ashamed of its cracks is, I think, a thoroughly Christian beauty.

photos/2026-11-03/3.alt: A narrow Naples street with a greengrocer's stall
photos/2026-11-03/3.description: A narrow street climbs upward, turning into steps at the very end, with a strip of sky between the balconies above it. Along the left side motor scooters stand in a row, by the butcher's shop there is a red refrigerated display case right on the sidewalk, and on the right a greengrocer's under a green awning. Crates of cabbage, broccoli, greens, peppers, and bunches of red hot peppers hanging under the awning. The pavement is old dark stone slabs, here and there yellow road markings, wires, air conditioners, laundry. This is the real Naples I was talking about: from a car window it seems like chaos, but on foot it begins to make sense. Everything here is on the street: trade, conversation, scooters, children. The shop is not behind a door but right on the pavement, and the seller doesn't wait for you inside but stands by the crates chatting with a neighbor. Naples is built on hills, and the streets that run up from the sea often end in steps — a car can't get through there, but a scooter, if it really wants to, will get through anywhere. Neapolitans, by the way, ride them in places where back home it would be scary even to walk. The red peppers under the awning are not only for cooking here. In Naples people love the little red horn-shaped amulets, and the pepper, by popular habit, is also considered a thing “against the evil eye.” Here, as a priest, I'll keep quiet, but I'll smile to myself. We walked streets like this all day and were in no hurry to get anywhere. It smells of frying, coffee, vegetables and a little of gasoline from the scooters. This, of course, isn't Rome. Rome is solemn, while here life is laid bare, with all its cracks.

photos/2026-11-03/4.alt: A fish stall at a Neapolitan market
photos/2026-11-03/4.description: A fish stall right on the street. On sloping white boards strewn with parsley, silvery fish lie in rows, then pink slices, squid, small fry on round trays, mussels and something I couldn't identify. Next to them plastic buckets, yellow crates, wet glistening pavement. At the back of the shop a sailing ship is painted on the wall, and a red life ring and an anchor hang there, as if you were not at a market but in a port. Across the street is a bakery with a sign and people at the entrance. A market in Naples is not a shop but a continuation of the street. Fish is sold here from morning until it runs out, and the pavement is hosed down with water to keep everything fresh. The sellers praise their goods loudly here, but more for form's sake than pushily. To be honest, I looked at these stalls and remembered the Gospel. After all, the first apostles — Peter, Andrew, James and John — were fishermen, and the Lord called them straight from their nets: “Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men.” The fish became one of the very first Christian symbols. In Greek, “fish” is “ichthys,” and the first Christians read this word as the initial letters of the phrase “Jesus Christ, Son of God, Savior.” Little fish like these were drawn on the walls of the Roman catacombs. And in Naples, a city by the sea, fish is simply daily life. It was probably like this in Capernaum too: noise, wet stones, the smell of the sea and people working with their hands from early morning.

photos/2026-11-03/5.description: By an old stone wall covered in graffiti, a little street studio has set up. On a black stand, samples are hung with clothespins — caricature portraits in pencil, with huge noses and grins from ear to ear. Above is a sign reading “Caricature” with prices, and to the side a small table with colored drawings. On a folding chair sits an artist in a brown jacket with a board on her knees, drawing something intently. Opposite her, on a little green stool, is a young woman with bright red hair in a light blue coat. Who was drawing whom, and whether they were drawing each other, was hard to tell from the outside: the redhead also has something like a tablet on her knees. Perhaps they are just two artists waiting for customers and passing the time. The sun was already sinking toward evening, the light was warm, and the scene practically begged to be photographed. Street artists are a long-standing tradition in Italy. Here, in every town with tourists, someone sits with a chair and an easel and in a few minutes turns a passer-by into a funny caricature. It is a special skill: to catch what is essential in a face and exaggerate it just a little, but so that the person isn't offended and laughs instead. In my opinion, that is a good skill for life in general, not only for drawing: to see what is essential in another person and treat him with a smile rather than with anger. We didn't order a caricature of ourselves. I'll admit that some features of my face don't need exaggerating anyway — they speak for themselves even without an artist.

photos/2026-11-03/6.alt: The tomb of judge Cesare Gallotti in San Domenico Maggiore
photos/2026-11-03/6.description:
A marble widow presses her cheek against her marble husband. Or rather, against his bust on a tall pedestal. She is in a long dress and veil, holding a wreath of flowers in her lowered hand, and her eyes are closed. He looks straight ahead, calmly, as if none of this concerns him anymore. On the pedestal, under the bust, there is a short inscription: “He looked upon death without fear, for the Giver of life was with him.” And below, on a large slab, a long text, and I made it out almost entirely.

The monument was erected to Cesare Gallotti, a Neapolitan judge. He was born in 1787 and died “serenely” in February 1860, and he was a director at the ministry of justice. His wife, Carolina Pulieri, is called “the inconsolable widow” on the slab. And then about him: he valued nobility of heart above nobility of birth, lived modestly, was an incorruptible judge, suffered for justice and triumphed, “was a martyr of labor” and an unrelenting defender of the law. At the bottom his three children signed. The monument itself, as I read later, was made by the sculptor Luigi Pasquarelli in 1870.

It stands in San Domenico Maggiore, and behind it, beyond a wrought-iron grille, is a chapel with colored walls and a Gothic window. On the wall to the right you can see pieces of much older tombs, with a relief of Christ in the tomb.

It is interesting that Gallotti died seven months before Garibaldi entered Naples, and soon the kingdom he had served ceased to exist. He did not have to see that.

What I liked most was that short inscription at the top. An incorruptible judge, a ministry, distinctions — all that is good. But the main thing about the man is said in one line: he was not afraid of death, because he was not alone.

photos/2026-11-03/7.alt: A marble altar with Dominican images in San Domenico Maggiore
photos/2026-11-03/7.description:
A side altar in San Domenico Maggiore, the great Dominican church of Naples. It is entirely of colored marble: pink, grey and beige slabs, with yellow panels set into them bearing delicate floral patterns in stone. Neapolitan craftsmen were famous for this work, stone fitted to stone so that it becomes almost painting. Above are white Baroque scrolls, and on the altar table a lace cloth. In the center is a painting: on the right a monk in the black-and-white Dominican habit sits in a chair, on the left a nun in the same habit stands with her hand on her breast. Exactly who is depicted I couldn't make out, and I won't guess.

On the other hand, two portraits with inscriptions hang on either side. On the left “B. Francesco de Posadas,” on the right “B. Colomba.” These are two Dominicans. Francisco de Posadas was a Spanish preacher from Córdoba who died at the beginning of the eighteenth century. Colomba of Rieti was a young Dominican tertiary who lived in the fifteenth century and is venerated in Perugia. The letter B before the name stands for Beatus, “blessed.”

Here, by the way, it is useful to know one subtlety. For Catholics, “blessed” is the step before canonization: the person has already been glorified, but for now for local veneration. Whereas with us the word “blessed” (blazhenny) more often refers to the fools for Christ, like St Basil the Blessed. One word, but a different meaning, and in conversation with Catholics it is easy to trip over this.

I liked that the Dominicans surrounded their altar with their own. Not the great and universally known, but their own, their dear ones, whom few people outside the order know about. In this very church, incidentally, Thomas Aquinas, their most famous brother, lived and taught. But on this wall there was room too for a humble preacher from Córdoba.

photos/2026-11-03/8.alt: A chapel with a marble altar
photos/2026-11-03/8.description: An empty chapel, not a single person, only marble, light from the windows under the dome, and a floor that deceives the eye. Slabs of grey, white and dark stone are laid so that the floor seems to be made of three-dimensional cubes, and you are afraid to step on it — what if you fall through? In the center is an altar of colored marble with inlay, above it in a niche a statue of the Mother of God in a light-colored robe, and on either side two more niches with statues of saints. Above, little angels sit on the cornices dangling their legs, and over it all, a cross. On the side walls are tall glass-fronted cabinets, with something glinting behind the glass. Which chapel exactly I photographed I can no longer say for certain from the picture: that day we visited San Domenico Maggiore and Santa Chiara, and by evening Neapolitan marble merges into one endless pattern. There are said to be several hundred churches in old Naples, and a large church may have a dozen chapels or more. Each was built by its own noble family or its own confraternity, each with its own coats of arms, tombs and saints, and then the families competed over whose was richer. Hence all this abundance. As an Orthodox priest, I always miss icons and lamps a little in chapels like these. But this silence, this emptiness and this light from above — those are missing in our noisy churches too. Sit on a bench for a couple of minutes, and the noise of Spaccanapoli, just a few steps away, seems to stay outside the door. Such minutes on a trip are worth more than any guided tour.

photos/2026-11-03/9.alt: A maiolica bench with a country scene
photos/2026-11-03/9.description:
Another bench from the cloister of Santa Chiara, and on this backrest there is a little story of its own. A peasant house under a tiled roof, steps leading up to the door, and in front of the house an arched footbridge over a stream. On the steps stands a man in a long brown robe with a staff, looking like a pilgrim or a monk, and in the window above him someone is looking out. Next to him a man in a hat carries a long pole on his shoulder, and another is busy with something at his feet. On the right is a gnarled tree with sparse leaves, with birds above it. All this in a frame of yellow scrolls and blue Baroque waves.

The tiles have put up with a lot over almost three centuries. In places the glaze has chipped off and the reddish clay shows through, cracks run right across the sky and through the tree, and here and there patches have been inserted. Sun, salt from the sea, thousands of visitors who sat down to rest. And yet the colors are alive; the blue and yellow glow as if the tiles had just come out of the kiln.

Maiolica is clay covered with a white tin glaze, on which paints are applied before it is fired again. The name, it is believed, comes from the island of Majorca, through which Spanish painted pottery was once shipped to Italy.

I don't know what exactly the artist intended in this scene. Perhaps simply a day in the country. But I keep seeing a pilgrim at a stranger's door, and it seems he is about to be let in. And for the nuns who once walked here along these benches, such a scene was very easy to understand. Hospitality in a monastery is almost a commandment. “I was a stranger, and ye took me in.” So if I am mistaken about the subject, I am mistaken, I think, in the right direction.

photos/2026-11-03/10.alt: A fresco in a gallery of the cloister of Santa Chiara
photos/2026-11-03/10.description:
A gallery wall in the cloister of Santa Chiara. Gothic windows behind close-set iron grilles, old grey stone between them, and frescoes on it. Here, in a frame, is a large scene: at the door of a pink little house with a red roof stands a woman in a lilac dress and white veil, her arms crossed on her breast. Before her is an old man with a long grey beard, in a light-colored hooded cloak, a staff in one hand and in the other something golden, resembling a book or a tablet. Behind them, trees, a meadow and two roe deer. Above this scene you can see the lower part of another fresco, with clouds and figures, and below, under the frame, a Baroque scroll painted as if it were molded in plaster.

The walls of this cloister's galleries, as far as I know, were painted in the seventeenth century: saints, allegories, scenes from the Old Testament. Much has faded and crumbled, in places the paint is hanging on by a thread, and still the figures are alive.

I found no caption for this scene. I would like to think it is the prophet Elijah and the widow of Zarephath: the prophet came to a poor woman during a famine and asked for bread, and she had only a last handful of flour left. She gave it, and the flour in the barrel did not run out until the end of the drought. In the West Elijah was often depicted just like this, as a grey-haired elder in a light monastic cloak. But I won't insist; it is only a guess.

If the guess is right, then it is a very apt choice for a convent of Poor Clares. Christ Himself recalled this widow in Nazareth: there were many widows in Israel, but the prophet was sent only to her, a foreigner. God comes to those who have a last handful left, and asks for exactly that. The nuns, who gave Him their whole lives, understood this story, I think, better than we do.

photos/2026-11-03/11.alt: A gold vestment in a museum
photos/2026-11-03/11.description: I couldn't walk past this display case. Behind the glass of a museum case, a vestment hangs on a stand: pale silk, entirely covered in gold embroidery. Flowers, leaves, scrolls, ribbons with bows, in the center of the back some kind of baskets or cornucopias with tassels, a gold border along the edges, and on the inside you can see a scarlet lining. Behind the case are the white walls of the museum hall, small windows and statues. Judging by the cut, it is most likely a Latin cope — a mantle-like cloak worn not for Mass but for processions, Vespers and solemn services of prayer. The Orthodox Church has no direct twin for it, but in spirit it is a relative of our phelonion. I myself have served in vestments for many years and know what gold embroidery is. It is not simply beautiful. Every such scroll is hours of work: thread of gilded metal is laid on the fabric and fastened with tiny stitches, centimeter by centimeter. A whole mantle means months, if not years, of painstaking work by needlewomen. And it weighs accordingly: you can't stand for long in such a vestment, your shoulders will remind you. The priest was meant to shine in it like an angel, and the point is not his personal beauty but that divine worship is an image of the Kingdom of Heaven, where everything is in light. Nowadays such things are hardly ever worn in churches; they hang in museums and are looked at as works of art. That makes me a little sad. The needlewomen sewed this not for a display case but for prayer. I hope that at least some of the visitors, passing by, remember them too.

photos/2026-11-03/12.description: A whole collection of reliquaries behind glass. At the bottom is a silver shrine with glass sides, like a little house with a sloping roof, with gilded Baroque scrolls and medallions. Something lies inside on a red cushion, but through the double glass you can't really make it out. On the roof of the shrine stands a dark figure of an old man with a halo, one hand raised, and in the other he holds a long object — apparently an instrument of martyrdom, by which saints are identified in the West, but which saint exactly I wouldn't venture to say from the photograph. And on the shelf above are two gilded cabinets in the form of little churches with pediments, and in each about fifteen compartments holding small bundles wrapped in colored silk — blue, pink, red. These are particles of relics. On either side stand gilded angels with folded hands, as if keeping guard. To some people all this looks strange, almost like a cabinet of curiosities. But to an Orthodox person it isn't strange at all. We too venerate relics, and in every antimension on the altar a particle of a martyr's relics is sewn in; without it the Liturgy is not served. The tradition goes back to the first centuries, when Christians gathered to serve on the tombs of martyrs — in the very catacombs we had seen in Rome. The Seventh Ecumenical Council specifically affirmed this veneration. The point is not in the little bones, but in the fact that the body of a saint was a temple of the Holy Spirit and will be raised. The saints are not dead heroes of the past but living members of the one Church. That is why at reliquaries like these I don't admire the jewelers' work so much as silently greet them.

photos/2026-11-03/13.alt: The Bay of Naples and Vesuvius
photos/2026-11-03/13.description: A blue sky, a blue sea, a single cloud as if painted on, and beneath it Vesuvius. The volcano has two peaks: on the left the old mountain of Somma, on the right the cone of Vesuvius itself. Along the shore stretches a long pale strip of towns clinging to its foot; on the left a huge cruise liner at the pier has driven into the frame, next to it a stone breakwater, and on the right a red tanker sits on the water. This is the view from the waterfront, on the way to Castel dell'Ovo. Here I have to say the main thing. Vesuvius isn't asleep, it is just resting.
