In 79 it buried Pompeii and Herculaneum in ash, and Pliny the Elder died then, having sailed across this very bay to rescue people. The volcano last erupted in 1944 — the same year that Monte Cassino, where we had been the day before yesterday, was bombed. And now hundreds of thousands of people live at its foot and somehow get along with it: grapes grow superbly on the volcanic slopes, and so does the wine. Neapolitans, I think, generally know how to live next to danger without unnecessary panic — whether behind the wheel or under a volcano. We stood on the shore and looked at this mountain. The strangest feeling: everything is very peaceful and very beautiful, yet you know that under this calm, fire is boiling. It happens that way with people too. In the next few days we were planning to go to Pompeii, to the very foot, to see what was once left after that calm.

photos/2026-11-03/14.alt: An old building with laundry on the balconies
photos/2026-11-03/14.description: If I were asked to describe Naples with one photograph, I would probably choose this one. A tall old building, the walls peeled down to the stone, the plaster hanging in patches like a map of an unknown continent. On top, extra floors have been added, little balconies, awnings, some sort of extensions that clearly appeared later and without any architect's permission. Green shutters, air conditioners, flowerpots. And laundry everywhere: on lines along the balconies hang shirts, towels, socks, a huge red sheet, white tablecloths. From below, the white roof of someone's van has driven into the frame — a Neapolitan street won't let you photograph even a building in peace. Laundry outdoors in Naples is not disorder but a whole tradition. The apartments are cramped and there are no dryers, but there is sun and a wind from the sea. Lines are strung across balconies, and sometimes across the whole street, from window to window, to the neighbors opposite. I like it. Here people don't hide their lives behind high fences. Everything is on view: poverty, and order, and clean sheets, and added-on floors. In America that isn't how things are done: there laundry is hidden away in the dryer, and the houses stand perfectly neat and all alike. But here every balcony tells its own story. Christ, after all, was born not in a palace but in an ordinary town, among ordinary people and their ordinary, not always beautiful life. Naples seems not even to try to look better than it is.

photos/2026-11-04/1.alt: The Gothic façade of Naples Cathedral
photos/2026-11-04/1.description: Naples Cathedral from below, from the square, and once again you have to tilt your head back. The façade is pale, almost cream-colored, all pointed gables, turrets, lancet windows and stone lacework. Above the main portal there are statues in the tympanum, above them a round window, and at the very top a cross. People sit on the steps, some taking pictures, some simply warming themselves in the November sun. Thin clouds in the sky. It all looks very medieval, and here there is a small catch. The cathedral itself really is old: it was begun under the Angevin kings, at the end of the 13th century. But the façade in its present form appeared only at the turn of the 19th and 20th centuries, in the Neo-Gothic style, that is, “in imitation of the old.” The genuine, medieval parts here are the portals; they were made at the beginning of the 15th century and carefully preserved during the rebuilding. So looking at this façade, you see two eras at once. Inside the cathedral is kept the blood of St Januarius, patron of Naples, a martyr of the 3rd century. Three times a year, on the Saturday before the first Sunday of May, on 19 September and on 16 December, it is brought out to the people, and the Neapolitans wait to see whether the dried blood will become liquid again. If it doesn't, it is considered a bad sign for the city. I don't presume to judge such things. But I like that a whole city, noisy and far from devout, gathers in church three times a year and prays for itself. The rest of the time the cathedral simply stands and patiently waits. And the people on the steps go on warming themselves in the sun, and the cathedral, it seems, only enjoys it.

photos/2026-11-04/2.alt: A sign with currency exchange terms
photos/2026-11-04/2.description: I didn't photograph this sign for its beauty, but as a lesson to myself and to you. It stands on the counter of an exchange office, in a red frame, in English and Italian. Let's read carefully. Fixed fee — 9 euros 90 cents. Commission on buying banknotes — 24.90 percent. Commission on selling foreign currency — also 24.90. Card transactions — 21.90 percent. And at the bottom, in eight languages, including Japanese and Chinese, the most important thing is printed: once you have handed your money to the cashier, no refund is possible. That is, if you bring a hundred dollars, almost a quarter of it simply vanishes into thin air, plus a tenner on top. And all of this is written honestly, in big letters, right under your nose. No law is being broken — read it and agree. Friends, the advice is simple and free, unlike this outfit: in Italy you shouldn't change cash at places like this. Pay by card where you can, and withdraw cash from the ATM of a real bank. Exchange offices in tourist spots are a sport of their own, in which the same side always wins. I stood over this sign and remembered the Gospel episode where the Lord entered the Temple in Jerusalem and overturned the tables of the moneychangers. I used to think He was angry only because they were trading in the Temple. Now I suspect their commissions were about the same as these. That's a joke, of course. And in the evening of the same day, the closed funicular cost us eleven euros forty cents, and compared with this sign, that was still a very cheap lesson.

photos/2026-11-04/3.alt: Nativity scene figurines on San Gregorio Armeno
photos/2026-11-04/3.description: Your eyes don't know where to look, and that's exactly the idea. The shelves rise upward, and on each one is a little world. Bakers in white caps stand by brick ovens wielding long peels, a pizzaiolo takes a pizza out of the oven, a fishwife has laid out her fish, next to her a flower girl with an armful of roses, and further on cottages with thatched roofs, stables, rocks, mills. Each figurine is the size of a finger, yet all the faces are different, and everyone is busy with something. Wires and sockets run between the shelves: many of the scenes here are lit up, and some, judging by the little motors, even move. On the right, someone's hand holding a phone got into the shot: on Via San Gregorio Armeno every other person is taking pictures, and it's so crowded you can only walk shoulder to shoulder. I've already told you about the street itself, so I'll add something about the tradition. The first Nativity scene, as is well known, was set up by St Francis of Assisi in 1223 in the Italian town of Greccio: on Christmas night he placed a manger in a cave, brought a live ox and donkey, and celebrated a service there. And in Naples in the 18th century it became a real art: wealthy families and even kings commissioned huge Nativity scenes with hundreds of figures, and in them, besides the Holy Family, there was always the whole of Neapolitan life — with taverns, markets and bakeries. Looking at these tiny bakers, I thought it was very much in the spirit of the Gospel. After all, Bethlehem means “house of bread.” And in this house of bread, bakers were probably quite at home.

photos/2026-11-04/4.alt: A statue of a recumbent saint on a red cover
photos/2026-11-04/4.description: In one of the churches of Naples, right by the pews, on wooden trestles covered with red velvet, lies a life-size statue of a saint. A grey monastic habit, a white rope belt, bare feet in sandals, a dark beard, a hood on his head, a cross in his hands. His head rests on a golden pillow, and olive branches are laid out around him. Behind are rows of pews, columns, a marble floor, and by the far wall a statue of the Mother of God. A habit with a rope is Franciscan, and by all appearances this is St Francis of Assisi himself on his deathbed. Every year, on the evening of October 3, the Franciscans commemorate his death, and for this they put out recumbent statues like this one. Apparently they just haven't got round to putting it away since October, or else it stays here permanently. Francis died in 1226 near Assisi. According to tradition, he asked to be laid on the bare ground, without any clothes, and met death as a sister. He even added a line about her to his famous “Canticle of Brother Sun”: “Praised be You, my Lord, for our sister, bodily death.” But the Italians, as you can see, laid down velvet and a pillow for him all the same — they love their saints and spoil them. I looked at this statue, and somehow there was no feeling of mourning at all. Francis's face is calm, almost content, like that of a man who has finished a long road and is just about home. For a Christian, I think, that's how it should be. And on San Gregorio Armeno, by the way, they sell Nativity scenes — and it was he who came up with the very first one.

photos/2026-11-04/5.alt: “The Liberation of St Peter” by Battistello Caracciolo at the Pio Monte della Misericordia
photos/2026-11-04/5.description: At first I thought I was looking at another Caravaggio, and no wonder: the same dark background, the same harsh light snatching the figures out of the darkness. But this is a different painting from the same church of the Pio Monte della Misericordia. In it an angel in white bends over an old bald apostle in a yellow cloak, and below, in the foreground, a half-naked soldier sleeps in red cloth. This is the liberation of the Apostle Peter from prison, if I understand correctly, the work of Battistello Caracciolo, a Neapolitan pupil and follower of Caravaggio. Below the painting is an altar with Florentine mosaic of coloured stone, with a cross and candlesticks on it. The story is from the Book of Acts, chapter twelve. Herod threw Peter into prison and set a guard over him, and at night an Angel appeared, woke him, the chains fell from his hands by themselves, and Peter walked out, thinking it was a dream. The Pio Monte is a confraternity of mercy, founded at the beginning of the 17th century by a few young Neapolitan aristocrats. In the centre of the church is Caravaggio's “Seven Works of Mercy,” and the side altars continue the same theme, and this painting is about the work “visiting the prisoner.” And here is what I noticed: two days ago, on the Appian Way, at Domine Quo Vadis, we recalled how Peter was leaving Rome to escape persecution and went back to his death. And here, on the contrary, he is being led out of prison to freedom. The Apostle Peter accompanies us all along the way, now by the stone on the Appian Way, now in paintings. It seems he watches over the pilgrims who follow in his footsteps, even if they travel by car and without a ticket for the autostrada.

photos/2026-11-05/1.description: From above, from the top rows, the Large Theatre of Pompeii looks like a shell laid on a hillside. Down below, on the semicircular orchestra, stands a tour group, about forty people, all with their heads tilted back listening to the guide, while I look at them from on high and listen only to the wind. The sky is so blue it seems it's not November but May. Behind the stage are trees, behind the trees mountains, and it feels as if the theatre was built not in a city but right in the landscape. That's how the Greeks liked it: they set the seating on a natural slope so that the earth itself held up the stands. This theatre appeared as early as the 2nd century before the Nativity of Christ, when Pompeii had no thought of being Roman, and later it was rebuilt and enlarged more than once. It held, it is thought, about five thousand people, very respectable for a provincial town. Down below you can clearly see wide low steps: these were the places for honoured citizens, and chairs were brought there for them. The rest of the audience sat higher up, like me now, and probably squinted at the sun in just the same way. The brick wall behind the stage was once faced with marble and adorned with columns; now only bare bricks remain of that splendour. On the other hand, the wooden boards on the stage are quite new: the theatre, as far as I understand, is still alive today, and in summer performances are held here again. So it turns out that for more than two thousand years people have been coming to this place to watch and listen. Empires, languages and faith have changed, but the habit of gathering together in front of a stage has stayed the same. There is something comforting in this: man changes much less than he thinks.

photos/2026-11-05/2.alt: The Quadriporticus of the Theatres in Pompeii
photos/2026-11-05/2.description: A large green lawn, a colonnade of grey stone around the edges, on the left the rows of the Large Theatre rising above the wall, and on the right, in a gap between the ruins, Vesuvius. In Pompeii it always appears unexpectedly, like a stern relative at a family party: you walk along, chatting, turn around, and there it stands, watching. This courtyard is usually called the Quadriporticus of the Theatres. It was conceived as a foyer: during the interval or in the rain, the audience came out here from the theatre, strolled under the roof of the portico, talked, showed themselves off. But in the last years of the city's life the courtyard was adapted as barracks, and here, archaeologists believe, the gladiators lived. Their weapons and richly decorated helmets were found here. So people walked on this grass who, a few days later, would face the arena. In the middle of the lawn stand modern slabs with some kind of signs, apparently someone's exhibition: the ancient city readily welcomes today's artists. I confess I wouldn't venture to decipher the meaning of these signs. Here it is hard for a priest not to remember how the story of the gladiators ended. According to tradition, at the beginning of the 5th century in Rome a monk named Telemachus went out into the arena to separate the fighters and was killed by the crowd, and after that the Emperor Honorius banned gladiatorial combat. One unarmed man did what centuries of philosophy could not. Now it is quiet here, cypresses, even grass and not a single spectator, except us and Vesuvius.

photos/2026-11-05/3.alt: The walls of a Pompeian house
photos/2026-11-05/3.description: I took this shot for the sake of the walls. Nothing famous, no sign, just a corner where several eras of building meet at once. On the left is a long wall of uneven stone, as if built from whatever came to hand: chunks of solidified lava, tuff, limestone, all set in mortar. The Romans called this kind of masonry opus incertum, that is, “irregular work.” In the middle is a neat corner of brick and pale dressed blocks, with the remains of a pilaster, and above it a tiled roof, laid by the restorers so that the rain doesn't wash away what lay under the ash for almost two thousand years. On the right the wall is quite different, with bands of brick every few courses of stone. And in the foreground are shapeless grey lumps from which you can no longer tell what they once were. Pompeian walls read like a chronicle. In one place you can see the house was built before the Romans, with large blocks, in another that it was patched up in a hurry. In 62 the city went through a strong earthquake, and when 79 came, many buildings were still under repair. People were restoring their houses, laying new bricks, haggling with craftsmen and, of course, didn't know that no one would ever finish this repair. For me this is perhaps the most human thing in Pompeii: not the temples and not the forum, but an unfinished patch on a wall. We too are always fixing something, rebuilding, and putting off the most important things for later, as if we had eternity in reserve.

photos/2026-11-05/4.alt: The ruins of Pompeii and a field
photos/2026-11-05/4.description: In early November, yellow flowers bloom in Pompeii. I'm no botanist and don't know their name, but among the grey walls they look as if someone had deliberately scattered a handful of sunshine across the grass. Beyond the field stretch the remains of roofless houses: doorways, niches, fragments of walls, a whole quarter resembling a honeycomb. And on the horizon, above the ruins, stands a white modern house with a terrace. That's how two cities live side by side here: the ancient one below and the present one, also Pompei, above. The ancient city is huge. About two thirds of its area has been excavated, it is thought, and the rest still lies underground, and not out of laziness. Digging began here in the 18th century, and the first excavations, to be honest, were more like a treasure hunt for royal collections than science: much was carried off, and some things were destroyed through inexperience. That's why today's archaeologists are in no hurry and deliberately leave work for those who will have better tools than ours. I liked this thought: not to grab everything at once, but to leave something for the next generations. And I'll repeat my advice to friends: Pompeii is not a one-hour museum. Here you need to walk for a long time, turn into side streets, and sometimes just stand, as I did here, looking at the field, the flowers and the empty windows behind which people once cooked supper and quarrelled over trifles.

photos/2026-11-05/5.description: Next to the Large Theatre stands the Small one, also called the Odeon. In the daytime it is half in shadow, and that makes it seem almost homely: rows of stone benches in a semicircle, the pale floor of the orchestra below, and along the edges of the parapet kneel stone figures carved from tuff. One of them is clearly visible on the right: a bearded atlas who has been holding up the edge of the parapet for two thousand years and, judging by his face, is tired. This theatre was built in the first years after Pompeii became a Roman colony, that is, at the beginning of the 1st century before the Nativity of Christ. Unlike the Large one, it was roofed, it had few seats, somewhat over a thousand, and it was intended not for loud performances but for music, the recitation of poetry, perhaps for meetings. Under a roof the voice sounds better; you don't have to shout over the wind. I thought that for its time this was something like a small town's concert hall. People came here in the evening to listen to a musician or a poet, and then went home along the very streets we walked today. The stone of the benches is worn smooth, the steps between the sections are steep, and going down them is much more pleasant in comfortable shoes than in Roman sandals. In places like this I'm always touched not by scale but by proportion: everything is made for a person, to his height, his voice and his hearing.

photos/2026-11-05/6.alt: A fresco with ornament above a door
photos/2026-11-05/6.description: Above the doorway a band of painting has survived, and I stood there with my head tilted back. Below is a rich red wall, above it a dark, almost black band along which run pale scrolls with rosette flowers, and higher still a light zone with thin red lines, like on a technical drawing. In places the plaster has fallen off, and through the holes you can see the rough stonework. The result is a cross-section, like in a textbook: here is the wall, here is the layer of mortar, here is the paint. Almost all Pompeian painting was done on wet plaster. The paint was applied before the mortar set, and the pigment became part of the wall, which is why it survived the ash, two thousand years and the excavations. The master worked quickly and with no room for error: tomorrow you could no longer fix this section. These scrolls above the door reminded me of a grapevine. In a Roman house it was simply a beautiful ornament, but a few centuries later Christians took the same vine into their churches, because the Lord said: “I am the vine, ye are the branches.” The Roman masters, of course, meant nothing of the kind. But I like that the Church didn't invent a new language for itself, but took what was around and filled it with new meaning. The wooden lintel over the doorway, by the way, is new, put in by the restorers, and behind it is the darkness of the next room, where tourists are no longer allowed.

photos/2026-11-05/7.description: Red and yellow. This is the corner of a wall at the entrance to a room, and in it you can see straight away how the Romans loved to deceive the eye. On the flat plaster are painted columns, cornices, delicate architectural details, as if the wall recedes into depth and the room is bigger than it really is. Below is a dark plinth with a small ornament, above it a bright field, higher still more light painted architecture. In places the paint has flaked off, and the white patches look like clouds. Around the corner you can see the next room, also with red panels, and at the entrance a metal post with a chain: no further. There's one story I learned not long ago, and since then I look at Pompeian walls differently. The famous “Pompeian red” was not always red. Italian researchers have shown that some of the walls were originally painted with yellow ochre and turned red from the scorching gases during the eruption: yellow ochre turns red when heated. That is, some of these walls we see not as their owners saw them, but as Vesuvius made them. Here, on this corner, yellow and red stand side by side, and of course I wouldn't venture to say where the paint is original and where it has been scorched. But the thought itself is a good one and, I think, very true to life: fire changes colour, and not always for the worse.

photos/2026-11-05/8.alt: A painted room of a Pompeian house
photos/2026-11-05/8.description: The sun peeks into this room through the door and falls on the wall in a slanting strip, as if on purpose to light up the painting. Red and ochre fields, a dark plinth below, above it light painted pavilions and frames, and in the middle little pictures. In one you can see several figures in long robes, some kind of scene, perhaps from a myth. What exactly, I don't know, and I won't guess. On the left is a narrow passage closed off by a grille, and beyond it a sunlit courtyard. Overhead are wooden beams: the roof was restored so that the rain wouldn't wash away the paint. Roman masters painted rooms according to an established scheme, and it can be seen clearly here. The lower part is dark, since it got knocked by feet and furniture anyway. The middle part is the main one, with large coloured fields and a picture in the centre. The upper part is the lightest, with airy architecture, so that the ceiling doesn't feel oppressive. This didn't stop each owner from showing off his taste and his wallet. In rooms like this I always want to imagine who lived in them. Here stood a bed or a couch, here they sat in the evening, and in the morning the light fell in from the door just as it does now. And the owners saw these little pictures on the wall every day, just as we see the icons in our homes, stop noticing them, and then one day suddenly look at them closely.

photos/2026-11-05/9.description: A long covered gallery with columns: on the left a low wall and a row of white fluted columns, behind them the greenery of a garden, on the right a wall with remnants of red paint and a barred window, overhead new wooden beams. The floor is of ancient mortar with fine stone chips, patched here and there with grey cement, and these patches look like puddles that will never dry. This is a peristyle, an inner courtyard with a garden, surrounded by a portico. The Romans picked it up from the Greeks and grew very fond of it. A Roman house was arranged like this: first the atrium, where the master received guests and clients, and further in, deep inside, the peristyle, just for their own people, for the family, with flowers, a fountain and shade. The columns look like marble, but most often they were built of tuff or brick and covered with fluted plaster. Roman thrift, nothing to be done about it. I walked along this gallery and thought how much it resembles a monastery courtyard. And that's no accident: monastic cloisters with arcades around a garden grew out of the same ancient habit of building a quiet place inside the house, shut off from the street. And the next day we stood in the Cloister of Paradise at the cathedral in Amalfi, and there I remembered this thought once again. Shade, a garden, footsteps on stone, and the noise of the city left somewhere outside.

photos/2026-11-05/10.description: The room is small, but you walk in and want to speak in a low voice. The walls are red, divided into panels by thin frames; in the middle of one there is a small faded picture, on another wall a dark rectangle where there was once an image too. Up above you can see a bit of ceiling plaster with a pattern; the rest has been replaced by a new wooden roof. But the floor here is perhaps the best thing in the room: dark, ruled with white lines of tiny pebbles in a diagonal grid, diamond after diamond. I'd put a floor like that in at home, only I suspect I'd be scrubbing it until Christmas. The Romans knew how to make floors that lasted for ages. First several layers of tamped base, then mortar, and on top a pattern of pebbles or bits of marble. That's why the floor is often better preserved than everything else: the roof collapsed, the walls were burnt, but you could walk on the floor even today, only visitors are no longer allowed in, the entrance is blocked by a little wooden fence. What the room was used for I can't say; it could have been a bedroom or a dining room. But you can see it was made with love and not for just a year or two. And here's another thing about Pompeii that won't let me go: the people who lived here put effort and money into the beauty of their home, into what would bring joy every day. Not one of them intended to leave here for good on a single August or autumn day.

photos/2026-11-05/11.description: This is a difficult shot, but I still put it on the site, because without it the story of Pompeii would be untrue. Under glass, in sand and ash, lie human bones. Skulls, ribs, bones of arms and legs, several people together, close to one another. The glass is dusty, light is reflected in it, and through it everything seems even more distant, though in reality they are half a metre away. The famous Pompeian figures that everyone has seen in photographs are plaster casts, filled hollows in the ash. But here there is no cast; here are the people themselves, or rather what is left of them. Most of the inhabitants, by all accounts, managed to leave the city in the first hours, while pumice was falling from the sky. Those who died were the ones who stayed to wait it out, hoped to save their house, or simply couldn't leave. They were overtaken by flows of scorching gas and ash the next morning. More than a thousand such people have been found already, and they are still being found. I don't know their names and I don't know what they believed in. Most likely in their household gods; perhaps they had never even heard of Christ. But when you stand over them, the prayer comes by itself: “Give rest, O Lord, to the souls of Thy departed servants.” That is probably the first thing such a place teaches. Not fear, but remembrance. And also that none of us has a guaranteed tomorrow, so it's better not to put off what matters.

photos/2026-11-05/12.description: On a palm are three small pieces: green, light green with ochre, and pinkish red. These aren't pebbles from the road; they're fragments of painted plaster, and on one you can even see a clean border between two colours, as if the brush had only just passed. Nearby on the ground are someone's black boot, the fluffy sleeve of a sweater and a lock of fair hair, and two fingers are holding one of the fragments to look at it more closely. In Pompeii such things literally lie underfoot, especially at the edges of the excavations, where the walls are slowly crumbling. You pick up a piece and realise that two thousand years ago someone diluted this paint, mixed it and laid it on a wet wall. Let me say right away for strict readers: you may not take anything away from Pompeii, and that's right. If each of the millions of visitors takes a pebble, in a few years nothing will be left of the city. And for those whom the law doesn't convince, there's a story of its own. Parcels regularly arrive in Pompeii from all over the world: tourists return fragments, frescoes and mosaic they once stole, and in their letters they write that ever since, their lives have been nothing but misfortune, and they ask for forgiveness. The museum collects these letters. I don't believe in curses, but I do believe in conscience, and I like that it works even after many years and across an ocean. So let these pieces stay here, and we keep the photograph.

photos/2026-11-05/13.alt: A street in Pompeii along a high wall
photos/2026-11-05/13.description: A long street between high walls of dark volcanic stone, greenery sprouting at the top of the walls, and at the very end, as if in a gunsight, stands Vesuvius. The sun strikes from the side; one side of the street is in shadow, the other blazes. Walking down a street like this is strange: not a single door, not a single window, only stone, and all the time you feel the mountain looking at your back when you walk away from it, and in your face when you walk toward it. The inhabitants of Pompeii, by the way, didn't know they lived under a volcano. For them it was simply a big green mountain covered with vineyards, and the wine from its slopes was prized. In 73 before the Nativity of Christ, Spartacus hid with his men on the summit of Vesuvius, and no one at that time considered this mountain dangerous. The last eruption before 79 had been so long ago that it was forgotten. And the mountain itself looked different then. The present cone, which we see in the photograph, grew only after that catastrophe, inside the old destroyed summit, of which the semicircular ridge of Somma now remains. I looked at this silhouette at the end of the street and thought how easily a person gets used to danger if it stays silent for a long time. Vineyards, wine, Spartacus, ordinary life. And then one morning that changes everything. I don't think it's a reason to live in fear. Rather, a reason to live watchfully, as the Gospel says.

photos/2026-11-05/14.description: This picture isn't a photograph but a modern reconstruction illustration, and I put it here deliberately, because after a whole day among the ruins you want to imagine how it was. A narrow street with red and yellow walls, a wooden balcony, tiled roofs. Above the city rises a huge column of dark smoke, the sun barely breaks through it as a pale spot, and little stones are pouring from the sky. A woman in a red cloak runs, clutching a child to her. Behind her a man leads a donkey and covers his head with something like a rolled-up bundle; a few more people carry bundles on their heads. It's remarkable that the artist follows an eyewitness account here almost word for word. Pliny the Younger, who saw the eruption from the other side of the bay, wrote that people going out into the street under the falling stones tied pillows to their heads to protect themselves. In the first hours pumice really was falling from the sky, light porous stones, and roofs caved in under their weight. It was terrifying, but you could still get away from it, and many did. What came afterward was what proved deadly. I look at this woman with her child and think that at such a moment the most important thing is always in a person's arms. Not a chest, not silver, but the one you love. I hope she made it to the sea.

photos/2026-11-05/15.alt: A marble table by the impluvium in an atrium
photos/2026-11-05/15.description: In the middle of the atrium stands a marble table on a single thick fluted leg, and next to it, in the floor, are two round openings covered with metal lids. From above, through an opening in the roof, the sun falls and lies on the wall in a slanting ray, as in an old painting. The floor around is of white mortar strewn with black pebble dots, with a dark border at the edge. All this explains very well how a Roman house was arranged. In the centre of the atrium the roof had a square opening; through it light came into the house, and in the rain water ran down. Beneath the opening in the floor was a shallow pool, the impluvium; from there the water went into an underground cistern, and the round openings next to it are the mouths of the cistern, through which water was later drawn. It made a household water supply without any pipes: what God sent from heaven, that's what they drank. The table was usually placed right here, at the edge of the pool. They say the best tableware was displayed on it, so that a guest, coming in, would see at once that the house wasn't poor. Today the table stands empty, without silver and without owners, but it hasn't lost its place. I looked at that ray of light for a long time and thought that the atrium was the heart of the house not only because of the water. It was the place where the family welcomed guests, where the household shrines stood, where life went on in plain view of everyone. In our homes, I suppose, the role of the atrium is played by the kitchen.

photos/2026-11-05/16.alt: A garden in a fresco in a Pompeian house
photos/2026-11-05/16.description: In a small niche the whole back wall is painted as a garden. On a dark, almost black background grow trees, bushes and flowers, and birds fly between the branches. Lower down a lattice fence is painted, with vases on it, and in the centre a fountain basin. Lower still is a dark plinth with coloured diamonds, and a crack runs across the whole wall like a white scar. To the side stand modern spotlights for illumination. And in the centre, on the main tree, coiled around the trunk, sits a snake. The Romans loved painting gardens on walls, especially in small windowless rooms: you open the door, and there is eternal spring, birds and water. In a Roman house the snake is not a symbol of evil; on the contrary, it was considered a kindly guardian spirit of the house and the place, and was often painted by household altars. But a Christian, seeing a tree with a serpent coiled around it in the middle of a garden of paradise, of course immediately thinks of something else. A garden, a tree, a serpent. I stood before this wall and couldn't shake off the thought that the artist, without knowing it, had painted the first page of the Bible. He was painting his own paradise, without sin and without exile, peaceful, with birds and a fountain. But we know how that story ended, and we know it didn't end with the exile. There is another Tree, and through it the road to the garden is open again. A fine sermon from a Roman house painter, though he had no idea of it.

photos/2026-11-05/17.description: In one of the rooms, which you can only peer into through the doorway, lie amphorae. Whole and broken, with handles and without, pointed, pot-bellied, stacked in modern plastic crates like potatoes in a warehouse. Nearby is a pile of empty blue crates: work is going on, everything is accounted for and awaits its turn. On the wall behind them are remnants of red painting, and a tuft of grass sticks out of one crate. In the ancient world an amphora was everything at once: barrel, bottle, container and packaging. In them they shipped wine, olive oil, the fish sauce garum, which the Romans added to almost everything. The pointed bottom was no hindrance; on the contrary, an amphora was stuck into sand or set in special stands, and in a ship's hold they were laid in rows. Pompeii lived by both trade and winemaking; the slopes of Vesuvius were covered with vineyards, and the local wine travelled far beyond Campania. Archaeologists find amphorae in Pompeii by the thousand, and many still bear painted inscriptions: what's inside, where from, whose. These are, in essence, two-thousand-year-old waybills and price tags. Storerooms like this touch me more than palaces. Someone ordered this wine, waited for the delivery, maybe argued with a merchant over the price. Ordinary household life that suddenly stopped in mid-sentence. And now, so many centuries later, the amphorae lie in a storeroom again, only now they are not goods, but memory.

photos/2026-11-05/18.alt: A courtyard with a portico in Pompeii
photos/2026-11-05/18.description: A spacious open courtyard, trampled earth, on the right a long portico under a tiled roof with a row of columns, in the background a façade with openings, and on the left, above the ruins, stands a modern canopy on metal supports, protecting something from the rain. People walk around the courtyard; someone is taking pictures, someone is reading a sign. The sky is enormous, with cirrus clouds, and that makes the courtyard seem even wider. In the bottom corner someone's heads got into the shot; I didn't crop them out: it's more honest that way, the courtyard is alive after all, people still walk here today. What this courtyard is, I can't say for certain. Pompeii has many such open spaces with porticoes: at baths, at public buildings, at large houses. The Romans loved porticoes in general. It's a very practical thing for a southern city: in summer, shade under the roof; in winter, shelter from the rain; and between the columns you can meet, talk, strike a deal, or just stand around. The Greek philosophers, the Stoics, got their name precisely from a portico, the stoa, where their founder taught. And the Apostle Paul, when he preached in Athens, talked with people in the marketplace and argued with those very Stoics. I looked at these columns and thought that for people in antiquity the portico was what the church porch or the churchyard after the service has become for us: a place where everyone meets and where half of life's questions get settled.

photos/2026-11-05/19.alt: A vaulted hall of the baths
photos/2026-11-05/19.description: Under the high vaults it is cool and quiet; light comes only from the doorway at the far end, and your eyes take a while to adjust. These are the thermae, the public baths. The vaults are decorated with stucco, crumbling in places, a row of niches runs along the right wall, and the floor is paved with pale stone slabs. By the entrance stands the attendant's folding stool, the only modern furniture in the whole hall. The niches in the wall, by all signs, were for clothes: in halls like this people undressed, left their things and went on, from a cool room to a warm one and a hot one. A Roman bath was a whole system. Under the floor of the hot rooms hollow spaces were left, through which hot air came from the furnace; the walls were heated too, through hollow bricks; and the water was heated in large boilers. For its time it was real engineering. People went to the baths not only to wash. It was a club, a gym and a place for news: people came here almost every day, met friends, discussed business, politics and the price of grain. Pompeii had several public baths, and by all appearances they were never empty. For me, living in Florida, where there's more than enough hot water and sunshine, it's hard to fully understand what this luxury, available for a small coin, meant to a Roman. But I understand the main thing: people need a place where they can come, where they're known and where they can catch their breath. That's worth remembering for us too, when we think about what parish life should be like.

photos/2026-11-05/20.alt: A narrow alley with moss between walls
photos/2026-11-05/20.description: One of the narrowest alleys of the whole day. On the right a wall of red brick, on the left a lower part of large dark stone with masonry of uneven rubble above, and underfoot an old pavement of big grey slabs, with green moss grown thick between them. On the right a narrow raised sidewalk runs along the wall, and at the end of the alley a bright opening appears: steps, columns and distant mountains. In November it's damp in Pompeii, and on the stones where the sun doesn't reach, the moss feels entirely at home. In summer this alley probably looks quite different, scorched and dusty. Pompeian pavements are made of solidified lava, the very volcanic stone with which Vesuvius itself once supplied the surrounding area. The slabs were fitted together without mortar, and two thousand years ago carts rolled over them, leaving ruts, while the sidewalks were made higher so that pedestrians didn't walk through mud and water. Sometimes the streets also served as drains: in the rain, water flowed along them. A cart, of course, couldn't have squeezed into such a narrow alley. This is a path for pedestrians, for neighbours who took a shortcut to the forum or the baths. I like places like this more than the grand streets. There's nothing showy here, only walls, stone and light at the end. To be honest, there's something very familiar in this shot for any Christian: a narrow way, hard to walk, but with light at the end of it.

photos/2026-11-05/21.description: And this is already evening, Agerola, and antiquities of a quite different kind. Bottles of local wine stand on a wooden shelf; the round white labels read Selezione Chapeau, Agerola, Alta Costa d'Amalfi. The labels are designed to look like ancient wall painting: on one there is a horseman and the words “L'amore delle api”, that is, “The love of the bees”, on another a figure in a horned headdress and the word “Incontro”, “Meeting”. Next to them lies a cork with the price written on it by hand. After a whole day among the Pompeian frescoes these labels look like a continuation of the tour: the same ochre, the same red paint, the same Greek meanders around the edges. Agerola, in fact, is better known for its cheese than for its wine. This mountain plateau above Amalfi is famous for its milk and dairy products, while wine is made here in small quantities on little vineyards clinging to the slopes. On the Amalfi Coast the grapes grow on narrow terraces that for centuries have been cut out and propped up with stone walls, and they have to be worked by hand. So each bottle like this, if you think about it, is paid for not so much in euros as with someone's back. And for a priest wine is no casual thing. The Lord worked His first miracle at the wedding in Cana of Galilee, turning water into wine so as not to sadden the young couple. And at every Liturgy we once again take bread and wine into our hands. I particularly liked the name “Meeting” here: good wine really is best drunk when people meet.

photos/2026-11-06/1.alt: Cliffs above the path to Amalfi
photos/2026-11-06/1.description: This is what the path we went down to Amalfi looks like. Underfoot is an old stone path paved with flat slabs, with a low stone parapet on the side of the drop. All around are dry grass and bushes in autumn patches of russet and yellow, and above it all rises a huge pale cliff, sheer, full of cracks and ledges. If you look closely, on the ledge to the right, almost in the middle of the frame, a tiny white house clings to the rock, either a little chapel or an old watchman's hut. How people got up there and why they built there, I don't know, but it looks as if it is holding on to the cliff with its last strength. There are a great many paths like this on the coast. Until the 19th century, when the coastal road was built, they were the main roads: people walked along them, drove mules, carried firewood, milk and cheese down, and salt, fish and everything that came by sea up. Every step and every slab was laid by someone's hands. The slopes around are cut into terraces held up by dry-stone walls, and it is precisely this man-made landscape, not only the sea and the cliffs, that got the Amalfi Coast onto the UNESCO World Heritage list. Walking here is not hard if you are walking down. True, by the end of the descent your knees start asking questions. But when it is so quiet all around that you can hear only footsteps and birds, it is easy to understand the monks and hermits who in the old days went off to live on slopes just like these.

photos/2026-11-06/2.alt: Sunrise over the Gulf of Salerno
photos/2026-11-06/2.description: This is where it all began. Morning, we are standing on a terrace high above the sea, and the dawn is kindling over the Gulf of Salerno. The sky is full of pink and orange feathers of cloud, along the horizon there is a band of golden light, on the far side of the gulf the mountains stretch in a dark line, and the sea below is smooth and pearly, with a lone boat you can hardly see. In the foreground are wrought-iron railings, an old lamp on a post and a stone urn with flowers that refuse to give up even in November. You really don't see something like this every day. So we decided we ought to go out for a fifteen-minute walk. How that walk ended is told in the story of the day; I'll only say that the next shots were taken a good deal lower down. The Gulf of Salerno lies south of the Amalfi Coast, and the sun rises here right over the water and the distant mountains. Somewhere over there, on the far shore, is the plain where the ancient Greek temples of Paestum stand, and beyond it the mountains of the Cilento begin. You can't make them out from here, of course, but it is nice to know you are looking in that direction. To a priest the dawn says a great deal. Every morning we read about light in our prayers, and at Matins in church we hear “Glory to Thee who hast shown us the light”. Usually you say these words in a half-dark church, by candlelight. But here you just want to say them out loud, looking at the sky, and on a morning like this gratitude takes no effort at all.

photos/2026-11-06/3.description: Already on our way, at the start of the descent. Below us is the old tiled roof of some shed or outbuilding: the tiles are askew, in places they have slid down, wooden beams stick out from under them, and the edges of the roof are hemmed in by bushes with yellow and white flowers. On the left stands a gray house with small windows, with wires running to it. And beyond, right behind the roof, is the drop and the enormous sea, on which the morning sun paints a wide bright path. The sky is still in a light haze, the horizon is drowned in light. What I like about this shot is precisely the combination. Below, everything is old, dilapidated, overgrown, in a farmyard sort of mess, and beyond it a vastness that takes your breath away. This is how people live here: on tiny scraps of land, on slopes where every flat spot has been won from the mountain, with a henhouse, a shed, a woodpile, and with a view that elsewhere people would pay millions for. For the locals it is simply the view from the window, and the shed is there to keep tools in. The tiles on this roof are the classic half-round kind; for centuries they were shaped from local clay and fired, and roofs all along the coast are still covered with tiles like these. I looked at this poor roof and thought that the beauty of the world is not given only to those who have money for a villa with a terrace. God is generous, His sun rises over everyone, and over the owner of this shed perhaps even more brightly, because he gets up earlier.

photos/2026-11-06/4.alt: View from the mountain of the sea and a village
photos/2026-11-06/4.description: From here, from the slope, the coast is laid out like a map. Below, on a headland, the white and pink houses of a small village huddle together, and next to it a dark rock rises out of the water. The sea is vast, silver under the low sun, and the clouds lie over it in layers, as if someone had stacked them in a pile. In the foreground is a slope with scrub and the dry stalk of some umbellifer, withered since the summer and sticking up proudly right in the frame. I didn't crop it out: let it serve as a measure of scale. I can't say for certain what this village is called; on the Amalfi Coast towns and hamlets follow one after another, and from above they are easy to mix up. But you can see the main thing: below, the sea and a narrow strip of life by the water, and above, the mountains and the paths that tied it all together. Before there was a road, the way from here to the next village could take an hour on stairs, and people walked, because there was no choice. By this point the fifteen-minute walk planned in the morning had long since turned into a real journey. Going down is easy, but your calves and knees keep their own count. To jump ahead, I'll say that we went back up by bus, and we were right to. But the view that opens up to someone on foot you won't see from a bus window. In general it seems to me that this is just what distinguishes a pilgrimage from tourism: it is better to come to a holy place on foot, little by little, so that there is time to think about where you are going.

photos/2026-11-06/5.alt: Old houses on the road in Agerola
photos/2026-11-06/5.description: An old house on the road, on the way down. Once upon a time it must have been smart: a pale orange façade with pink bands, arched windows, wrought-iron balconies, little round porthole windows, molded cornices. Now the plaster has peeled, the stonework shows through underneath, one corner is wrapped in ivy, and right up against it stands a modern house with identical balconies, and the difference between them is obvious at first glance. A gray cliff hangs over the roof. Cars are parked by the house, and here they look like chance visitors. You come across houses like this often on the coast and in the mountain villages. This one looks a hundred and fifty years old, or even more; houses like it were built for well-to-do families, merchants, owners of mills and workshops. Then times changed, the children left for Naples, for Rome, for America, and the houses stayed behind to grow old. Italians, by the way, left for America whole villages at a time, and a great many of them came from right here, from Campania. Who knows, perhaps the descendants of this house's owners now run a pizzeria somewhere in New Jersey. I like peeling façades like these more than freshly painted ones. You can see from them that the house lived a long time, that it was loved, and then that people didn't manage, or weren't able, to keep it up. It is like old icons in village churches: the paint has darkened, the gilding has worn away, but the face has remained. And I also thought that on this road every bend reveals something new, and that it is worth walking for the sake of unremarkable houses like this one too.

photos/2026-11-06/6.description: Here it is, the Cathedral of St Andrew in Amalfi, which we, without planning to, came down to from the mountains by noon. A wide, steep staircase climbs from the square to the façade; people sit on the steps and take photos, and above them is the striped façade of black and white stone with pointed arches, diamonds and crosses, and at the very top, on the pediment, a golden mosaic of Christ enthroned is shining. On the left a cliff with the remains of an old tower hangs over the town; the sky is overcast, and because of that the gold on the façade glows even more brightly. The façade, I must honestly say, is younger than it looks. The old one collapsed in the 19th century and was rebuilt in the spirit of the medieval Arab-Norman style so characteristic of southern Italy and Sicily. But the main doors behind the arch are genuine and very old: the bronze doors were cast in Constantinople in the 11th century, commissioned by a wealthy merchant of Amalfi. They are considered among the first Byzantine bronze doors in Italy. So even before the relics of the apostle were brought here, Amalfi was already linked to Constantinople both by trade and by faith. Climbing this staircase after several hours of going down mountain paths was a feat in itself: legs used to walking downhill suddenly remembered that there is such a thing as uphill. But with every step I understood where I was going. Not to a museum and not to a viewpoint, but to my heavenly patron, whose name I have borne all my life. Staircases like this are probably built for just that: so that people approach a holy place without hurrying.

photos/2026-11-06/7.alt: Statue of the Apostle Andrew in the crypt of Amalfi Cathedral
photos/2026-11-06/7.description: The crypt of the cathedral, the place for whose sake, by and large, I came down to Amalfi today. Above the altar stands a large dark bronze statue of the Apostle Andrew with his saltire cross behind him; around it are columns of dark marble, white marble statues of saints on either side, inlays of colored stone, gilding. On the altar there is an open book, a cross, candlesticks and red flowers, and in front a gilded wrought-iron grille with a pattern. Beneath this altar lie the relics of the apostle. All this splendor is Baroque, of a later period. The crypt was richly decorated in the 17th century, when devotion to the saint here was especially strong. But to be honest, it wasn't the marble I was looking at. For an Orthodox Christian the Apostle Andrew is especially close. The Church of Constantinople considers him its founder, and our ancient tradition says that he passed by the hills on the Dnieper. So Andrew the First-Called links Amalfi and Constantinople, Kyiv and Patras, and, it turns out, me too, a sinful priest from Orlando. The saltire cross on which he was crucified became his sign; he is recognized by it by Greeks and Russians alike, and by the Scots, who have it on their flag. Here in the crypt, according to tradition, an oily moisture called manna is exuded from the apostle's tomb, and, so they say, it is collected on special days. It is impossible for a priest to stand here and not pray, and what that prayer was about, let it stay between me and the apostle. And all this on a day that began with the intention of taking a fifteen-minute walk.

photos/2026-11-06/8.alt: Silver bust of the Apostle Andrew
photos/2026-11-06/8.description: A silver bust of the Apostle Andrew, with a modest label beneath it: “S. Andrea Ap. Sec. XVI”, that is, the 16th century. The face and hands are silver, the beard is worked down to every curl, the garments are gilded, and behind the head is a large golden halo. The right hand is raised in blessing, the left holds a book in a silver cover, a golden saltire cross rises behind his shoulder, and on his chest is a small reliquary with a particle of the relics. And from the left hand two silver fish hang on a little chain. This was the detail I liked most of all. Andrew was a fisherman on the Sea of Galilee, together with his brother Simon, until Christ said to them: “Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men.” The craftsman who made this bust five hundred years ago did not forget where the apostle came from, and put his fisherman's past into his hand. Holiness does not erase one's life story, it transfigures it: the fisherman remained a fisherman, only the nets are different now. Reliquary busts like this were made so that the relics could be carried in processions. In Amalfi the apostle is venerated as the patron of the city, and on his feast the image of the saint is carried through the streets. This bust stands in the cathedral halls under glass, on a wooden pedestal with a coat of arms on its base, with other reliquaries nearby. Through the glass everything glints a little, but you can see the expression of the face well: stern and at the same time kind, like an old fisherman who has seen a great deal. It is hard to walk away from it. I suppose that is how one looks at a portrait of a beloved great-grandfather, if, of course, the great-grandfather is cast in silver.

photos/2026-11-06/9.alt: Fountain with a siren in Amalfi
photos/2026-11-06/9.description: After the cathedral, on the square below, there is a fountain it is impossible to walk past. At the top stands a statue, of which only the feet and the hem of the garment got into the frame, and on the very rim of the basin a pigeon has settled, the only one here who is in no hurry to go anywhere. Under the basin is a Latin inscription in which you can read “sacramus fontem”, that is, “we dedicate the fountain”. Below are two plump marble cherubs riding dolphins, from whose mouths water flows, between them a coat of arms with a crown, and at the very bottom, waist-deep in the water, a siren with water pouring straight from her breasts. The Baroque sculptor, it seems, was not overly concerned about modesty. This fountain on the cathedral square is dedicated to the Apostle Andrew, and the statue at the top depicts him. The result is a curious pairing: the apostle, the fisher of men, stands above a siren, who, according to the ancient myths, destroyed sailors with her songs. These parts have long been associated with the sirens: opposite Positano small islands rise out of the sea which in antiquity were thought to be their home. Odysseus, in order to sail past, had himself tied to the mast. The Fathers of the Church later loved this image: the ship is the Church, the mast resembles the cross, and by holding on to it one can pass by any sweet voices. It seems to me the craftsman who put the siren at the apostle's feet was thinking of something like that. Or perhaps he just wanted a beautiful fountain. I would have liked to sit here longer, watching the water and the pigeon, but after the descent and the cathedral staircase my legs were already asking for the bus, and it carried us back up.

photos/2026-11-07/1.alt: A street in Herculaneum with its paving
photos/2026-11-07/1.description:
A street where people last walked in peace almost two thousand years ago. The paving is made of large dark stones of irregular shape; this is lava, and the Romans fitted it stone to stone so tightly that you can still walk on it today. True, after rain the stones gleam and are slippery, and water stands in the potholes. On the left is a colonnade: the brick columns were once plastered and painted; now the plaster has peeled off and you can see what they are really made of. On the right is a high sidewalk with stumps of columns, and at the very end of the street a white sheet is stretched across; beyond it, apparently, there is no way through.

We walked here in the morning, our last morning in the south. There were few people, and it is a special feeling: you are almost alone on an ancient street, and above the wall on the right you can see cypresses and the small figure of a person at the top. Up there is a completely different level, both in height and in time. I caught myself walking exactly in the middle of the road, as if a cart were about to come rolling round the corner and I would have to jump onto the sidewalk.

The excavation of Herculaneum began as early as the eighteenth century, and at first in a miner's fashion: they dug underground tunnels and hauled statues up to the surface for the royal collections. The city was uncovered to the open sky gradually, mostly in the twentieth century, and even now only part of it has been excavated. The rest lies under modern Ercolano, under somebody's kitchens and garages. So this street quite literally runs up against other people's lives. It occurred to me: one day someone will walk our streets like this too and wonder how we lived. It would be good if he found something kind to say about us.

photos/2026-11-07/2.alt: The Herculaneum excavation pit and the modern town above
photos/2026-11-07/2.description:
This is the view from the walkway by which you go down into the excavations. Below are grass and ivy; in front of us is an ancient house of brick and stone with rounded window arches, and behind it more roofless walls. And above all this, on the edge of the pit, stand ordinary apartment buildings: a white one, a yellow one, with balconies and satellite dishes, and a dark cypress beside them. On the right, the red hair of one of our party and the steel cable of the railing got into the frame. That is the whole composition: below, the first century; above, the twenty-first; and in the middle, us, holding on to the railing.

Standing on this walkway, you understand well why so much has survived here. The walls of the pit, these gray-yellow cliffs, are exactly what came from Vesuvius: red-hot flows of gas, ash and stone, which later hardened almost into rock. They did not sweep the city away; they filled it, like a mold. The wood was charred but did not burn, and here and there you can still see beams and doors.

For a long time it was believed that almost all the inhabitants of Herculaneum managed to escape. But in the eighties of the last century, by the former shoreline, in vaulted chambers right by the water, the remains of about three hundred people were found. They had gone there and were waiting to be taken off by sea. They were not. In those days the sea came right up to the city; now the shore has moved far away. It is known that Pliny the Elder, in those very hours, was trying to come with ships to the aid of the people on this bay, and died himself. You stand up above, the sun is shining, there is green grass below, and you think of the people who were waiting for a boat. You want to remember them in prayer, though no one knows their names. The Lord knows.

photos/2026-11-07/3.description:
A fragment of ancient wall: a deep red background with cracks across it, and on the left the plaster has fallen away down to the gray base. On the red a winged boy is painted, most likely Eros, or, as the Romans called him, Cupid. The wings are gray and light, the face is almost worn away, and the garment falls in folds so that you can see the movement. Lower right, someone has scratched some letters. I can't say whether they are ancient scribbles or someone's modern prank, but they look very human.

In Herculaneum there are many paintings like this, and they turn up where you least expect them: in a passageway, on a corner, in a small room you glance into in passing. I lingered at this one longer than at the others. This red is called Pompeian red. They say research has shown that some of the walls we now consider red were once yellow and turned red from the heat of the eruption. So two worked on these walls: the artist and Vesuvius. Which of the shades here is whose, I of course don't know.

Who lived in this house, who commissioned this winged boy and admired him in the evenings, we will never know. But he himself hangs there as he always did. It is interesting that a few centuries would pass and Christian artists would take up similar wings when they began to depict angels. The language of beauty proved tenacious; it was simply filled with a different meaning. I have always found this very comforting: nothing good made by human hands is ever entirely wasted, even if at first it was about a pagan godling.

photos/2026-11-07/4.alt: Fountain with a mask on a street in Herculaneum
photos/2026-11-07/4.description:
An ordinary Roman street fountain. A stone trough, white, with chipped edges, and above it a slab with a bearded face. Water once flowed from the mouth; a rusty streak still runs down from the hole, as if the fountain had just been turned off. I don't know for sure who is depicted: perhaps some sea deity, perhaps Hercules himself, after whom, according to legend, the city was named. Behind it is a brick pillar and a wall of dark blocks, and to the side a modern barrier cord, so that tourists don't sit on the edge.

I liked this fountain more than many statues. Statues were put up for beauty and for pride, but people came here every day. Most houses had no water of their own, and people went for it to the corner, to a trough just like this, with jugs and buckets. This is probably where they heard the news, and quarrelled, and arranged matches. The water came to such fountains by aqueduct from far away, from the mountains, through lead pipes under the paving, and flowed constantly, and the overflow ran off down the street.

I stood a while, pictured that queue with jugs, and thought that for many people in the world water at the pump still looks just like this. And I also remembered that one of the most profound conversations in the Gospel, with the Samaritan woman at the well, also began with an ordinary jug and ordinary thirst. Water always brings people together.

After Herculaneum came three hundred kilometers north, a long day in the car, and in the evening dinner, already on the rock of Orvieto. And for me the south has remained just this bearded face, which for two thousand years has been looking at the street with the same surprised expression.

photos/2026-11-08/1.alt: The shore of Lake Bolsena with autumn plane trees
photos/2026-11-08/1.description:
The shore of Lake Bolsena towards evening. On the right is a row of plane trees; in November their leaves are russet and gold, and half of them are already lying on the path. The path is laid with flat stones, with grass along it, a weeping willow right by the water, and further along the shore more trees, just as orange. The water is perfectly smooth; both the clouds and the willow are reflected in it. In the distance, under the trees, two small figures are walking along the shore, and on the far side low mountains show blue.

We came to Bolsena after lunch in Civita and at some point simply went for a walk along the water. It was quiet and warm, nobody was in a hurry, and neither were we. For us Floridians an autumn like this is an event in itself. In Orlando the leaves don't really turn yellow in November, the trees stay green, but here real autumn rustles underfoot, and it smells of leaves and water. I kept stopping with my phone.

The lake is large, almost round, and it is not an ordinary lake but the flooded bowl of ancient volcanoes. Looking at this smooth surface, you can hardly believe it: everything is so peaceful, the willow, the ducks, the benches. But the stone on which all this land stands, from Orvieto to Civita, came out of those same volcanoes. So the gentle local countryside rests on a very turbulent past. It's the same with people, I think: the most peaceful of those I know have usually been through a great deal. And then we stayed by the water right until sunset, but that's the next pictures.

photos/2026-11-08/2.description:
Sunday morning in Porano. The street is paved with small cobbles, and the houses on either side are plastered in warm colors: peach, ochre, pale pink. The shutters are wooden and brown, there are wrought-iron lamps on the walls, and on the left a little balcony with a railing. There too is a yellow PT sign, the Italian post office, and of course it is closed: it's Sunday. In the middle of the street, near the far house, a lone figure is walking; there is nobody else on the street.

We came to Porano for Mass. It is a small town very close to Orvieto, without any particular tourist fame, and that is exactly why we wanted to go there. In a big city on a Sunday you are still a tourist, but in a small one you become a parishioner for a while. The service is not ours, the language is not ours, much is different, but people have gathered in church because today is the day of the Resurrection, and that we have in common. I stood listening to words whose meaning was familiar in a foreign language and prayed in my own. And on such a morning the streets are quiet: the whole town is either in church or already at the Sunday table.

Towns like Porano have stood on these hills since ancient times. Etruscan tombs are still being found around Orvieto, and the streets themselves, like this one, took shape over centuries, house by house, without any master plan. Hence this gentle curve, and the different heights of the houses, and a lamp fixed wherever someone found it too dark. I like streets like this more than grand squares. You can see in them that people lived, rather than posed.

photos/2026-11-08/3.description:
A narrow lane in Porano, so narrow that two people with bags could no longer pass each other. The left wall is old, reddish, pitted, with stone buttresses jutting out; the right one is gray-beige, with a heavy mahogany door under an arch of gray stone. At the far end is a brick house, and right across the lane a line is strung, with dark trousers, sweaters and something else drying on it. Under the washing are a wooden bench and pots of greenery and a little palm, and above it all a lamp.

In Porano it is worth turning off the main street, and you find yourself in something like this. Another of my favourite Italian sights: washing on a line. You can talk about the Renaissance and marble as much as you like, but the real flag of Italy, in my opinion, is this, trousers hanging across the street, and nobody is embarrassed by it. Someone did the washing in the morning, hung it out and went off to church, or to the market, or to their mother's for lunch. And the bench is placed so that any passer-by can sit on it. I like that too: a man put a bench by his house not just for himself.

The walls here are built of local stone, which was later plastered over, and over the long years the plaster has crumbled in some places and darkened in others. Doors under stone arches like these once led into houses where livestock was kept downstairs, along with wine and tools, while people lived upstairs. Now behind them there are most likely ordinary apartments with a television. Yet the town has not become a museum; it has remained a town, and that is its chief merit. The Sunday lane with its washing and its bench turned out to be no less important a part of that morning for me than the service itself. Faith, after all, lives not in a museum but in lanes just like these.

photos/2026-11-08/4.alt: A little street with an arch in Civita
photos/2026-11-08/4.description:
A little street in Civita. On the left is a yellow house with burgundy shutters, under the roof a wooden canopy on a bracket, by the entrance a trellis twined with ivy, and a whole row of flowerpots. Ahead the road dives under an arch, beneath a house, and to the right of the arch wide, shallow steps climb upward. Above the arch a lamp hangs on a wrought-iron bracket, and a garden hose runs along the wall. The sky is overcast, the light is soft, with no harsh shadows.

You get to Civita on foot, over a long bridge; there is no other way. The bridge rises to the gate, you go through it and find yourself in little streets like this, where no car could possibly be. For me, after the parking in Naples, this was a pleasure in itself: no one honks, no one is looking for somewhere to squeeze in. People walk slowly because there is nowhere to hurry to; the town is small, you can walk round all of it in half an hour if you don't stop. But you stop at every step, at every arch.

The town was founded by the Etruscans, and its trouble has always been that it stands on soft tuff above clay. The rains wash away the clay, the edges of the rock collapse, and houses go over into the abyss. At the end of the seventeenth century there was a strong earthquake here, and after it many of the inhabitants moved to neighboring Bagnoregio. Ever since then Civita has been emptying. But someone waters these flowers in the pots, and the hose isn't lying there for nothing. So the town is still alive, however often it is called dying. It seems to me that every little street like this has its keeper, a person who simply didn't leave. And afterwards we had lunch right here, stewed donkey. I hope the keepers don't hold it against us.

photos/2026-11-08/5.alt: Staircase in a little courtyard in Civita
photos/2026-11-08/5.description:
A small courtyard that the lane leads into. Right in front of us is a house of large pale stone blocks with brown shutters, with two outside staircases leading up to it. The left one, wide, rises to a door with pots of geraniums on the railings; under the right one is a stone arch, and under the arch a dark passage leading somewhere down. On the left is a wall with green shutters, with terracotta pots hanging on it and a house-number plate. Overhead wires stretch across, and an aerial sticks out at the side. The cobbles here are old, with grass coming up between the stones.

We turned in here at random and for a while simply stood. The silence in such places is special: no cars, no music, only somewhere behind a wall people speaking Italian. It occurred to me that this is probably how courtyards have looked in all the little towns around here for the last five hundred years or so, only the aerials have been added.

Outside staircases like this one are typical of these parts. Downstairs, under the staircase and in the half-basements, they kept the household things: firewood, tools, wine, sometimes livestock, and they lived on the second floor, which is where the steps lead. An outside staircase also saved space and served as a porch where people sat in the evening. In Viterbo and the surrounding area such staircases with a landing at the top even have their own name. And I noticed one more thing: there are flowers on every ledge here. A town that is slowly slipping into the abyss is stubbornly decorated with geraniums. To my mind this is hope in its simplest form: not reasoning about what will happen, but watering the flowers today.

photos/2026-11-08/6.description:
An outside staircase in Civita, with a pot on every one of its steps. The wall of the house is built of yellow-gray tuff blocks, porous like pumice; this is the stone the whole town stands on. The steps are gray stone, with wrought-iron railings along the wall. In the pots are cyclamens, pink and crimson, and something green and trailing. Below, along the wall, is a long stone bench with another pot on it, and on the left you can see an arch with worn steps.

This staircase is probably the most photographed spot in Civita after the bridge. We, as you see, couldn't resist either. Someone looks after it: the flowers are fresh, in November, and the pots are neatly arranged, one to a step. Going up it, though, is now only possible sideways.

Tuff, which all this is built of, is compressed volcanic ash. It is soft, it can be cut with a saw, and that is why it is so convenient to build with and so convenient to dig cellars in. But the same softness is its undoing: the rock beneath the town crumbles year after year. St Bonaventure came from these parts, a Franciscan, a learned theologian, Minister General of the Franciscan order and a cardinal, who wrote the life of St Francis. According to tradition, the very name Bonaventure came about after Francis, having healed the boy, exclaimed: “O, buona ventura”, that is, “O, good fortune to come”. I stood by this staircase and thought that the good future of a town slipping into the abyss probably really does rest not on stone but on people like that. And on those who water the cyclamens every morning, too.

photos/2026-11-08/7.description:
The sun is setting into Lake Bolsena. Half the sky is covered by a heavy dark cloud, and beneath it, right at the horizon, is a narrow strip of clear sky, yellow and orange. On the right the sun is already touching the distant hills, and from it a golden path runs across the water. On the water are a few buoys, small dark dots. The foreground is almost black: the shore, pebbles and sand, already gone into shadow.

We stayed until sunset, although we had meant to leave earlier. We sat on the shore; nobody talked much. It had been a long day: Mass in Porano in the morning, then the bridge to Civita, the donkey stew, the Basilica of St Christina. And it ended like this, with silence over the water. At moments like these I always remember the words of Vespers, “O Gladsome Light”: “having come to the setting of the sun, having beheld the evening light, we praise the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit”. It is one of the most ancient Christian hymns; it was sung when the evening lamps were lit. And here you have literally come to the setting of the sun, you are sitting on the shore and seeing that very evening light. I didn't sing aloud, but I sang it to myself.

The lake we were looking at formed where the craters of ancient volcanoes once collapsed, which is why it is almost round and surrounded by gentle hills. The sun sets behind its western shore, and there, beyond the hills, the Tyrrhenian Sea is not so very far away. In November it gets dark early, and very soon all that splendor was reduced to gray water and lights on the shore. We drove home, to near Orvieto, in the dark.

photos/2026-11-08/8.description:
Overhead, branches with the last dry leaves; below, stones and fallen leaves; and between them the huge water, in which the whole sky is reflected as a second layer. The clouds are gray and heavy, with pink edges, at the horizon there is a strip of sunset, and all of it is repeated in the lake almost without distortion, only a little darker. On the right, on the far shore, there is a dark hill and lights.

The lake was this smooth until it got dark. There was no wind at all, and the water lay like a mirror. I took several shots from that shore, and in each of them you can't tell where the sky ends and the water begins. Anyone would say it's a filter. No, that's how it was.

Bolsena is a deep lake, more than a hundred meters in places, and its water is famous for its clarity. It is filled by rain and underground springs, and only one small river flows out of it, so the water is renewed very slowly. You stand on the shore and realize that you are looking into the bowl of a former volcano, which over thousands of years has become one of the calmest waters in Italy.

Mirror-like scenes like this always remind me of one simple thing. To reflect the sky, the water doesn't have to do anything, only become still. While waves are running across it, there is no reflection, only ripples. It is the same with the soul, I think: we keep trying to do something so that heaven is reflected in it, but often we just need to stop being agitated and grow quiet. That is easy to say and hard to do, especially for a priest with a parish and endless tasks behind him. But that evening on the shore I managed it, for twenty minutes at least.

photos/2026-11-08/9.alt: Lake Bolsena at sunset under the branches
photos/2026-11-08/9.description:
Another shot from the same shore, just a little later. A branch with yellow leaves hangs down from above like a frame, the clouds have grown even darker, and the sunset on the left has flared up more strongly. Everything is reflected in the water: the clouds, the gaps between them, the gold. On the right, by the shore, there are thickets of dry reeds, and on the water, if you look closely, sits a small dark bird, a duck or a coot, I can't tell them apart. In the distance, on the right-hand shore, there are lights and houses.

We stood and watched this bird calmly swimming about; it couldn't care less about the sunset. And I was thinking that it is with this very lake that the story of St Christina is connected, the saint for whose sake we had come here today. According to tradition, she was the daughter of the local pagan ruler and, while still very young, came to believe in Christ. Her father tried to force her to renounce Him and in the end ordered a heavy stone to be tied to her and for her to be thrown into the lake. But the stone did not sink, and the girl came out onto the shore alive.
