Later she was martyred all the same, but this story about the stone that floated is remembered here, and they show it to pilgrims.

St Christina is venerated in our Church too; her feast is at the end of July. It was interesting to look at this water and realize that for the people here it is not just a beautiful lake but the very place from her Life. We are used to reading the Lives of the saints as old stories about faraway lands. And here it is, that faraway land: a branch overhead, a duck in the reeds, and the water into which a girl was once thrown, and the Lord did not give her up. The water that evening was very still, as if it remembered this too.

photos/2026-11-08/10.alt: An island and the sunset on the lake
photos/2026-11-08/10.description:
Here it is almost evening. On the left a dark promontory of stones juts out into the water, and at its very tip stands a weeping willow, quite see-through against the sky. The sun is already right at the line of the far shore, the clouds above it are lit up orange, and the water repeats all of this, only in blue-grey tones. Near the shore you can see stones in the water, and barely noticeable ripples spread across the surface.

I especially liked this promontory with the willow: a lone tree growing by the water, afraid of neither wind nor winter.

Somewhere over there, where the sun is setting, in the middle of the lake lie its two islands, Bisentina and Martana. I won't try to make them out in this photo. But there is a story about Martana that I learned in these days and that really caught hold of me. In the sixth century the queen of the Ostrogoths, Amalasuntha, the daughter of Theodoric, was exiled to this island. She was an educated woman, knew Greek and Latin, and tried to reconcile the Goths with the Romans, and the nobility disliked her for it. Her cousin, whom she herself had made co-ruler, betrayed her, and she was killed on the island. Her death became the pretext for a long war: the Emperor Justinian sent troops into Italy, and that war devastated the country for twenty years.

So it is that on a quiet lake, on a small island, a knot is tied that then drags whole nations along behind it. You look at this beauty and remember that human history is rarely as quiet as the water. And the willow still stands, and the sunset is still the same.

photos/2026-11-08/11.alt: The sun setting behind the trees by the lake
photos/2026-11-08/11.description:
A summer café on the shore, which in November is already taking a rest. Under big trees stand wooden tables, with chairs turned upside down on some of them; around it is a white picket fence, and light bulbs, not lit right now, hang on wires. On the left is an open pavilion with glass walls. And through the foliage, right between the branches, the sun is setting, and beneath it a golden strip stretches across the water. Everything in the frame is warm, yellow-orange, while the trunks and leaves against the light are almost black.

We stopped by this picket fence simply because the sun had settled so perfectly, exactly between the trees. The café was closed, the season was over, and, to be honest, we weren't hungry at all: at lunchtime in Civita we'd had stewed donkey, and it hadn't gone anywhere yet. But I imagined what it's like here in summer: every table taken, glasses clinking, children running down to the water. Now it is empty, and there is a charm of its own in this emptiness, as if the place is resting until spring, as we too will one day rest.

Bolsena has fed people since ancient times, and not only tourists. The eels from here were once famous throughout Italy. They say that Pope Martin IV, who lived in the thirteenth century, loved Bolsena eels stewed in wine so much that Dante placed him in Purgatory in the “Divine Comedy,” among the gluttons, where he purges himself by fasting of the Bolsena eels and wine. So if you see eel on a menu by the lake, you will be eating a dish that made it into a great poem. We didn't eat it, though; the café was closed, and the donkey was enough for us for the whole day. We'll leave the eel for next time, if God grants us to come here again.

photos/2026-11-08/12.alt: A chapel with majolica in Bolsena
photos/2026-11-08/12.description:
A quiet chapel with warm pink-terracotta walls. The ceiling here is not plastered but bare, rough stone; it looks like this is a part of the church cut into the rock. In the middle is a simple stone altar, and above it, in a niche, a relief of glazed ceramic: on a blue background the crucified Christ, with two standing figures on either side, most likely the Mother of God and the Apostle John, all in a green frame of leaves and fruit. On either side are wrought-iron lamps, on the right a narrow pointed window and a candle stand. And in the corner a grey metal cabinet on castors, which doesn't fit into a medieval chapel at all. But let it stay in the frame: the church is alive, services are held here, and the things they need are kept here.

We were in Bolsena, at the Basilica of St Christina, after lunch in Civita. The church itself goes partly into the hillside; below are grottoes and ancient underground passages, and everything there breathes stone. It was here, at St Christina's, in 1263 that the miracle I've already written about took place: blood on the Holy Gifts in the hands of a doubting priest. And here they also show the stone, the very one, according to tradition, with which the saint was thrown into the lake and on which the prints of her feet remained.

Glazed-clay reliefs like this one were invented in Florence in the fifteenth century, in the workshop of Luca della Robbia, and were later made all over Italy. Whose work this one is, I won't venture to say, but the manner is recognizable at once. And one more thing. We call her Christina of Tyre, but here they are sure she is from here, from Bolsena. I didn't argue. The saint is one, and she prays for everyone who comes to her, whether from Tyre or from Florida.

photos/2026-11-09/1.alt: Two riders before the ride at La Cacciata
photos/2026-11-09/1.description:
A riding club near Orvieto, half past nine in the morning, and we haven't set off yet. On the left, on a light, almost white horse, sits our companion in black, red hair sticking out from under her helmet, grinning from ear to ear. On the right, on a black horse, is the second one, in a helmet, blue jeans and a black top, turned towards the first and saying something to her. Under the black horse's saddle is an orange checked saddle blanket. Behind them are old olive trees with silvery leaves, a wooden fence, plastic crates, and in the distance on the left you can see fields.

This is La Cacciata. The guide spoke Italian, and it seems the horses also understood only Italian. That didn't bother us. Before setting out everyone was given helmets, everything was checked and tightened, and there you are sitting up high, on this huge, warm, living back, and you suddenly realize that all your confidence now depends on what mood the horse is in. Ours, thank God, were in a good mood.

Notice the olive trees. November in Umbria is just the time of the olive harvest; all around the area in these days they spread nets under the trees and gather the crop, and the olive mills make the new oil. The olive tree lives a very long time, some stand for several hundred years, and these ones, gnarled and thick, were clearly not planted yesterday either. In Scripture the olive is always a sign of peace and of God's blessing; it is no accident that the dove brought Noah an olive leaf of all things. A good start for a horse ride: olive trees, sun through the clouds, and two riders having a wonderful time.

photos/2026-11-09/2.alt: A selfie in a helmet on the ride
photos/2026-11-09/2.description:
A selfie straight from the saddle. In the foreground is a face in a black helmet, fair hair in a plait, the helmet strap under the chin, a fluffy black top. Behind, on the path, walks a white horse with a red-haired rider on it, and behind her one more person in a helmet. To the right and left are vineyards: bare vines on stakes, the leaves already fallen, the grass green, and further off woods with yellow patches and a blue sky with clouds.

I love this photo because it shows what the ride was really like. Not a grand parade, but an unhurried walk in single file along a path between the vines, when the horses know the way themselves and all you try to do is not get in their way. Two hours went by just like that, among vineyards and olive trees. We had our ride, everyone loved it, and I think you can see it on her face.

The vineyards near Orvieto are no accident. The local white wine, Orvieto Classico, has been known since ancient times, and the cellars for it have been cut right into the tuff rock under the town since Etruscan times. They say the craftsmen who painted the cathedral were paid partly in wine. Now, in November, the harvest is long since gathered, the vines are resting until spring, and soon they will be pruned. Looking at these bare bushes, you remember: “I am the vine, ye are the branches.” In winter the vine looks completely dead, a dry stick on a stake. But in spring it comes to life again and bears grapes. A good image for November, when both in nature and in the soul there can be a season like this.

photos/2026-11-09/3.alt: A rider on a white horse by the stables
photos/2026-11-09/3.description:
This is what the stables at La Cacciata look like. A long, low building of yellowish-brown stone blocks, apparently the same tuff that Orvieto stands on, under a slate roof, with semicircular openings and green stall doors. On the right, on the wall, all sorts of gear: a floodlight, an electrical box, hooks, brushes, a bucket. In the foreground is a light-coloured horse, and on it a rider in black, red hair showing from under her helmet, sitting side-on to us and smiling at the camera.

By the stables we wanted to photograph every horse together with its rider, as a keepsake. This white one, I think, behaved impeccably: standing still, putting up with it, posing.

By the way, about colour. Horses that we call white, horse people usually call grey. Such horses are often born dark and get lighter over the years, and by old age become almost completely white. So a white horse is most often an experienced horse. In the language of the Bible and the Church the white horse is something special altogether: in Revelation the One who is called Faithful and True rides out on a white horse, and St George in icons is also on a white horse. I remembered this as I looked at this calm horse by the old stables, and, to be honest, it seemed to me that she had exactly that expression, wise and patient, like an elderly nun who has already seen everything.

The morning turned out better than we expected. Next on the plan were the warm waters, but more about that in the story of the day.

photos/2026-11-09/4.alt: With the black horse by the stables
photos/2026-11-09/4.description:
By the stables. On the left is the green iron door of a stall, on the right a wall of porous yellow stone blocks, and between them our companion in a black top and blue jeans, fair hair down to her shoulders. She is holding the black horse by the muzzle and saying something to him, face to face. The horse is big, all black, with a leather halter, and on his back a saddle on an orange checked saddle blanket. To the right, behind him, is the darkness of the stall and hay on the floor.

We quickly made friends with the horses, and nobody wanted to leave them. The horse stands calmly, listening, as if he understands everything, whatever language you speak to him in.

There is something about horses that calms people. The animal is huge and strong, with one movement it could knock you down, yet it stands quietly and nuzzles your palm. In the Book of Job the Lord, showing man the world, asks him: “Hast thou given the horse strength? hast thou clothed his neck with a mane?” And then follows a whole description of the horse, which “mocketh at fear” and “is not affrighted.” It is one of the most beautiful passages about animals in all of Scripture. People have got so used to horses that they no longer marvel at them, and God seems to be saying: look closely, this is a miracle, you know.

Looking at this photo, I see exactly that kind of attentiveness. Not “had a ride and off she went,” but she stopped, looked the horse in the eyes and thanked him. A good habit, and not only with horses.

photos/2026-11-09/5.description:
The last shot from the stables. The same green door, the same wall of yellow porous blocks, and the same black horse, only now everyone is looking at the camera. Well, almost everyone: the horse is looking off somewhere to the side, while our companion has pressed her cheek against his head, laid her palm on his forehead and is smiling broadly. The horse has a small white star on his forehead, his mane is tousled, and on his back is a saddle on an orange checked saddle blanket.

There are photos that simply came out well, and there are ones in which you can see that the person is happy. This is one of the second kind. After two hours in the saddle your legs ache, your hands smell of horse, and on your face there's this.

Soon after the ride a question ripened in us: where are the warm pools around here, we want to bathe. And we drove to Tuscany, to San Casciano dei Bagni, a little town of hot springs. There, as is well known, I nearly climbed in to bathe in an old washhouse. In Italian towns these public washhouses, lavatoio, often stand under a roof, with stone troughs and running water, so it wasn't hard to make a mistake. Women washed their laundry there for centuries and, probably, gossiped no less than at a Roman fountain in Herculaneum. Good thing I asked first. In the end we bathed in a real thermal pool, and after the horses it was exactly what we needed.

And the horse with the star stayed at La Cacciata. I hope he remembers us too, at least when he's given a carrot.

photos/2026-11-09/6.description:
The façade of Orvieto Cathedral at night. It is lit from below, and the marble seems warm, pinkish-gold against a completely black sky. Below are three portals, the central one the tallest, with dark bronze doors. Between the portals are flat marble pilasters covered in fine carving. Above them, on the cornice, are the dark silhouettes of bronze figures. Higher up are three triangular gables with mosaics, in the centre a round rose window in a square frame, surrounded by niches with little figures, and at the edges four slender spires. Under the lights the mosaics glow blue and gold.

At about half past seven in the evening we were finally standing in front of it. Finally, because before that we had spent a long time walking the little streets and couldn't find it. The cathedral, which can be seen from the plain kilometres away, hides behind the houses in the town itself, and you come out onto it suddenly, from a narrow street into the square. And then it simply comes crashing down on you with all its height. The square on a November evening was almost empty, and we stood in the middle of it with our heads tilted back until our necks ached. We listened to the story of the cathedral: about the corporal from Bolsena, about Maitani, about Emilio Greco's doors.

I have already written about the first stone, laid on 13 November 1290. I'll only add that the anniversary falls exactly on this Friday. It took almost three centuries to build, the architects changed, but the idea held: the cathedral as an ark for a single holy relic. Down below, on the pilasters, is the whole Bible, from the Creation to the Last Judgment, and at the very top the Coronation of the Mother of God in Heaven. First the story of man, then his hope.

And then we went to have dinner in an old trattoria, and I ordered pigeon Umbrian-style, alla ghiotta, and kept asking again whether it really was pigeon. Pigeon. In Italy, as it turned out, they serve even stranger things for dinner, and very tasty ones.

photos/2026-11-10/1.alt: The rooftops of Orvieto from above
photos/2026-11-10/1.description: This is what Orvieto looks like if you climb the Torre del Moro, which is what we did towards midday. There are more than two hundred steps, and on the last flights you are thinking not about beauty but about your age. But at the top you forgive everything. Below lies the town, built as if from one and the same roof tile: the roofs grey with ginger, faded, with little chimneys like tiny houses, with aerials, here and there a terrace on which someone has grown a whole little garden in pots. Through the middle of the frame a street runs off into the distance straight as a string, still wet after the morning rain. Tiny people walk along it, some with umbrellas, some without, and a little red van drives by. And further on, beyond the last houses, there are already fields, yellow autumn trees and a misty valley. From here you can clearly see how closely people lived here. The houses stand shoulder to shoulder, the little streets between them can barely be made out, and there isn't a metre of free space. The reason is simple: Orvieto stands on a rock of tuff, on a flat summit, and it had nowhere to grow except upwards and downwards. Tuff, as I said in the travel recording, is compressed volcanic ash; it is soft and easy to cut, so over the centuries hundreds of caves, cellars and wells were hollowed out under the town. So it turns out we are looking only at the top floor. I like that from the tower the town looks not like a postcard but like a family: all together, crowded, a bit higgledy-piggledy, but under one roof. And somewhere very close, behind our backs, stands the cathedral, for whose sake all of this once came together.

photos/2026-11-10/2.alt: A painted choir loft above the crucifix in an Orvieto church
photos/2026-11-10/2.description:
In the morning it was raining in Orvieto; we were walking around the town following my list, and in one of the churches not far from the cathedral I looked up and saw this. Above the crucifix hangs a wooden balcony, a choir loft, painted all over. On it chubby little angels play pipes, funny horned masks peep out from the scrolls at the edges, and garlands of flowers twine about. And in the centre, in a round medallion on a red background, is a small scene: the Mother of God with the Child sits under a palm tree, beside her Joseph with his staff and a donkey, and above an angel flies. This is the Rest of the Holy Family on the Flight into Egypt. Below the loft the wall is painted with a gold pattern, like costly fabric, and against this background hangs a crucifix with a radiance around the cross.

Where exactly I took this, I can no longer say for sure from memory. It isn't the cathedral itself: there the walls are austere, striped, of black basalt and light stone, while here it is Baroque, white pilasters, gold.

A choir loft, or in Italian cantoria, is a gallery for the singers and the organ. Music sounded from here during services, which is why the angels on it have instruments. The palm tree on the medallion isn't there for nothing either. There is an old apocryphal tradition that during the flight into Egypt a palm tree bent down to the weary Mary so that She could pick its fruit.

I liked how all of this is arranged. Above, music, angels and a family on the road, fleeing from Herod. Below, the Cross. Christ's whole life from the very beginning was heading towards this Cross, and the flight into Egypt was its first alarm. The singers sang above the crucifix, and the crucifix silently bore all this joy upon itself. To my mind, a very honest pairing.

photos/2026-11-10/3.description: The morning in Orvieto began with rain, and we went for a walk following my list of addresses made in advance, while along the way the town kept slipping us houses like this one. Pink, or more precisely that warm apricot-pink colour which for some reason never looks sugary in Italy. Grey shutters, grey bands across the façade, at the top roof tiles and a whole forest of TV aerials, as if the house is picking up signals from the entire peninsula at once. On two balconies there are geraniums and some other flowers in pots, and this in November, in the rain. On the left is another house, with a long wrought-iron balcony and stone blocks painted on its corner, and in front of it a tree with stiff, glossy leaves, a magnolia, I think. At the bottom, the top of a café umbrella has crept into the frame; they hadn't folded it, apparently in the hope that the rain would change its mind. I kept catching myself thinking that Italians decorate their houses not for tourists but for themselves. Nobody puts these geraniums on show on purpose; they are simply watered every day, because that's the done thing, because a window without flowers looks like an unmade bed. The shutters here are called persiane; they are wooden, with slanted slats, so that in summer they let the air in and keep the sun out. In summer in Umbria you probably couldn't survive without them, but now they just stand half open, like the eyes of someone who hasn't quite woken up yet. An ordinary house on an ordinary street, and it is exactly houses like this that make a town alive rather than an open-air museum.

photos/2026-11-10/4.alt: An arch over a cobbled street
photos/2026-11-10/4.description: This is a covered passage, of which there are many in Orvieto: the street dives under a house and comes out on the other side. Overhead is a low vault of dark tuff blocks, in patches of damp and old whitewash, and along it runs a string of light bulbs, switched off in the daytime, of course. Underfoot are wet cobbles laid in a fan pattern, on the sides iron lanterns on brackets, a window behind a grille and some sort of wooden board on the wall whose purpose I never did work out. And at the end, where the vault ends, it is bright: yellow walls, greenery in pots, a whole avenue of plants along the houses, and it seems the weather is already different there. Passages like these came about from lack of space. A town on a rock can't sprawl outwards, so houses were built right over the streets, rooms were thrown across from one side to the other, and below a passage was left for people and mules. The stone is the same, the local tuff, of which everything here is made: walls, vaults, cellars. Places like this always remind me of one simple thing that I sometimes say at confession: darkness can be short if you don't stop in the middle. You walk under a heavy vault, it is damp and cramped, and twenty steps later there is already light and flowers. Here you could see it literally, without any sermon.

photos/2026-11-10/5.alt: Flowers on a wall in a side street
photos/2026-11-10/5.description: Sometimes the most interesting thing in a town hangs right on the wall at eye level. In this side street in Orvieto identical terracotta pots are fixed all along the wall, and ivy hangs down from each one in long trails almost to the pavement. I went up closer and took one pot in close-up, while the street behind it dissolved into a soft blur: wet cobbles, yellow and pink walls, more pots, more greenery, a lantern. The ivy leaves are dark, veined, some already with brown autumn edges, and from the top sticks out a long, narrow leaf of some other plant, which has clearly ended up in someone else's pot and feels perfectly at home there. It was November, it was raining, and everything around was grey and brown, except for this greenery. Ivy is an amazing plant altogether. It doesn't need much soil, it clings to stone, grows in shade and in cold, and stays green all year round. No wonder that since ancient times it has been regarded as a sign of faithfulness and eternal life; it was carved on tombstones and woven into ornaments. Someone living in this side street evidently decided that the grey wall lacked life and hung it there with their own hands, pot by pot. I liked this more than many museum halls. The museum was made for us, but the pots were hung up for themselves and for the neighbours, and that made the side street feel like a shared courtyard where everyone knows each other.

photos/2026-11-10/6.alt: A yellow house with a restaurant sign
photos/2026-11-10/6.description: A yellow house on a cobbled square, and on it a simple inscription in old-style lettering: “Ristorante.” We didn't go in; it was a little after eleven in the morning, and an Italian restaurant at that time is only just waking up; people have lunch late here. But I couldn't walk past. Look at the doors: they are framed with stones of two colours, dark grey and light, laid alternately, in stripes. Exactly the same device as in the cathedral, where the walls are built of black basalt and light travertine, as if the church had been drawn in pencil. So it turns out the town speaks one language, from the main church to the door of an ordinary trattoria. Along the wall stand pot-bellied clay pots with some sort of prickly little shrubs, lanterns hang above the doors, there are blue shutters on the windows, and a flower box under one little window. Down below the plaster has already gone patchy and peeled: the stone draws moisture from the ground, and people here have evidently lived with that for centuries without worrying much about it. The pavement underfoot is of dark stone, wet and shining after the rain. I like façades like this for their honesty. The house doesn't pretend to be a palace; it is old, a bit worn, with wires and pipes on the outside, but people clearly live and cook in it, and in the evening it is probably noisy here and smells of garlic. And in the morning it stands quiet, yellow, under a grey sky, patiently waiting for the town to get hungry.

photos/2026-11-10/7.alt: A wrought-iron grille with the cathedral's lights
photos/2026-11-10/7.description: Through a wrought-iron grille you can see the Chapel of the Corporal in Orvieto Cathedral, for whose sake, by and large, the whole cathedral was built. We came here in the morning, in the rain. On the left are twisted columns of light stone, spiralled like candles, and further on a grille of iron quatrefoils, and through it a golden half-light: walls covered entirely in frescoes, lamps, pews, a few people sitting on the pews. On the grille is a sign: “Al culto del SS. Corporale,” that is, a place for the veneration of the Most Holy Corporal. This is not an exhibit but a chapel for prayer, and you can feel it: tourists here start whispering of their own accord. The corporal, let me remind you, is the linen cloth that is laid on the altar during the Liturgy. In 1263 a priest, Peter of Prague, who doubted that Christ is truly present in the Holy Gifts, was celebrating Mass in Bolsena, and blood seeped from the Host onto the cloth. The cloth was brought here, to Pope Urban IV, and a year later the Pope instituted the feast of Corpus Christi. The cloth itself is kept in a silver reliquary which, as I said in the audio recording, looks like the cathedral's façade in miniature. The day before yesterday we stood in Bolsena at the place where it all happened, and now we were standing by the cloth itself. For me, as a priest, there is nothing museum-like here. At every Liturgy I myself take the chalice in my hands and say the same words, and this story about a doubting priest feels very close to me. The Lord did not scold him for his doubt. He simply answered.

photos/2026-11-10/8.description: The pavement a few steps from the cathedral, photographed from above, right underfoot. Dark stones and light stones mixed together, in stripes here, any old how there, with grass pushing through between them. Higher up are the broad slabs of the steps, covered in patches of lichen, white, grey, greenish, so that each slab looks like a little map of an unknown archipelago. At the bottom is a straight kerb of light stone, and in the very corner of the frame lies a ginger autumn leaf. I photographed this because after the cathedral its stripes, black basalt and light travertine, were still before my eyes, and suddenly the same thing turned up underfoot. Of course, there is no great design behind this pavement. It's simply that in these parts there are two kinds of stone: a dark, hard one of volcanic origin, and a light, limy one. From them they built cathedrals, roads, steps and the thresholds of houses. But I still like to think that someone laying these stones had the walls of the cathedral before his eyes and did the same, as best he could. Lichen, by the way, grows very slowly, and patches like these build up over years and decades of clean air and quiet. That means people walk on these steps but don't trample them. The grass between the stones also says something of its own: the town is old, but the life in it is stubborn. It will find a crack and grow through.

photos/2026-11-10/9.alt: The tiled roofs of Orvieto in the mist
photos/2026-11-10/9.description: The roofs of Orvieto under a heavy grey sky, photographed near the cathedral, almost level with them. The tiles vary: on the far houses they are grey, old, as if sprinkled with ash, on the nearest house ginger, recently relaid. Chimneys stick up above the roofs, and each one is topped with its own little tiled roof, on some a gabled one, on others one like a tiny house with slits for the smoke. On the left is a wall of unplastered yellowish-brown stone, green shutters and a small balcony with a railing, and below yellow and white houses with arched windows. The sky at that moment was completely white, and the shot came out almost like a drawing. I looked at these chimneys for a long time. Here they are like a master's signature: every town has its own, and in Orvieto they are like this, with little roofs so that the rain doesn't flood the hearth. The stone wall on the left is built of tuff, the very stone the whole town stands on. It is soft, porous and easy to cut, so building with it is quick and cheap, and in summer these houses are cool. Tuff, let me remind you, is volcanic ash, once thrown out by the volcanoes where Lake Bolsena now lies. So, looking at these houses, I am looking at very ancient ash turned into walls in which people were born, married, baked bread and prayed. A quiet shot, nothing special, but for some reason it is dear to me: this is what an ordinary November day looks like in a town that has been living its own life for more than two thousand years.

photos/2026-11-10/10.alt: The “Last Judgment” relief on the façade of Orvieto Cathedral
photos/2026-11-10/10.description: This is hell. More precisely, the lower right part of the Last Judgment relief on the façade of Orvieto Cathedral, the very section about which I said in the audio story that it probably sent shivers down the spines of medieval parishioners. Yesterday evening we saw the façade under the lights, and today in the daytime we went right up close, and I realized that it sends shivers down modern spines too. The whole space is crammed with bodies. Snakes coil around the sinners, demons with bat wings seize them by the arms and by the hair, someone covers his face with his hands, someone screams with his mouth open, someone is already lying at the bottom, crushed. In the centre sits the chief demon, entwined with snakes, and under his feet flames are seething. Above all this, in the upper row, you can see the legs and bodies of those being led into hell. All the figures are naked, because before God there is nothing to cover. This is the work of the workshop of the Sienese Lorenzo Maitani, the master of the façade, from the beginning of the fourteenth century. The marble is delicate, almost lacy, with reddish traces of time on it. It's interesting that in our Orthodox churches the Last Judgment is traditionally painted on the west wall, so that a person sees it as he leaves the church for the world. But here it is on the façade, to the right of the entrance, and you see it before you go in. It seems to me this is not meant to frighten. Rather, it is so that a person stops on the threshold and honestly thinks about what he is bringing with him. And inside, in the Chapel of the Corporal, the answer awaits him: a mercy that is stronger than this whole nightmare.

photos/2026-11-10/11.alt: Sinners: a detail of the Last Judgment relief
photos/2026-11-10/11.description: A close-up of the same Last Judgment scene on the cathedral's façade. Here I went right up close and shot almost from below, so the figures loom over the viewer. These are the condemned. They are not being dragged by demons, they are not being burned, at least not in this fragment; they simply stand in a tight crowd, and one long, supple band, like the body of a snake, girds them all, binding them together. And then the faces. One has clutched his head, another has pressed his palm to his cheek, a third is gripping his own fingers, a fourth looks off to the side with the expression of a man on whom it has only just dawned. Someone with his mouth open, someone else, on the contrary, with a bitter, crooked smirk. Not a single face is the same. In places the marble has darkened and become covered in brown streaks, but this has only made the expressions stronger, as if the people were weeping stone. Maitani's craftsmen worked on these columns at the beginning of the fourteenth century, and I am struck by what psychologists they were. They could have depicted the sinners as caricatures, with horns and tails, but they depicted ordinary people. People like us. This is probably the most frightening thing about this relief: you look and recognize familiar expressions. They are all bound together, and that is no accident either. Sin is rarely the business of one person alone; it always drags others along with it. And salvation, if you think about it, doesn't happen alone either.

photos/2026-11-10/12.alt: A detail of the relief on the cathedral façade
photos/2026-11-10/12.description: This is perhaps my favourite fragment on the whole façade of Orvieto Cathedral: the resurrection of the dead, the lower left part of the Last Judgment relief. People are rising from stone coffins. In the centre is a woman, still waist-deep in a sarcophagus, holding her head with both hands as if from a deafening sound, and looking bewildered, as if she had been woken too early. To her left is another figure, curly-haired, leaning over the edge of the coffin; to her right a man, with a burial shroud thrown over his shoulders, is stepping over the side. At the right edge someone is pushing aside the lid of a sarcophagus, and on the lid you can see inlays of dark coloured stone. Above, out of frame, angels are blowing trumpets, and perhaps that is exactly why the woman has covered her ears. The marble has darkened, become covered in reddish spots and worn away in places, but the liveliness hasn't gone anywhere because of it. At every Sunday Liturgy we sing in the Creed: “I look for the resurrection of the dead.” This is not a metaphor and not just beautiful words. From the very beginning Christianity has believed that not only the soul but also the body will rise, this very body, with hands, curls and a bewildered face. And the fourteenth-century sculptors from the workshop of Lorenzo Maitani depicted it in a very human way: without solemnity, with surprise, with awkwardness, with the way a person clambers out of a cramped space. I really like that the first emotion of the risen here is not fear but amazement. That's probably how it will be. We'll wake up and won't believe it at first.

photos/2026-11-10/13.alt: A marble pilaster of Orvieto Cathedral
photos/2026-11-10/13.description: One of the four marble columns, or pilasters, of the façade of Orvieto Cathedral, in its entirety: the right-hand one, with the Last Judgment. It is hard to photograph so that it all fits in; I had to step back and hold my phone up high. It reads from top to bottom, like a page. At the very top is Christ in glory, in an oval radiance, with angels around Him, and the apostles seated in rows on either side. Below are several tiers of the righteous; they are led by angels and stand in calm, orderly groups. And at the very bottom everything divides in two: on the left people are coming out of their graves, on the right is that same hell with snakes and demons that I photographed in close-up. And running through the whole relief from bottom to top are winding stone stems, branches and scrolls, which divide the scenes into tiers and at the same time bind them into a single whole. Four such pilasters stand between the doors of the cathedral, and together, as I said yesterday in the audio recording, they make up a Bible in stone: from the creation of the world on the left one, through the prophets and the earthly life of Christ, to the Last Judgment on the right one. The master of the façade was the Sienese Lorenzo Maitani; the work went on in the first half of the fourteenth century. What I like about this composition is that there is no chaos in it. Even the Last Judgment here is built like a church: at the top is Christ, and everything looks to Him. People tend to see only catastrophe in the end of the world, but the medieval master saw order. The Judgment is just, the Judge is merciful, and the last word belongs not to the demons in the bottom corner but to the One who sits at the top.

photos/2026-11-10/14.alt: View of the cathedral over the rooftops
photos/2026-11-10/14.description: Again the view from the Torre del Moro, but now in the other direction, toward the cathedral. Heavy clouds hung over the town, and over the hills in the distance light was breaking through them, so that half the sky was dark gray and the other half almost silver. The cathedral rises above the roofs like a ship above little boats. You can clearly see its striped side, its long roof and the façade with its pointed pinnacles, where last night the gold of the mosaics glowed in the floodlights. Everything else, the tiled roofs, the yellow and pink houses, the octagonal dome of some church in the foreground, the cypresses on the right, looks like a toy next to it. In the morning we had been inside, by the corporal of Bolsena and the frescoes of Signorelli, and now we were looking at the same cathedral from above, and that is a completely different feeling. From inside the cathedral is huge and quiet, but from outside you can see how it holds up the whole town. They began building it in 1290, on the thirteenth of November, that is, almost exactly in these very days, only seven hundred and thirty-six years ago. And they kept building it for almost three hundred years. Just think: whoever laid the first stone never saw the façade, or the mosaics, or the frescoes, and knew he would not see them. They built for their children and grandchildren, for people they would never meet. It seems to me that this is the main lesson of such cathedrals. We like to do things whose results we will see ourselves, but here people worked for the future for three centuries in a row and did not complain. Probably because they worked not for themselves, but for God.

photos/2026-11-10/15.alt: View of Orvieto from the Torre del Moro
photos/2026-11-10/15.description: One more view from the Torre del Moro in Orvieto, this time toward the side where the town drops away into a green valley. In the foreground are tiled roofs of old dark stone and green shutters, and on the right a large building with a bell wall, in whose arches you can see the bells, and with a round window in the pediment. In front of it tall dark cypresses stand in a row, like a guard of honor, and between them the autumn trees have already turned yellow. Beyond the town are hills, woods, fields, and all of it in a light haze, as if an artist had gone over the background with white paint. This is still Orvieto; the shot was taken from the same tower around noon, before we left. Which church exactly this is, I can't say with certainty, and I don't want to guess. But the cypresses here are certainly no accident. In Italy they have long been planted by churches and cemeteries: a slender evergreen tree reaching upward long ago became a sign of remembrance and eternity. Next to one it is good to think of those who have departed. The belfry itself is made as a wall with arches, the bells hang right in the openings, in plain view, and they probably ring across the whole valley. What I especially love in this shot is the light: overcast, soft, without shadows. In such weather stone looks warm and greenery looks deep. A couple of hours later we were already driving from here to Lake Bolsena, and this view stayed in my memory as the last picture of Orvieto from above.

photos/2026-11-10/16.description: A narrow lane on the western edge of Orvieto, taken just before we left, around two in the afternoon. On the right is a wall of large brown tufa blocks, uneven, as if molded by hand; on the left a house with windows behind diamond-patterned grilles; underfoot wet cobblestones with blades of grass along the walls. And ahead there is an arch thrown between the houses, with a lantern on a bracket, and in the gap beneath it emptiness suddenly opens up: the town ends, beyond is a cliff and a green valley far below. I like that it is like this everywhere in Orvieto: you walk along a cramped street, and suddenly it runs into the sky. The town stands on a huge tufa rock, and on three sides there are sheer walls dropping down from the last houses. People have lived on this rock since Etruscan times. Most historians think that the Etruscan city of Velzna stood here, one of the richest in Etruria. In 264 before the Nativity of Christ the Romans took it and destroyed it, and moved its inhabitants down to the shore of Lake Bolsena. The rock then stood almost empty for a long time, and when people settled on it again, the town came to be called simply Urbs Vetus, that is, “the old city.” From this Latin “old city” came the name Orvieto. And that very day we were driving to Lake Bolsena, in the footsteps of those same resettled Etruscans. There is something in this arch of a door into another world: behind you stone, damp, grilles, and ahead open space and air. And so we said goodbye to Orvieto. The town on the rock saw us off politely, without fuss, simply opening a view of the road at the end of the street.

photos/2026-11-10/17.alt: A walk under a red umbrella in Montefiascone
photos/2026-11-10/17.description: Montefiascone met us with rain and fog. One of my girls is walking along the wet cobblestones under a red umbrella, long red hair, black coat, and I am photographing her from behind. On both sides of the street are little Italian cars, parked as tightly as only Italians can manage. On the right is a large old house: a portal of rough-hewn bulging stones, grilles on the windows, a brick wall. On the left, peeling orange plaster. Somewhere ahead, beyond the fog, the Rocca dei Papi, the papal fortress, was supposed to be standing, with the best view of Lake Bolsena. To be honest, we pictured the view from the description; the fog ate everything. Before this I had proudly parked our car under a “residents only” sign, so the walk began with moving it, but that is another story. Montefiascone stands on a high hill above the lake, and its huge dome of the cathedral of St Margaret can be seen from dozens of kilometers away. The Via Francigena runs through the town, the ancient pilgrim road from Canterbury to Rome, along which for a thousand years people walked on foot to the tombs of the Apostles Peter and Paul. We walked much less, and with umbrellas, but I liked thinking that underfoot were the same stones the pilgrims had trudged over, wet, tired, with the one hope of getting there. In general I liked that this little town in the rain does not pretend to be a resort. It simply lives: cars, shutters, shops, and a red umbrella in the middle of a gray street, like a small celebration.

photos/2026-11-10/18.alt: A bottle of local wine in a shop
photos/2026-11-10/18.description: In a shop in Montefiascone they showed us this bottle, and it was impossible to walk past it after we had spent the whole drive from Orvieto listening to the story of the bishop and his servant. The dark blue label reads: “Est! Est!! Est!!! di Montefiascone,” and below it is a small picture in medieval style with horsemen. The bottle is held by the man behind the counter; in the frame you can see only his beard, striped sweater and a ring on his finger, and in his other hand he has a corkscrew at the ready. Behind him are blurred taps and big bottles; you can see that here wine is not only sold but also poured. The legend is well known. In 1111 a German bishop, Johann Fugger, was traveling to Rome and sent his servant Martin ahead to write “Est,” that is, “it is,” in chalk on the doors of inns with good wine. In Montefiascone the servant wrote it three times, with three exclamation marks. The bishop arrived, tasted it, and went no further toward Rome. His grave, they say, is still shown today in the church of San Flaviano at the foot of the town. The wine is white and local, and the grapes for it grow on the volcanic slopes around Lake Bolsena. What I like about this story is that it is funny and a little edifying at the same time. The bishop was traveling to Rome, to the Apostles, but got stuck at a wine barrel and never made it. A good occasion for a sermon about the distracting joys of life. But I did not preach it in the shop, especially since the Lord's first miracle was at Cana of Galilee, where He turned water into wine, and that wine, according to the governor of the feast, turned out to be the best.

photos/2026-11-10/19.alt: Fresco of a grape press on a wall
photos/2026-11-10/19.description: Right on an old wall of dark tufa blocks in Montefiascone there is a large painting, and of course it is about wine. On the left a man carries a basket of grapes on his back; next to him stand two ladies in long dresses, one in red, the other in pink. In the center is a big wooden vat full of grapes; a young man stands in it treading the grapes with his feet, and another hands him a jug from above. A girl in orange holds a jug under the stream of must that flows from the vat into a tub. To the right of the tree a lad in a russet jacket and white stockings is dancing or walking, with a bunch of grapes in his hand, and next to him on a small plaque are Roman numerals, apparently a date. Under everyone's feet is a meadow of tiny flowers, as on old tapestries. The painting is done in the spirit of medieval miniatures, bright, naive and very joyful. The grape harvest in these parts was always a feast for the whole village, and judging by this painting, they trod the grapes with their feet, merrily and as a whole family. Montefiascone has lived by wine for many centuries, and all its fame rests on the legend of “Est! Est!! Est!!!” that we heard on the way. This picture reminded me that in the Bible the vineyard is one of the most frequent images: the Lord says, “I am the true vine,” and there are the parables of the husbandmen. Land, labor, shared joy and wine on the table. All of this is very much in the spirit of the Gospel, as long as you don't overdo the last item.

photos/2026-11-10/20.description:
Two old houses in Montefiascone, pressed against each other like old men on a bench. The one on the left is narrow and tall, orange, with brown shutters and a wooden door under a semicircular arch, with a fanlight above the door. The one on the right is a warm yellow; a stone staircase with iron railings rises to its green door, and moss grows in the cracks between the steps. The doors and windows are framed in dark gray stone, and the corner of the house is built of the same rough gray blocks. On the wall are mailboxes, wires, a lantern on a bracket. And on the left, beyond the posts with a chain, there is nothing, only white fog.

Somewhere out there, beyond the fog, Lake Bolsena was supposed to be. Montefiascone stands on a high hill, and on this side the town drops away, and on a clear day you can probably see the whole bowl of the former volcano from here. We got a white wall. But in such fog the houses looked as if they were painted on an old postcard.

The gray stone around the doors here is almost everywhere the same. Most likely it is peperino, the volcanic stone of these parts. Its name comes from the word for “pepper”: the gray stone is sprinkled with dark specks, like ground pepper. In Tuscia it has been used for centuries to frame doors and windows and to make steps and fountains.

That day I learned the local news: near Acquapendente, quite close by, there had been a small earthquake, a 2.6. A very weak tremor; we didn't even feel it. The land here is volcanic and still alive, yet the houses stand for centuries. It brings to mind the Gospel words about the house built upon a rock: the rain, and the winds, and the fog, and still it stands. Here, true, all the stone is volcanic, but judging by these walls, it holds up pretty well.

photos/2026-11-10/21.description:
Montefiascone met us with fog so thick that the street simply dissolved into white at the end. This is one of those little streets we climbed up toward the Rocca dei Papi. The wet cobblestones gleam, the walls are orange and ochre, on the windowsills are pots of some hardy greenery that November doesn't bother at all, and the old stone house on the left is half overgrown with ivy. Across the pavement are drain grates: the town stands on a high hill, and the water here is always hurrying down to the lake.

We climbed without hurrying. First, though, we had to go back and move the car from under the “residents only” sign I had so proudly started with. At the top, they say, is the best view of all of Lake Bolsena, of the bowl of the former volcano with its two islands. We took that view on faith: the fog ate it whole. But in such fog the town was quiet, empty and somehow honest, without the postcard gloss.

The Via Francigena runs through Montefiascone, the old pilgrim road from Canterbury to Rome. For a thousand years people walked on foot over stones just like these, to the tombs of the Apostles Peter and Paul, and they probably got soaked too and didn't see the lake either. For some reason I find this comforting: a pilgrimage, after all, is not about the view from the mountain, but about where you are going. And for those who still need a landmark, above the town stands the huge dome of the cathedral of St Margaret, one of the largest in Italy. On a clear day it can be seen from dozens of kilometers away. That day we couldn't make it out properly either.

photos/2026-11-10/22.alt: Gate in an old wall with a bust of a pope, Tuscania at night
photos/2026-11-10/22.description:
In the evening Tuscania turned out to be empty, and that is putting it mildly. A Tuesday, November, no one on the streets, only lanterns on the walls and dark cobblestones. This shot is exactly about that emptiness. An old stone wall, a brick arch with a fan-shaped grille, and behind it a little inner courtyard glowing with yellow light, as if someone had forgotten to switch off the sun in there. On the right, in a lit niche, a white bust of a pope. The pavement goes down in steps, each stretch separated by its own strip of stone, so that both the pedestrian and the car have something to grip on the slope.

We walked through the town slowly, in no hurry, because there was literally nowhere to hurry to. And in such silence the old town suddenly comes to resemble a stage set from which all the actors have stepped out for a minute. The walls here are thick, of that same volcanic tufa on which this whole land stands, and they hold the darkness very well.

They tell a beautiful legend about Tuscania. Supposedly Ascanius, the son of the Trojan Aeneas, came here, found on the hill a dog with twelve puppies, and decided that this was a sign to found a city. Hence the name: “tus” and “cane,” dog. Scholars say, more dully, that the name comes from the Tusci, that is, the Etruscans. And in February of nineteen seventy-one there was a strong earthquake here; people died, and houses and both of the famous Romanesque basilicas were damaged. The town was restored for a long time, carefully, stone by stone. Looking at walls like these at night, you would never suspect it. And one more clarification that I kept repeating to myself all evening: we are not in Tuscany. Tuscania is Lazio.

photos/2026-11-11/1.alt: Dancers among trees, Tomb of the Triclinium
photos/2026-11-11/1.description:
The left wall of the Tomb of the Triclinium, closer up. Here is a dance in a grove. On the left a young man in a short transparent chiton holds something to his chest, apparently a lyre; next a dancer in a patterned dress with a dark cloak spread out like wings; then a man dancing with his arms flung up; and one more woman in a long dress with small dots. Between them are slender little trees, and on the branches sit birds, one right above the head of the first dancer. Below runs a band with a running wave, and the ceiling above it all is in a red-and-white check.

Notice how the artist showed the fabric. The dancer's dress is decorated with a fine pattern, while the young man's chiton is almost transparent; you can see his leg through it. All this with a few lines and one or two colors. The men are reddish-brown, the women light; that was the custom among the Etruscans. And everyone is in motion: not a single figure that is simply standing.

Time is visible in the photo too. The plaster has flaked off in places, and here and there are white patches where the paint has not survived. In the lower right the glass of the barrier is reflected. Over such a wall you want to stand in silence: there is not much to say, you just want to look.

Scholars think that such a dance is connected with the festival of Dionysus, the god of wine. For the Etruscans it meant the fullness of life, which they wanted to take with them over there. For me this is a little sad and very human. People who loved life so much that they painted their grave with it. David, too, danced before the ark with all his might. Joy, in my view, does not contradict faith at all.

photos/2026-11-11/2.alt: Brick arch with a grille and a bust of a pope in a niche, Tuscania
photos/2026-11-11/2.description:
In the morning the gate looked quite different than at night. Yesterday evening it was in darkness, with a lantern and yellow light behind the grille, but now you can see everything: the wall is built of reddish tufa mixed with gray stone, the arch of old brick, a wrought-iron fan above the opening, and the iron gate leaf thrown open inward. Beyond the gate is a small paved courtyard, a dark wooden door with a stone frame, and in front of it a white statue. On the right, in a pinkish niche, a white bust of a pope beneath a coat of arms with the keys of the Apostle Peter. Simple life around very old stones.

Ahead lay a long Etruscan day. Tarquinia is twenty-five minutes from here, and the whole way we listened to a talk about the city of the dead, which for two and a half thousand years has been looking across the valley at the city of the living. But before going down underground, it was nice to see this living little town in daylight.

In the Middle Ages Tuscania was one of the main towns of the whole region, more important than Viterbo, and very early on it got its own bishop. Then it lost the rivalry, grew poor and fell asleep. And, as often happens, poverty turned out to be the best restorer: there was no money for rebuilding, so much has remained untouched here. Arches like this, patched with brick over tufa, tell history better than any plaque. Every century mended something, throwing nothing away.

photos/2026-11-11/3.description:
An overcast morning in Tuscania, a small square in the old town. The cobblestones are laid in fans, the houses are yellow, pink and the color of old terracotta, the shutters dark green, and on the roofs are antennas and chimneys. A blue sign with the letter “T” honestly warns that there is a dead end ahead, and next to it is a no-parking sign which, judging by the cars by the yellow house, is understood creatively. On the right is a low stone parapet, beyond which the street goes down.

What I like most here are the outside staircases. Stone steps lead straight from the street to the door of the second floor, with a small landing at the top and iron railings. In these parts, in Tuscia, such staircases are a common thing on old houses: downstairs there was usually a shop, a workshop or a storeroom, and people lived upstairs. The pink house in the back has the same kind of staircase, only more modest, with a pot of flowers on a step.

We stood for a while, took some photos and headed to the car: ahead were Tarquinia, the necropolis and the museum. On such mornings the town has not yet fully woken up, and it feels as if you are peeking at it a little. Yesterday evening it was just as empty here, only dark.

Tuscania stands on a tufa hill above the little river Marta, in the very heart of the ancient Etruscan land. Around the town there are many underground tombs in the rocks, and noble Etruscan families lived here several centuries before the Nativity of Christ. It's rather funny: we went off for a whole day to see the Etruscans in the neighboring town, although they lie literally under our feet. But the most famous Etruscan paintings are, after all, in Tarquinia, and that is exactly what we were going for.

photos/2026-11-11/4.alt: Modern stone relief in the Etruscan spirit near the Monterozzi necropolis
photos/2026-11-11/4.description:
Even before going down into the first tomb, we got stuck by this block of stone in a yard under an olive tree. On the left a bearded man reclines, leaning on his elbow, exactly the way Etruscans recline on the lids of sarcophagi. Next to him, shoulder to shoulder, a whole menagerie: animal and human faces, an owl with huge round eyes, horses' heads with manes, some creature with a curled tail. Set into the stone is a small terracotta tile with a relief, like a signature or a seal. The whole thing stands on stone and brick supports, with grass all around.

At first we honestly decided that we were looking at something ancient, found somewhere nearby. Then we took a closer look at the background: a white van, a little shed, red plastic chairs. It turned out to be a modern work by a local craftsman. We could have been disappointed, but no. It is made with real knowledge, with the same love for the feast, for animals and for strange faces that we then saw all day on the walls of the tombs.

The motif of the reclining man is the main one here. The Etruscans depicted the deceased not lying motionless, but reclining at a feast, cup in hand, alive and content. That is how they wanted to remember him, and that is probably how he himself wanted to remain. The owls, horses and beasts around him are also from the same ancient vocabulary: the horse as an image of the last journey, the predators as guardians. This craftsman clearly knows that vocabulary.

I liked the very idea. Two and a half thousand years ago stone carvers worked here, and now once again someone sits in a yard on a plastic chair and carves stone. Sometimes a tradition continues not in a museum, but next to a van.

photos/2026-11-11/5.alt: Painting with predators and a festival among trees, probably the Tomb of the Jugglers
photos/2026-11-11/5.description:
Every tomb in the Monterozzi necropolis begins the same way: a small hut in the grass, a door, a steep staircase down, glass and a button. You press it, the light comes on, and out of the darkness comes a room like this one. A low gabled ceiling, a floor of bare tufa, and along the walls a wide band of painting above a dark dado.

In the triangle above the back wall are two predators on either side of a red projection that holds up the beam: on the left a ginger lion with its jaws open, on the right a gray-blue cat that looks like a panther. Below are stripes of red and blue, and beneath them a festival among slender little trees with blue leaves. A flute player, another musician, in the center a female figure with some object on her head, in front of her a man with his arm raised, and on the right an elderly man sits on a stool with a stick and watches it all like a spectator at a show. It looks like the tomb that is called the Tomb of the Jugglers: there a girl balances a stand on her head, and the seated old man, probably the owner of the tomb himself, watches the game. But that name is not in my notes, so I say it cautiously.

You can see how much plaster has fallen off: yellow patches all over the wall, like a map of unknown islands. And still the figures are alive, with movement, with a turn of the head.

This is the early, bright period of Etruscan painting. There are no demons at the doors here yet, no fear. Death for these people looked like a continuation of the festival: music, games, trees, spectators. You stand down there, in the cold tufa, and think that they very much wanted the festival never to end. And we know that the real feast is still ahead.

photos/2026-11-11/6.alt: False door and Charun demons, Tomb of the Charuns
photos/2026-11-11/6.description:
This is one of the latest tombs we saw, and you feel it at once. The Tomb of the Charuns. It was found in nineteen sixty, and painted around two hundred and seventy-five years before the Nativity of Christ, in a dark time when the Etruscans were losing city after city to Rome.

It is built on two levels. First a staircase leads into an antechamber with benches, where the relatives performed the memorial rite. And from the antechamber separate narrow staircases go down, each into its own simple burial room. The photo shows just such a staircase: stone benches on the sides, and between them a passage going down. Above it a false door is carved and painted in the wall, with bands and round studs, like a real one, heavy, iron-bound. Behind it is solid tufa, but the meaning is clear to anyone: this is the entrance to the afterworld.

On either side of the door stand demons, the Charuns. On the left a winged one, on the right a figure in a short red garment. Charun is the Etruscan double of the Greek Charon; he was painted with a hooked nose and disheveled hair, often with a hammer. By the heads you can see letters; these are their names in Etruscan. They are written from right to left, and the letters look like Greek ones, but of course I couldn't read them.

In the morning we had seen tombs with feasting, birds and dolphins, where a festival waited behind the door. Here, two and a half centuries later, the door is already guarded by sentinels. They don't attack, they just stand and wait. So you can see from the walls how a whole people's soul grew dark. I stood at this door and thought how lucky we are: we know Who said, “I am the door.”

photos/2026-11-11/7.alt: Tomb of Hunting and Fishing: birds and a boat
photos/2026-11-11/7.description:
This shot was taken through a doorway, and that is the whole point. The Tomb of Hunting and Fishing consists of two rooms, one behind the other, and you can't go into the second, main one, only look in from the first. The dark frame around the picture is the stone of the doorway.

At the top, in the triangle under the ceiling, the owners of the tomb are feasting, with servants around them, and something hangs above, apparently wreaths. And below, the sea begins. Birds fly over the water, red and blue, as if the artist had scattered them by the handful. Below is a boat with fishermen, on the right on a rock a man has swung back a sling, and at the edge of the water something like a dolphin is leaping out. Such a lively landscape is found almost nowhere else in the ancient art of that time. The tomb was painted around five hundred and twenty years before the Nativity of Christ, most likely by a Greek master from Ionia.

The most famous thing here is the young man diving headfirst from a rock into the sea. He is on the left wall of the second room, and from the first you can't see him, however much you crane your neck. We had to look at a photo on a phone. You stand a meter away from a fresco twenty-five centuries old and look at your phone. The twenty-first century in all its glory.

Scholars think that this dive is an image of the passage from life into death: a step off a rock into an unknown depth. Some thirty years later a similar diver would be painted at Paestum, in the south of Italy. And I was reminded of Jonah, who also went down into the deep and came out of it on the third day. The Etruscans did not know this story, but about the depths and coming out of them they seem to have had an inkling.

photos/2026-11-11/8.alt: Empty burial chamber with a flowered ceiling
photos/2026-11-11/8.description:
This room struck me with its ceiling. Both slopes are covered with a fine pattern of dark little flowers, like chintz fabric, and down the middle runs a broad red ridge beam. As if you are standing not in a stone tomb but inside a festive tent. Under the ceiling runs a band of red and blue lines, and in the triangle above the back wall two beasts with blue manes lie on either side of a red projection that holds up the beam. In the projection itself is a small face, like a mask.

And below, almost nothing. The walls are bare, light-colored, with damp stains; the painting on them has not survived, or there was hardly any. The floor is uneven, of tufa, and you can see small ledges and hollows in it by the walls. In similar tombs the legs of funeral couches were set into such sockets.

What this particular tomb is called, I can't say for sure from my notes, and I don't want to guess. We went down into it between others, and all that stayed in my memory from it is this flowered ceiling and the silence.

An empty room sometimes says more than a painted one. Nothing distracts you here, and you begin to think about the simplest things. Once a person was brought here, laid on a couch, and dishes with wine and food and lamps were set beside him. A flute played, the relatives said goodbye. Then the entrance was closed with a slab and covered with earth. And when the next one in the family died, the tomb was opened again. Almost all such tombs were sooner or later robbed, and the bones crumbled to dust. Only the walls and ceiling remained, which nobody had any use for. And it is precisely they that turned out to be the treasure.

photos/2026-11-11/9.alt: Artist's reconstruction of a funeral in an Etruscan tomb
photos/2026-11-11/9.description:
This is not a photograph, but an artist's reconstruction of that same room with the flowered ceiling from the previous shot. The same gabled ceiling with the fine pattern, the same red beam, the same bands and beasts in the triangle above the back wall. Only now it is not empty here, but as it might have been on the day of the funeral.

On a couch with a patterned cover lies the dead man, a wreath on his head, his hands folded on his chest. On the left stand women; one in a dark blue dress has pressed her hands to her face. On the right are bearded men in cloaks, quiet, with downcast eyes. On the floor are small oil lamps, a large bronze cauldron, a little table with cups, painted jugs with animals. By the right wall is a second couch, still free. It is waiting for the next member of the family.

I understand that any picture like this is a guess, not a document. How exactly people stood, what clothes they wore, how many lamps were burning, no one knows for sure. But some things are known reliably. The body was laid on a couch or on a stone bench in its best clothes; beside it were set food, wine, lamps, sometimes weapons or a mirror. A flute played, the relatives said goodbye, and sometimes a memorial meal was held right at the entrance. Then the tomb was closed, and it served the family for several generations.

This reconstruction helped me see a simple thing. An empty chamber in the tufa turns into a room where people grieve. And they grieve just as we do: they stand in silence, not knowing what to do with their hands. Our own burial service, after all, also begins with us simply standing by and praying.

photos/2026-11-11/10.alt: Artist's reconstruction: a funeral feast with dancing and musicians
photos/2026-11-11/10.description:
And one more artist's reconstruction, a noisy one this time. This is how a celebration in a painted tomb might have looked: not a quiet farewell, but a feast, music and dancing. This is not a photograph and not a wall painting, but a picture that is a guess, so it is worth looking at it as an illustration of what we had seen on the walls all day.

In the depths of the room the banqueters recline on couches, there are dishes on little tables, and along the left wall stand large vessels for wine. In the middle women are dancing: one has thrown her arms over her head, another is swirling a long veil, a third holds something like castanets in her raised hands. A serving girl bends over a table; someone in the back has flung up his arms. Wreaths hang on the walls, and by the right wall lie shields, a helmet and a chariot wheel. And in the foreground are two musicians: one in a laurel wreath plays the lyre, the other blows a long double flute. It was the double flute that we had seen in almost every tomb.

The most interesting thing is that the walls of this imaginary room are painted too: there are the same banqueters, dancers and little trees as in the real tombs. That is, the feast is reflected in its own paintings, as in a mirror.

In real life everything was probably more modest: the memorial meal, they say, was held at the entrance, not in the cramped chamber, so the picture brings a lot together. But for the Etruscans death really was connected with feasting, with wine, music and dancing in honor of Dionysus. They painted the feast on the walls so that it would never end. But Christ promised us a real feast: many shall come from the east and west, and shall sit down in the kingdom of heaven. Sit down, that is, recline at the table, almost like these Etruscans on their couches.

photos/2026-11-11/11.alt: Sarcophagus of a woman with a relief of the journey to the afterworld
photos/2026-11-11/11.description:
On the ground floor of the museum the sarcophagi stand in rows, and from each one a person looks at you. This one stayed in my memory more than the others. On the lid lies a woman, leaning on her elbow, as at a feast. A dress, a cloak on her shoulder, her hair arranged in a wave, her right hand resting freely on the edge of the couch. The lower part of the lid, where the feet were, has broken off and lies as a separate piece. The face is full, calm, a little tired. This is not an ideal beauty, but a quite specific person, as her family remembered her. Most likely the third or second century before the Nativity of Christ.

And on the chest below is a relief, and it has to be read from right to left, like a journey. On the right is the demon Charun with a hammer on his shoulder; he seems to be urging her on. Closer to the middle is a rider on a horse, probably the deceased woman herself or her soul: the Etruscans often depicted the last journey as a ride on horseback. In the center is a winged figure with a torch. This is most likely Vanth, the female demon of death, the same one who that morning in the Tomb of the Two Roofs was lighting the way for the deceased. Further left are two wrapped-up figures, a man and a woman, relatives who died earlier. And in the far left corner is a gate with crenellations at the top, like a city tower. These are the gates of Hades.

So on one stone there is the whole story. Above, the person as she was in life, at a feast. Below, the last road, from the demon with the hammer to the gates where her own people are waiting.

I stood by her for a long time. In our panikhida we pray that the Lord will give the soul rest where there is neither sickness, nor sorrow, nor sighing. The Etruscans, it seems, also hoped that someone would meet them at the gates.

photos/2026-11-11/12.alt: Black-figure amphora in the National Museum of Tarquinia
photos/2026-11-11/12.description:
A pot-bellied amphora with two handles, and people dancing across it. This is black-figure painting: figures in dark glaze on the reddish background of the clay, with details incised in a thin line. There are six dancers, and they go in pairs. The men are black, the women in patterned dresses of dark red, and their faces are light. It is by this light face, by the way, that you recognize a woman in this kind of painting. They hold hands and wrists; someone is looking back, someone has already run ahead. Around the neck of the vessel runs a band of lotuses and palmettes, like the border on an old tablecloth.

What dance this is, I won't venture to say. Perhaps a festival in honor of Dionysus, perhaps a wedding round dance. The style is very similar to Greek, Attic, of the sixth century before the Nativity of Christ, but without a label let that remain a guess.

But here is what is known for certain. The Etruscans were the best customers for Greek pottery in the whole ancient world. They loved it, collected it, set it out at feasts, and then took it with them into the tomb. That is why a great many Greek vases that stand in museums around the world today were found not in Greece but in Etruscan land. In the morning we had seen dances on the walls of the tombs, and here is the same dance on a vessel from which wine may have been poured at just such a feast.

What I like in these figures is their liveliness. Twenty-five centuries have passed, the glaze has cracked, the vessel has been glued together from pieces, and the people are still holding hands. Looking at this, you very much want someone, someday, to remember us like this too: not alone, but in a round dance.

photos/2026-11-11/13.description:
A shallow cup on a low foot, with two handles at the sides. A cup like this is called a kylix; people drank wine from it at a feast, and when it was empty, a picture appeared at the bottom. Here the picture is in a circle framed by a meander, that very Greek endless pattern. Inside are two young men wrapped in cloaks. The one on the left leans forward and rests on a long staff, holding something small in his hand. The one on the right stands facing him, his cloak slipping off his shoulder. It looks as if they are simply talking.

This is the red-figure technique: the figures are left the color of the clay, and the background around them is painted black. It is the reverse of the black-figure amphora in the neighboring case. In this manner lines can be drawn with a brush, finely and freely, so you can see the folds of the cloth, the muscles, the turns of the body. Most likely it is Greek, Attic work of the fifth century before the Nativity of Christ, but I won't give an exact date.

Around it in the case stand other cups just like it, and the glass reflects the museum hall, the light from the window and the corridor. There is a great deal of light in the Vitelleschi museum in general, and after a whole morning underground that was pleasant.

I like that the most beautiful part of the cup is visible only once you have finished drinking. The feaster raises the kylix, drains the wine and sees at the bottom two young men in conversation. A small reward. And the conversation of people in cloaks, calm and unhurried, was probably the chief adornment of a feast for the Greeks. Not the wine, but the conversation. To be honest, I agree with that.

photos/2026-11-11/14.alt: Votive offerings in a museum case
photos/2026-11-11/14.description:
This case is not about beauty at all, it is about requests. Here are votive gifts, that is, offerings made under a vow. A person would come to a sanctuary with a trouble or with a hope and leave the god a clay token of their request. The label next to one of the objects says that it is a votive knee, with an inscription, from the votive deposit at the temple of the Ara della Regina, third or second century before the Nativity of Christ. The same temple to which the Winged Horses belonged too, more about them a little further on.

On the top shelf are little clay domes that look like a woman's breast, ribbed objects, fragments of figurines. Above, on a separate label, bronze votive body parts. Below is a seated figurine, and next to it a long figurine of a swaddled baby, with only the face peeking out. On the English part of the big label you can see the words about swaddled infants. People prayed for children, for the health of the mother, for a bad leg. A person with a sore knee brought a clay knee, and for a baby, it seems, they prayed with a figurine of a swaddled child.

This was the time when Tarquinia had already come under the power of Rome, and such figurines become very numerous in the sanctuaries. They were made in series, in molds, like gingerbread, and sold at the entrance. For simple people, health and the birth of children were a condition of survival.

And this is very familiar to us. Silver hands, legs and little hearts are hung by wonderworking icons to this day in Greece, in Italy, and at home too. It is the very same human habit: to bring to a holy thing a token of one's pain. Ask, and it shall be given you. The Etruscans asked their gods. We, thank God, know Whom to ask.

photos/2026-11-11/15.alt: Corinthian perfume flasks: alabastra, aryballoi and a duck askos
photos/2026-11-11/15.description:
A whole shelf of little flasks, and each of them once smelled sweet. These are perfumes and oils of the seventh and sixth centuries before the Nativity of Christ, ware in the Corinthian style: some brought from Greek Corinth itself, some made here by Etruscan craftsmen who adopted the style.

The tall narrow little bottles, shaped like a carrot or a spindle, are called alabastra. Scented oils were kept in them. The small round pot-bellied flasks with a wide flat mouth are aryballoi, for the oil people rubbed on after the baths, or athletes before a contest. The mouth is made so that the oil flows out drop by drop straight onto the palm. There are also low bowls and a round flask with a little ring. And at the bottom right stands a vessel in the shape of a duck, an askos, also for oil. The sweetest object in the case, honestly.

Their painting is recognizable at once. On a light background, brown and red animals walk round in bands: panthers, goats, birds, and between them rosettes, so that no empty space is left. The Corinthian craftsmen seem to have been afraid of emptiness and filled everything.

The Etruscan nobility adored Greek perfumes, and Corinth was their main supplier at the time. Perfume was expensive, and a beautiful flask was a gift in itself. Such flasks were placed in tombs, especially for women, next to a mirror and a little box.

But looking at them, I remembered something else. The holy chrism with which we anoint right after baptism is also cooked from oil and many fragrances. For Christians, chrismation is not a luxury, but the seal of the gift of the Holy Spirit. People have always felt that fragrance is somehow connected with feasting and with eternity.

photos/2026-11-11/16.description:
Two alabastra in close-up, so as to make out the painting. These are those same tall flasks for scented oils from the Corinthian case. On the left, a larger one, pale and worn, covered with rosette circles that look like flowers and with almost rubbed-out patterns.
