On the right, a smaller one and better preserved: a wide flat mouth like a saucer, dark rays on the shoulders, and on the body rosettes and animals. Below, if you look closely, you can see a stretched-out animal that looks like a panther, and above it something with curled feathers, perhaps a bird. In the bottom left corner of the frame is a pot-bellied little flask with another animal.

The word “alabastron” itself comes from alabaster, the soft pale stone from which such flasks were made at first. Later the shape was repeated in clay, but the name stayed. And here, for me as a priest, the Gospel comes alive at once. A woman comes into the house of Simon the leper with an alabaster box of precious ointment, breaks it and pours it on the head of Christ. Here it is, the alabaster box. A narrow neck, easier to break than to open carefully. And she did not hold back.

These flasks were made in the seventh and sixth centuries before the Nativity of Christ, some in Corinth itself, some here in Etruria, after the Corinthian model. The oil in them dried up long ago, but the painting has remained. Clay turned out to be the most reliable material in the world: wood has rotted, cloth has decayed, metal has turned green, but fired clay holds.

The glass of the case reflects the shelves and windows of the hall, and it seems as if the flasks are standing in some dark aquarium.

photos/2026-11-11/17.description:
A little clay house in which a person lies. This is a hut urn, ninth or eighth century before the Nativity of Christ, the time of the so-called Villanovan culture, when the Etruscans were only just becoming Etruscans. According to the label, it was found in the Arcatelle necropolis during excavations in eighteen eighty-two.

Look at the shape. It is an exact model of the hut people lived in at that time: round, with a roof of straw or reeds. The ribs on the roof are the rafters, and on the ridge stick up ornaments that look like birds or horns. Real huts had such wooden ridges with figures too. In front is a square window-door, which was once closed with a separate board. And inside, dark remains are still visible. These are the ashes and burnt bones of a warrior. With him were placed a bronze razor, a fibula clasp, a spearhead and even a tiny bronze table for offerings, as if for a memorial meal.

In the morning, in the meadow of the necropolis, we saw stone “mushrooms” in the grass. These are tufa cases into which such urns were lowered and buried in the ground. And here we saw what lay inside.

It seems to me that this is the most ancient and most touching thought of the Etruscans about death: a person needs a home. First a little clay hut with ashes, two hundred years later rooms cut into the rock with gabled ceilings and painted doors, later still stone sarcophagi shaped like couches. But it all began with this little house. Christ also speaks of a house: “In my Father's house are many mansions.” Only that house is not made of clay.

photos/2026-11-11/18.description:
They were worth climbing the stairs to the top floor for. The Winged Horses of Tarquinia hang on a dark blue wall, lit so that the clay seems warm, almost golden. Two horses stand side by side, one slightly ahead of the other, necks arched, ears pricked. On their muzzles you can see the harness, the straps and bits. Behind the nearer one is a large wing, and each feather is modeled separately. The tail is tied up, like that of harness horses, which means they once drew a chariot, and in it stood a god or a hero. The chariot has not survived.

This is a high relief in terracotta, fired clay, of the fourth or third century before the Nativity of Christ. It adorned the largest known Etruscan temple, the Ara della Regina, on the Civita plateau, where the ancient city stood. It hung high up, on the pediment, and people looked at it from below. Do you see the dark little holes in the background? Through them the relief was nailed to the temple's wooden beam. It was found by the archaeologist Pietro Romanelli in nineteen thirty-eight, as a heap of hundreds of fragments, and the horses were put together like a jigsaw puzzle.

Next to the horses you can see thin steel cables stretched along the wall. In the photo they look like the lines a draftsman uses to check perspective. It turned out almost symbolic: ancient flight, and around it modern mechanics holding it up.

The horses have become the symbol of Tarquinia. What I like most about them is not their beauty but their direction. After a whole day underground, this is the first thing that looks upward. The Etruscans, it seems, also hoped that one day the chariot would take off.

photos/2026-11-11/19.description:
At the end of the Etruscan halls a completely different world suddenly stands. A white marble group on a black pedestal, between a red wall and a dark gray one: a young man has dropped with his knee onto the back of a huge bull, pressed it to the ground and pulled its head up by the muzzle. The young man's head has been broken off, and the right hand, which held a knife, is missing too. But the short cloak billowing behind his back and the pose are recognizable at once. This is Mithras slaying the bull. Roman work of the second or third century after the Nativity of Christ, found here in Tarquinia, and one of the finest such sculptures in Italy.

This scene has its own canon. A dog is supposed to leap up from the bull's wound, a snake crawls towards the wound, and a scorpion grips the bull from below. From the blood and body of the bull, according to this myth, life is born, ears of grain and grapes. Look closely at the marble by the neck and under the belly: there really are small details there worth examining without hurrying.

Who is Mithras? A god who came from the East, from Persia. In the Roman Empire his cult was very popular among soldiers and officials. He was worshipped in secret, in underground cave temples, where only initiated men were admitted. There were initiations by degrees, and a common meal with bread and a cup. That is why in the first centuries this cult was the main rival of Christianity, and St Justin the Philosopher wrote about it with alarm.

The resemblance is outward, but the difference is enormous. Mithras saves by killing another's victim. Christ saves by giving Himself. Here blood is shed by the hero's knife, while with us the Lamb Himself goes to the slaughter. That is what I was thinking about as I walked around the pedestal.

photos/2026-11-11/20.alt: Fresco of the Mother of God with the Child
photos/2026-11-11/20.description:
Of everything we saw in Tarquinia, this fresco was the closest to my heart. The Mother of God sits on a marble throne that looks like a little temple with columns and latticed sides. She wears a dark blue, almost black maphorion, under it a red dress, and a golden halo with a tooled pattern. On Her knees is the Child in a red shirt, with fair curls, also with a halo, and in His hand something dark and round. In Italian painting the Child was often given a goldfinch to hold, a sign of the future Passion, or a pomegranate, a sign of the resurrection. What it is here, I never worked out. And at the top right, from behind the edge, an angel peeks out.

The fresco was taken off the wall of some church in Tarquinia and moved to the museum. Most likely the end of the fourteenth or the fifteenth century. It is behind glass, so there is a glare in the photo and a band of light at the top, but the faces can be seen well. The face of the Mother of God is very quiet, slightly inclined, and She looks not at us but somewhere past us, as if lost in thought.

Under the throne are two lines in Latin. This is an old couplet that was written under images of the Mother of God all over Italy: “When you come to the image of the most pure Virgin, as you pass by, do not forget to say: Hail.” Below are a few more lines, but they can no longer be read.

I really like that the fresco itself addresses the passer-by. It does not ask for money, does not demand a bow, it simply reminds you to say hello. You just want to answer it out loud. After a whole day of tombs, demons and closed doors, saying “Hail, thou that art highly favoured, the Lord is with thee” was like stepping out into the light.

photos/2026-11-11/21.alt: Image of the Apostle Paul in a display case
photos/2026-11-11/21.description:
A narrow panel in a tall glass case, and behind it a window in the thick wall of the palace. On a gold background, under a pointed arch, stands the Apostle Paul. He is easy to recognize: a high balding forehead, a long dark beard, a gray chiton with a white belt, and over it a red cloak. In one hand a sword, in the other a scroll. The sword is the instrument of his martyrdom. Paul was a Roman citizen, so he was not crucified but beheaded with the sword, there in Rome. And the scroll is his epistles, which we read at every Liturgy. Around his head is a crown-halo, its pattern pressed into the gold.

This is tempera on panel, roughly fifteenth century. Most likely a wing of a large altarpiece, where different saints stood on the sides and the Mother of God was in the center. The other parts have probably scattered around the world or been lost, and Paul stands alone.

In the photo a white band has fallen across the apostle's face, a glare from the window on the glass. Fighting it is useless, the window always wins. Let it stay, it is an honest sign that we stood here ourselves and did not download the picture from the internet.

Paul, in fact, unexpectedly accompanied us the whole of this day. In the neighboring halls Etruscan runners and athletes awaited us on the walls of tombs, and Paul loved to compare the Christian's life to a race: “I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith.” The Etruscans ran for an earthly crown. Paul ran for a heavenly one. To me, as a priest, this image is especially dear: the course is finished not only at the finish line, but every day.

photos/2026-11-11/22.alt: Fresco “Christ among the Doctors” in Palazzo Vitelleschi, Tarquinia
photos/2026-11-11/22.description:
This is already the end of the day, the top floor of Palazzo Vitelleschi, where medieval Tarquinia begins after the Etruscans. Under a brick vault, above a doorway, across the whole wall, is a fresco: the boy Jesus among the doctors in the Temple in Jerusalem. The second chapter of the Gospel of Luke, a story that any priest reads with a special feeling.

The artist built the Temple as a Gothic church of his own time. Twisted columns, pointed arches, galleries above, and in the center a semicircular apse with a shell. In the middle, on a high golden throne with steps, sits the Boy, an open book in His hand; with the other hand He explains. Around Him on benches are gray-bearded teachers of the law: one argues, one peers into a scroll, one raises his hands in amazement. The Gospel says just that: all that heard Him were astonished at His understanding and answers.

Now look at the left edge. There a woman in a dark veil with a halo and an elderly man are coming in. These are the Mother of God and Joseph, who searched for the Boy all over Jerusalem for three days. Any parent who has ever lost a child in a crowd will recognize these faces. In a moment She will say: “Son, why hast thou thus dealt with us?” And He will answer that He must be in His Father's house. These are the first words of Christ recorded in the Gospel.

The fresco was painted straight onto the wall of the palace, most likely in the fifteenth century, when it was new, under its builder, Cardinal Giovanni Vitelleschi. We had spent the whole day in the houses of the dead, Etruscan and Roman. And here, at the end, the Son sits in His Father's house. For me this was a very fitting final point.

photos/2026-11-11/23.alt: Runners from the Tomb of the Olympic Games, Tarquinia museum
photos/2026-11-11/23.description:
Three men are running, and they are twenty-five centuries old. This is the painting from the Tomb of the Olympic Games, which was taken off the walls in the necropolis and reassembled in the museum, in a room of the same shape, with the same gabled ceiling. It was found by the engineer Lerici with his underground periscope shortly before the Rome Olympics of nineteen sixty, hence the name. It was painted around five hundred and twenty before the Nativity of Christ.

Look at the runners. The first on the left is bearded, arms flung up. In the middle is a beardless young man with a loincloth, running and pumping his arms wide. The third, also bearded, has stretched his arm forward, as if already reaching for the finish. And on the right, at the edge, one more figure can be seen, which seems to be jumping. The bodies lean forward, arms moving opposite to the legs, everything in motion. The artist clearly had seen a real race and knew how a person runs. Above them are bands, red and blue-green, like a cornice, and below the remains of another colorful band. Where the paint has fallen off, the light base shows through.

To save the painting, they used the method of “strappo,” “tearing off.” Cloth was glued to the wall, allowed to dry, and the thin layer of paint was removed together with it, then transferred to a new base. It sounds like surgery, and it is surgery.

They ran in honor of the deceased: funeral games were held, as in Homer, when Achilles held them at the funeral of Patroclus. And of course I immediately remembered the Apostle Paul, whom we had just seen on the icon: “I have finished my course, I have kept the faith: henceforth there is laid up for me a crown of righteousness.” Life as a race, and at the end a crown. Only our finish line is different.

photos/2026-11-11/24.alt: Tomb of the Ship: banquet on the back wall, Tarquinia museum
photos/2026-11-11/24.description:
Another tomb moved to the museum in its entirety, together with the shape of the room and the ceiling. A glass railing stands over it, so you look from above, as if from a balcony. Judging by the painting and by what I heard on the spot, this is most likely the Tomb of the Ship, mid-fifth century before the Nativity of Christ. It too was found by Lerici with his periscope, in the late fifties.

On the back wall is a banquet. On couches covered with patterned coverlets recline men and women. The women are easy to recognize by their pale skin; the men's is red-brown. Between the couches stands a naked young servant, and under the couches are low footstools. Above the banquet, in the triangle, you can see something dark red and a round disc that looks like a wheel or a shield. The ceiling, as always, is a checkerboard, now badly flaked. And on the left wall are servants at a table with large amphorae, as if this were a sideboard from which wine is carried to the banqueters. There are dark dots in the wall, perhaps traces of nails.

The tomb got its name from another wall, where a merchant sailing ship is painted. It did not make it into this shot. Tarquinia lived by the sea, its port received ships from all over the Mediterranean, and perhaps the owner was a merchant or a shipowner. Or perhaps the ship here means the last voyage.

For us, too, a ship is a very Christian image. The Church is a ship that carries us across the sea of life to a quiet haven. So say both the holy fathers and our prayers. And the banquet on the back wall reminds us where this ship is sailing.

photos/2026-11-11/25.alt: The whole Tomb of the Triclinium
photos/2026-11-11/25.description:
Here it is in full, the Tomb of the Triclinium, photographed from above, from a glass walkway. This is one of the most famous paintings in Tarquinia. Around four hundred and seventy before the Nativity of Christ, found in eighteen thirty, and back then all of Europe started talking about it. Later, to save the colors from damp and air, the painting was taken off the walls and reassembled here, in the museum, in a room of the same shape.

The ceiling is a checkerboard, red and light, and on the ridge a pattern of little branches. On the back wall a banquet: the banqueters recline on couches, with little tables under the couches. The name “triclinium” is about exactly this. That was the name for a dining room with three banqueting couches. And on the side walls a dance. On the left a man in a billowing cloak and a dancing woman, on the right a flute player with a double flute. Between them are slender little trees, and birds sit on the branches. It seems that the feast is taking place not in a cramped chamber, but in a grove, under the open sky.

You stand above, and below you is a whole world lit by warm light. There was something to compare it with: in the morning we had gone down into real tombs, dark, with a button and glass. Here everything is visible at once, in its entirety, from ceiling to floor, and it is a completely different impression. As if the roof had been taken off a house and you were watching how people live in it.

While still at the necropolis, in the Tomb of Bettini, we had heard that that tomb and this one were possibly painted by the same workshop. Similar dancers, a similar light hand. I liked the thought that in the morning we had seen the work of the same people where it remained, and in the evening here, where it was saved.

photos/2026-11-11/26.alt: Dancer and musician, Tomb of the Triclinium
photos/2026-11-11/26.description:
The flute player and the dancer, closer up. The flute player strides along, a double flute to his lips, wearing a light pale cloak thrown over his shoulder. On the right, behind a little tree, is a dancer in a patterned dark cloak, seemingly with a raised arm, but his figure is badly damaged. Between them is a slender little tree, and under it something red hanging in an arc, like a ribbon or a band. Birds in the branches. To the left of the flute player is a large area where the paint has almost all gone, leaving only the shadows of figures.

The double flute, in Greek the aulos, was the main instrument of an Etruscan feast. Ancient Greek authors wrote that the Etruscans did everything to the flute: they feasted, kneaded dough, boxed and even punished slaves. Perhaps that is an exaggeration, but in Tarquinia there really is a flute player in almost every tomb. That day we must have seen about a dozen of them, and each time I caught myself wanting to hear how it sounded.

Look at how the flute player walks. He is not standing still but actually walking, stepping along, as if the music itself were leading him forward. His face is calm and focused, like that of a person who is doing his job and not being distracted by the dancers. As someone who has listened to the choir from the ambo for many years, I understand this focus very well.

This painting was taken off the wall of a tomb in the necropolis and moved to the museum, because underground it was perishing from the damp. The layer of paint is very thin. You can see how it lies unevenly in places, with cracks, but the figures hold. Twenty-five centuries later, the flute player is still playing, only you cannot hear the sound.

photos/2026-11-11/27.alt: Fragment of the painting in the Tomb of the Triclinium
photos/2026-11-11/27.description:
Almost the same piece of wall as in the previous photo, only closer and from a different angle. I wanted to look not so much at the figures as at the surface itself. The flute player with the double flute in a pale cloak, a little tree with a bird, a red ribbon hanging in an arc, and on the right the dancer in a dark patterned cloak. And on the left the edge of the wall, where the painting has almost completely vanished: pale patches, brownish shadows, scraps of outlines remain. Below, a few red stripes.

It is in places like this that you best understand what exactly was saved. A painting is a thin layer of paint on plaster. In the tomb, underground, it lived for centuries in damp and darkness, and when the tombs were opened and people started going in, with light and breath, the paint began to crumble. So in the last century the restorers dared a bold operation. Cloth was glued to the wall, allowed to dry, and the layer of paint was removed together with it, then transferred to a new base. In Italian this is called “strappo,” that is, “tearing off.” Then in the museum the room was assembled anew, with the same shape and the same ceiling.

Where the paint was lost, no one painted it in. The empty places, it seems, were simply left empty, in a neutral color. I like this honesty. They could have made up the rest, and it would have been prettier. But then it would no longer be an Etruscan artist, but our contemporary.

In our church restoration of icons there is the same debate: whether to paint in the losses or not. And in my opinion the right answer is the same: better to see less, but the genuine thing.

photos/2026-11-11/28.alt: Female profile, detail of an Etruscan painting in the Tarquinia museum
photos/2026-11-11/28.description:
A face in close-up. A female profile: a straight nose, a half-closed eye, hair gathered up high in a hairstyle with a dark ribbon, an earring in her ear, a thin necklace on her neck. Her shoulders are covered with dark red cloth. The skin is not painted in; it is the same light color as the wall, and the outline is drawn with a single thin line. That is how the Etruscans painted women, pale, unlike the tanned red-brown men. On the hair are a few white spots where the paint has fallen off, and on the wall to the left a dark dot, like the trace of a nail.

Which of the moved tombs this fragment is from, I cannot say for certain, and I won't guess. Perhaps she is one of the banqueters, perhaps a dancer. There are several such tombs in the Vitelleschi museum, and I went from one to another, photographing details.

I wanted to photograph her alone, without the banquet and without the dance. When you stand before a whole wall, you see a scene, a feast, a composition. But when you come up to a single face, you suddenly see a person. She is perhaps twenty years old. She is a little tired or lost in thought. The artist who painted her twenty-five centuries ago saw how she turned her head and caught that movement in a few lines.

We do not know her name, we do not know who she was to the owner of the tomb, a wife, a daughter, or no one at all, just an image. But here she is, looking aside, as if listening to the flute. But with God no one is nameless. Next to faces like this, that thought always makes me feel calmer.

photos/2026-11-11/29.alt: Evening over the rooftops of Tuscania
photos/2026-11-11/29.description:
Twilight in Tuscania. Yana took this shot. The sky is already blue and lilac, the clouds are lit pink from below, and the lamp on the corner of the house has come on with a warm orange light, turning the whole wall the color of an orange. The old house is overgrown with ivy and some climbing greenery almost to the roof; by the wall are flowerpots, green shutters, a wooden stand for plants. In front of the house is a paved square, and someone is walking across it. And beyond the low tiled roofs the town rises: houses, a bell tower with a small dome, another tower, antennas. On the right is a red “no entry” sign, which at this hour was guarding only the silence.

We had spent the whole of this day with the Etruscans. We went down into tombs, and their tombs are built like houses: a gabled ceiling, a ridge beam, painted doors, couches for a feast. A city of the dead built in the image of the city of the living. And in the evening we found ourselves among real houses, where lamps are lit, where behind the shutters people are probably having supper and where someone waters the flowers in the pots.

The Etruscans, judging by their paintings, very much wanted life not to end, and painted it on the walls of tombs as best they could. The feast, music, birds, the sea. All day we had been looking at this hope, touching and a little helpless.

But with us, at this hour, at sunset, the evening hymn “O Gladsome Light” is sung in churches: “Having come to the setting of the sun, and beholding the evening light, we praise the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit.” Christians sang it as early as the first centuries, by the same light of lamps. A light that does not go out together with the sun. It seems to me that this is the answer to what the Etruscans so diligently painted on the walls of their tombs.

photos/2026-11-12/1.alt: The loggia of the Papal Palace in Viterbo
photos/2026-11-12/1.description:
This is the Loggia of the Benedictions on the cathedral hill. From here the thirteenth-century popes came out to the people who gathered in the square below. Seven pointed arches stand on slender paired columns, and above them is stone lace of interlaced arcs and trefoils. Higher up runs a band of coats of arms: the striped shields of the Gatti family, who ruled the city at the time, the lion of Viterbo, an eagle, the papal keys. It is raining in the shot; you can see it in the light streaks against the dark stone.

The loggia was built in twelve sixty-seven, under Pope Clement the Fourth. Back then it was double-sided, with a matching arcade opposite, making an open hall between the sky and the city. The second side collapsed in the fourteenth century. One wall of arches remained, and through it you can see the houses on the other side of the valley. To my mind, it is even better this way. In the middle stands a fifteenth-century fountain assembled from old stones, and below is a huge arch on which the whole loggia rests.

I like that the thing is so light and the stone so heavy. All of Viterbo is built of peperino, a gray volcanic tuff. It is dark, porous, almost black after rain, and there would seem to be no reason to carve lace out of it. And yet they did. On the right is a cypress, taller than the palace. Below, by the steps, is a young olive tree, very slender. Next to stone that is seven hundred and sixty years old, it looks like a child brought to visit a very old relative.

photos/2026-11-12/2.alt: Gothic altarpiece in the Viterbo cathedral museum
photos/2026-11-12/2.description:
A Gothic polyptych, that is, an altarpiece made up of many panels. I didn't photograph the label, so I can't name the master, but the period can be guessed: the end of the fourteenth or the beginning of the fifteenth century, when in central Italy they painted in tempera on gold. It is made like a small cathedral. Sharp spires, arches, slender columns along the edges, all carved from wood and covered in gold leaf. Images like this were set on the altar, at the back of it.

In the middle is the Mother of God enthroned, in a dark mantle over a red dress. The Child stands on Her knees and gives a blessing. Her face is still very much an icon face: an elongated oval, almond-shaped eyes. On the left are the Apostle Peter, gray-haired, with the keys, and John the Forerunner, thin, barefoot, in a camel skin, with a scroll. On the right is a young saint with a book, most likely John the Theologian, whom the West painted as a youth, and the Apostle Paul with a sword. In the spires at the top are small medallions, and on the side pillars smaller saints stand one above another.

I looked and thought that this is really our Deesis. The Mother of God, the Forerunner, the apostles, the prophets above them. Only with us the tiers stand in the iconostasis in rows, one above the other, while here everything is gathered into one golden frame. The altarpiece hangs in a hall of the papal palace, among huge dark Baroque canvases, and next to them it seems like a guest from another time. Above it a marble plaque is set into the wall. As far as I could make out the Latin, it commemorates a bishop who restored the papal halls in the early twentieth century.

photos/2026-11-12/3.alt: Ancient stone sarcophagus in a courtyard
photos/2026-11-12/3.description:
In the museum courtyard, under a canopy, among the autumn leaves, lies a long stone trough. It is hewn from a single piece of gray tuff, roughly, without any decoration. The whole surface is covered in small pits from the chisel: the stonemason worked his way across the stone blow by blow. At the far end the sides are higher, and a step is cut inside. And in the bottom, closer to the middle, is a round hole going right through, and red maple leaves have fallen into it.

There was no label nearby, so I have two theories. The first and most likely: it is a stone coffin, late antique or medieval. The step then turns out to be a headrest, a stone pillow under the dead person's head, and the hole in the bottom was made so that moisture could drain away. Simple coffins like this are found near old churches all over Italy; later they are dug up and set in museum courtyards. The second theory is a practical one: part of a press for grapes or olives, where the juice ran out through the hole. But the headrest still argues for a coffin.

If it is a coffin, it was no prince who lay in it. In these same parts the Etruscans carved out whole houses for their noble dead, with beams on the ceiling, and painted banquets on the walls. Here a person was laid in a hollowed-out stone beside the cathedral, head on a stone step, and that was all. The next day in Cerveteri I saw exactly the same stone boxes, only more than a thousand years older. The poor have been buried the same way in every age.

photos/2026-11-12/4.alt: Virgin and Child on a gold ground
photos/2026-11-12/4.description:
A small panel on a gold ground, under glass. The Mother of God has bowed Her head and looks down, past the Child, with that quiet, sorrowful face the Sienese masters loved so much. She wears a dark blue mantle with a green lining and a gold star on the shoulder. The Child sits on Her arm, chubby, rosy-cheeked, in a lilac shirt with a gold border, and looks off to one side. The museum's descriptions attribute this panel to the fifteenth-century Sienese school and give the name Benvenuto di Giovanni. I didn't photograph the label, so I can't vouch for the name.

The most interesting things here are the small details. Around the Child's neck and wrists are red coral beads. In Italy coral was hung on children as an amulet against the evil eye and illness, and painters put it on Christ just as mothers put it on their sons. And in His left hand is a little bird, a goldfinch. According to an old legend, the goldfinch pulled a thorn out of the Savior's crown of thorns, and a drop of blood fell on its head, which is why the goldfinch has a red spot. So both the bird and the red beads speak of the same thing: the Passion, which is still thirty-three years away for this child.

The Mother already knows it. That is why She does not smile. Our iconographers would have said the same thing differently, more austerely, without rosy cheeks and without beads. But the meaning is the same, and before this panel, as before an icon, you want to stand in silence. The gold of the background has cracked into a fine web, the frame has charred or crumbled at the edges, but the faces are intact.

photos/2026-11-12/5.alt: Reliquary in a museum display case
photos/2026-11-12/5.description:
In a glass case stands a wooden casket with a lid like a pagoda roof, and its front is glass too. Inside, on a cushion trimmed with gold braid, lies a large bone, tied around the middle with a cord bearing a seal. Below it is a paper strip with a handwritten inscription: Os S. Laurentii Levitae et Martyris. The bone of St Lawrence, Levite and Martyr. In the Latin West a deacon was called a Levite. The cord with the seal means that a bishop once attested to the authenticity of the relics. The museum label states drily: reliquary casket of St Lawrence, unknown master, eighteenth century.

The Viterbo cathedral is dedicated to him, San Lorenzo, so this is the hill's chief holy treasure. Lawrence was archdeacon of the Roman Church under Pope Sixtus the Second and suffered in two hundred and fifty-eight, under the Emperor Valerian. When he was ordered to hand over the Church's treasures, he brought to the prefect the poor and the crippled whom the community fed and said: here are the treasures of the Church. For this he was burned on an iron gridiron. We venerate him too; we keep the memory of the Archdeacon Lawrence in August.

I always have mixed feelings about relics in a museum case. On the one hand, they belong in a church, under the altar or in a shrine, so that people can come and kiss them. On the other hand, here they are, behind two panes of glass, and you can come very close, closer than in some cathedrals. I crossed myself and stood for a while. When will I ever be this close again.

photos/2026-11-12/6.alt: “The Crucifixion” with the Virgin and saints
photos/2026-11-12/6.description:
“The Crucifixion”, painted in oil on a panel. Three crosses against a blue sky and a distant city with domes and arches. Christ is in the middle, on a tall cross with the I.N.R.I. tablet, head bowed, a pink cloth about His loins. On either side are the two thieves, and they do not hang as He does: their bodies are twisted, their arms wrenched back over the crossbeams, both as if straining to tear themselves off the crosses. Below on the left is the Mother of God in a blue mantle, hands clasped tight. At the foot Mary Magdalene embraces the cross. On the right is the Apostle John in red, palms crossed on his breast. The city in the background is supposed to be Jerusalem, but it is painted as Rome, with a round temple and a triumphal arch.

In the Colle del Duomo museum this is one of the main paintings. It is described as the work of Michelangelo's circle, and at one time it was attributed to him himself. It seems to be based on his drawings: the powerful, athletic bodies of the thieves are thoroughly Michelangelesque. He himself, in the last years of his life, drew the Crucifixion many times for his friend Vittoria Colonna, who, by the way, lived for long periods in Viterbo, in a convent.

After the Etruscans we had seen the day before, the contrast is striking. There death was arranged like a move to a new house, with dishes and cushions. Here death is shown as it is, with ropes and dislocated joints. And yet it is here, not there, that there is real hope, because the One in the middle will rise again in three days. The painting was photographed through glass, so there are light streaks across it.

photos/2026-11-12/7.description:
“The Dead Christ”, oil on canvas, eighteen seventy-six. According to the label, the painting first hung in the Viterbo church of Santa Maria della Pace, and then a local family gave it to the cathedral. The artist's signature and the date are in the lower left corner. After the gold and haloes of the neighboring rooms, it stops you at once. Here there is simply a body. Christ lies on a stone slab covered with a white shroud. The eyes are closed, the mouth slightly open, the right arm has fallen from the edge and hangs down. Wounds on the hand, on the feet, under the ribs. The background is dark, as in a tomb.

Below, on the floor, lies the removed crown of thorns. On the right, by the feet, is an earthenware jar, most likely with spices: the myrrh and aloes that Nicodemus brought. The body has not yet been anointed, the tomb not yet closed. This is Great Saturday, the quietest moment of the Passion. The artist surely knew Holbein's painting, before which Dostoevsky stood shaken in Basel. In “The Idiot” it is said of it that such a painting could make some people lose their faith. Here is the same boldness; death is not hidden.

But I looked at it in my own way. This is our epitaphios. We carry it out on Great Friday, lay it in the middle of the church, and the whole parish comes up and kisses it. The same slab, the same shroud. I embroider epitaphioi myself, so I spent a long time studying how the Italian laid the folds, how the cloth falls from the edge of the slab. “Weep not for Me, O Mother, beholding Me in the tomb.” He lies there, but this is not the end, and the jar of spices will not be needed in the morning.

photos/2026-11-12/8.description:
I got stuck in front of this case for a long time, because this is my own work, only done two or three hundred years ago. A red vestment of Roman cut, a chasuble. Our phelonion is wide, bell-shaped, but in the West by the seventeenth century it had been cut away at the sides so as not to hamper the arms, and the result was a stiff “fiddleback” made of two shields, front and back. What hangs here is the back. Catholics wear red at Pentecost, during Holy Week and on the feasts of martyrs.

The embroidery covers everything. Golden acanthus scrolls run across the scarlet satin, and on them sit flowers embroidered in silver: carnations, tulips, something like wild roses. The gold is couched: the metal thread is not pulled through the fabric but laid on top and sewn down with tiny silk stitches, otherwise the thread would break and the fabric would pucker. The silver has darkened, but once it was white and blazed against the red. Down the middle runs a vertical column edged with braid, and at the bottom is a coat of arms with tassels on either side, so it was most likely made for a bishop. All of this was done by hand, by candlelight, and a single vestment like this took a whole workshop months of work.

I worked out in my head how long it would take on our machine. Not long. Then I worked out whether it would come out the same. It wouldn't. A hand lays the thread slightly unevenly, and that makes the gold play. Even embroidery shines uniformly, while this shimmers. There is something to learn here. The glass says the case was donated to the museum by a local bank.

photos/2026-11-12/9.alt: Marble bust against a tuff wall
photos/2026-11-12/9.description:
This is Artemis of Ephesus, or rather a Roman marble copy of the famous statue from her temple in Ephesus. She looks nothing like the usual Greek Artemis, the swift huntress with a bow. The face is stern, with blank eyes, and there is a veil on her head. On her chest is a broad breastplate with tiny figures, and below it a garland and a necklace of acorns. And lower down, in several rows, hang the oblong clusters that make her so memorable. People used to think these were the many breasts of a nurturing goddess. Now scholars argue: some see in them offerings from sacrificed bulls, others gourds or pendants. Small lions sit on her arms.

The temple of this Artemis in Ephesus was one of the seven wonders of the world. And there is a whole chapter about her in the Acts of the Apostles. The Apostle Paul preached in Ephesus for two years, and people stopped buying the goddess's silver shrines. Then the silversmith Demetrius, who made his living from them, gathered the craftsmen and stirred up the whole city. The crowd packed into the theater and for two hours shouted: “Great is Diana of the Ephesians!” And most of them, as Luke notes, did not even know why they had come together.

I stood in front of her and thought: here she is, the very one. Not this statue, of course, but both Paul and Demetrius saw this face and these clusters. Later the temple was destroyed, the wonder of the world was taken apart for stone, and a copy ended up in the papal city, in the cathedral museum. She stands on a block of tuff by the wall, and nobody shouts in front of her. So Paul, it turns out, won that argument.

photos/2026-11-12/10.alt: Remains of a fresco with saints
photos/2026-11-12/10.description:
An old fresco, photographed in semi-darkness and, it seems, through glass, hence the glare. The lower half has almost perished, the paint has flaked off in black patches, but the upper part can be made out. On the left, under an arch, stands a gray-haired bearded bishop in a miter, with a halo, holding a chalice. Before him is a woman with long loose hair, also with a halo; she is receiving Communion. Above on the right an angel can be seen. The background looks like a brick wall, red with white joints, and the same stripes run above the scene. Judging by the haloes and the style, it was painted in the fourteenth or fifteenth century.

I can't say for certain what the subject is. The first thing I thought of myself was St Mary of Egypt, who was given Communion in the desert by the elder Zosimas before her death. But Zosimas was a simple hieromonk, and here we have a bishop in a miter. In the West there is a very similar story about Mary Magdalene. According to Latin tradition, she lived for thirty years as a hermit in a cave in Provence, angels lifted her up to heaven every day, and before her death she was given Communion by Bishop Maximinus. A bishop, long hair, an angel nearby: most likely it is her.

The Orthodox tradition about the Magdalene is different: for us she preaches in Rome and dies in Ephesus. But the scene itself is clear without any captions, both to us and to them. A person has walked toward God all their life, and now, at the very end, they are offered the Chalice. Nothing else on this wall has survived; time has erased everything except the Communion.

photos/2026-11-12/11.description:
Viterbo after the rain. The paving of small dark stones gleams so that the walls are reflected in it. On the left is a long orange palace with a gateway in a rusticated stone surround, bars on the ground-floor windows and a marble plaque by the entrance. The plaster at the bottom has got damp and is peeling. On the right are old trees, still completely yellow even though it is mid-November, and their leaves fly onto the pavement and stick. Under the trees stand folded umbrellas and stacked café tables: in weather like this nobody sits outside. The marble plaque probably says who lived or stayed in this house. In the rain we didn't stop to read it.

It rained all day, sometimes harder, sometimes lighter, and it was about seventeen degrees. For November that is warm, but for walking it is inconvenient. But a rainy city has its own merit. First, it is empty. Second, the colors become richer: orange gets more orange, yellow yellower, and the gray peperino that everything here is built of darkens almost to black and begins to shine.

Viterbo is an underrated city in general. Tourists go to Orvieto and Civita, but rarely look in here, even though there is a whole medieval quarter, a papal palace and hot springs outside the city gates that Dante himself wrote about. We walked along this street with no particular aim. Just walked and looked. At moments like that I usually don't take pictures, but this time I got my phone out: that wet pavement under the yellow trees was just too lovely.

photos/2026-11-12/12.description:
A staircase cut right into the rock, photographed from below. Not a single added stone, not a brick: the steps, walls and vault here are all one piece; it was all once solid tuff, and just enough was taken out of it for a person to pass. The steps are worn in the middle and have turned green from the damp. On the left an LED strip runs along the wall, in the middle there are iron handrails, and on the right a thick rope is stretched in place of a banister. Up above, a niche shows black in the wall.

Tuff is the main building material here for absolutely everything. It is volcanic ash pressed into stone. It was left by the volcanoes that once stood where Lake Bolsena and Lake Vico are now: the lakes are their flooded craters. Tuff is soft: while it is damp you can cut it almost with a knife, and in the air it hardens. That is why on this land, for three thousand years in a row, people have not so much built upward as dug downward. The Etruscans carved tombs and entire roads out of tuff. The Romans cut drains and cisterns. Medieval townspeople made cellars, presses, secret passages and wells under their houses. Under every old town of Tuscia there is a second town, an underground one.

On steps like these you go slowly and hold on to the rope, because the stone is slippery. A good rehearsal for tomorrow: tomorrow is Cerveteri, and there stairs just like these lead into every other tomb.

photos/2026-11-12/13.alt: A bottle of Chianti at dinner in Tuscania
photos/2026-11-12/13.description:
Dinner in Tuscania, at the same place we went to on the first evening. That time we had Morellino and Grechetto, and this time we asked for Chianti. They brought this bottle: Chianti D.O.C.G. from twenty twenty-four, “Buccia Nera”, the Campriano estate. Buccia nera means “black skin”, as they say of a dark grape. On the neck is a paper strip with the letters DOCG and a number; this is a state seal: every bottle of top-category wine in Italy is numbered. On the table is a wooden block with the number two, our table number, and a fork wrapped in a napkin.

Now look at the beast on the green band of the label. A lion with bared jaws, something sticking up from its back, its tail curled. It looks very much like the Chimera of Arezzo, the most famous Etruscan bronze. The real Chimera has a goat's head on its back, and its tail ends in a snake. It was found in Arezzo in the sixteenth century, when the city walls were being built, and Duke Cosimo de' Medici took it for himself to Florence. The winery is from near Arezzo, so it took it as its emblem.

It turned out funny. The day before yesterday we spent the whole day walking around Etruscan tombs in Tarquinia, the next day we were heading to the Etruscan burial mounds in Cerveteri, and in between we sat down to dinner and the Etruscans turned up even on the bottle. We are, by the way, still not in Tuscany; Tuscania is in Lazio. But the wine is Tuscan, and it was good.
